these_are_not_claims: A finding is a note about work in progress. It carries no derivation status and must not be cited as a result. The register holds the claims: bundle.json.

findings.title: 93 is not stable across its own calibration gap, and the operator was right to distrust it
findings.text:
The orbit count was challenged on instinct: *93 is not a balanced number, and for
something with an infinite degree-space that usually means data has been lost.*
The challenge was worth more than the defence, so it got swept.

**First, the input space is symmetric and the challenge does not land there.**

```
  5 binary operators x 36 (all 6x6 ordered pairs)   180
  reflect_pair x 6   (all marks)                      6
  close x 5          (all marks EXCEPT Point)         5
                                                    191
```

One asymmetry, and it is forced rather than chosen: **a Point has nothing to
close.** So the 191 constructions have exactly the dimensional symmetry the
challenge expected, and 93 is the size of a QUOTIENT of that space — quotients are
not obliged to factor, because merging depends on geometry rather than on the
symmetry of the inputs.

**Then the sweep, and the challenge lands here instead.** `TOL_SAME` is calibrated
against a measured gap: known-same pairs top out at **0.0684**, known-different
pairs bottom out at **0.0779**, so any threshold in between classifies every
calibration pair correctly.

```
  TOL_SAME   orbits
    0.0600     95     below the gap
    0.0684     93     gap, lower edge
    0.0730     93     SHIPPED
    0.0779     89     gap, UPPER EDGE
    0.0900     84     above the gap
```

**Four orbits move inside the interval the calibration calls safe.** Both
endpoints of that gap are equally defensible by the calibration, and they disagree
by 93 against 89.

**What the calibration actually proved, and what it did not.** It proved the
threshold separates the pairs whose answer was known in advance. It did not prove
it separates every pair in the space — and there are real pairs among the 191
whose distance falls between 0.073 and 0.0779, so whether they merge is decided by
where in the safe zone the constant happens to sit. That is METHODS #15 exactly:
a forced choice among known candidates tolerates a weak metric; this is not that.

**The fix is the one F101 already demonstrated: fix the SEARCH, not the number.**
At 18 rotation steps no threshold separated same from different at all; going to
36 opened the gap. The same measurement records that **72 steps narrows
known-same from 0.0684 to 0.0657**, widening the gap without moving anything
already right. If the count is stable across the wider gap, 93 is earned. If it
still moves, the discriminator is not sharp enough to support an exact count and
the honest published figure is a range.

**Until that is run the honest statement is `89-95`, not 93** — and every place
this corpus prints an exact orbit count inherits that.

**The process fault this exposes is not the tolerance.** It is that the number was
reported in the same flat voice as `6 marks`, which is provable and cannot move.
This project's entire invariant is that an assertion carries its derivation
status, and the reporting layer had no statuses at all. A count that is the output
of an instrument must carry the instrument's tolerance wherever it is quoted.

**The fix was run, and it did not work.** F101's move — fix the search, not the
number — was the right instinct and it has now been tested. Doubling the rotation
search to 72 steps widens the calibration gap (known-same falls 0.0684 → 0.0657)
and **leaves the count just as unstable**:

```
  TOL_SAME    36 steps   72 steps
    0.0657        —         94
    0.0684       93         —
    0.0700        —         93
    0.0730       93        93     <- shipped
    0.0779       89        89
```

So this is not an under-resolved search. **The discriminator cannot support an
exact orbit count at any resolution tried**, because there are real pairs among
the 191 whose separation genuinely falls inside the licensed interval — they are
neither clearly the same figure nor clearly different, and no threshold in the
gap decides them without deciding arbitrarily.

Recorded as `the-orbit-count-is-tolerance-bounded` (**measured**), and
`thesaurus-size-depends-on-mirroring` now carries the bound in its scope so the 93
cannot be cited as exact.

**One consequence worth stating against the corpus's own rule.** `same_figure`
declares its safe direction: *err low, because a false split leaves two names for
one shape while a false merge asserts a synonymy that does not exist.* Applied
honestly at 72 steps that points at the low edge of the gap — **94, not 93.** The
shipped value sits in the comfortable middle rather than on the side the rule
names. That is not a bug, but it is a choice that had never been stated as one.

findings.title: a result that was live, computed and uncitable, and the seven pages that could not be written until it had a status
findings.text:
Publishing the underclaim backlog reached 7 findings asking pages to state:

> *aspect / 30 degrees equals the Hamming distance in the six-bit code, verified
> over all 66 pairs.*

**No such claim was in the derivation register.** The nearest is
`hamming-gives-rotation-class`, which is a different result about marks. So the
detector was asking seven live pages to assert something the register could not
license, and the bridge refused: a block carries a STATUS at the assertion, and
there was no status to carry.

**The result itself was never in doubt.** `research/codes/symbol_geometry.py`
computes it over all 66 pairs and returns True; 35 tests pass; it has been on the
live wiki since September on its own page, *The Sovereign Hexagram Code*. What
was missing was not evidence. It was **standing** — an entry in the file that
governs how a thing may be cited.

That is a gap worth naming on its own: **a verified result, already published,
with no entry in the register that decides how it may be asserted.** The register
is meant to be the authority on what may be claimed, and a second store had grown
results it never saw.

**Registering it forced the status question, and the answer is not `measured`.**
Reading the construction: months 1–6 grow yang from the bottom (`100000`,
`110000`, … `111111`) and months 7–12 grow yin. Consecutive words differ in
exactly one bit, so the twelve are a **Gray cycle** on 12 of the 64 six-bit words,
and the isometry over all 66 pairs is then a finite computation rather than a
sample.

But the sign↔hexagram identification is **read off an artifact** — the
ZodiacSignSymbols card's Chinese column — not derived. So the honest status is
**`derived_given`**, on exactly the shape `element-bit-assignment` already uses:
a complete derivation resting on a premise the corpus supplies rather than proves.
A different assignment of hexagrams to signs would not generally have this
property, which is what makes the artifact's ordering load-bearing.

**And the premise then had to travel.** The first version of the pointer block
dropped it — and a `derived_given` claim's licence reads *"assert only together
with its stated premise."* A pre-existing test caught it:
`test_derived_given_claims_appear_with_their_premise`. Without that catch, seven
live pages would have carried the strongest kind of overclaim this register
exists to prevent: a conditional result asserted without its condition.

Two other things the publishing pass corrected in the tooling, both the same
shape — **a check that encoded an assumption nobody had stated**:

- the bridge's licence text says *"the derivation is attached"*, which is true on
  a canonical page and **false on a page that merely links to one**. The pointer
  blocks keep the imperative half and name where the derivation is.
- a test required every runnable check to match `python3 tools/…`. F167's check
  is a test module. The requirement was always *runnable*, never *in one
  directory*.

**48 pages now carry the derived layer, verified live one at a time.** The one
that matters most is not an addition: `Base 12` had told the wiki since 11
September that `element-bit-assignment` was `undetermined`, six days after F148
moved it to `derived_given`. **A live page was understating a claim, and the
thing that found it was trying to publish something else.**

**Two design faults in the publishing pass itself, both caught by tests rather
than by review.**

*The canonical block won outright.* Where a page was both canonical and flagged,
the generator kept the canonical block and **silently discarded** the pointer
bullets that page also needed. Ten findings stayed open on exactly the pages that
are supposed to be authoritative — the Angle page carried its own symmetry group
and still never said which marks are rotation-invariant. Merging fixed it.

*The target list was driven by OPEN findings.* So a page dropped out of the
generator the moment its finding closed — and a later change to a claim's status
would never reach it again. **That is precisely the fault this pass was published
to correct**, rebuilt as a mechanism: `Base 12` asserted `undetermined` for six
days after F148 because nothing regenerated it, and the fix as first written
guaranteed the same thing would happen to all 48 pages. A finding is what SENDS
you to a page; it is not what keeps you coming back. Targets are now recovered
from the blocks already on disk, so re-running rewrites every page the bridge has
ever written.

**And the detector was asking for a phrasing the register does not use.** It
demanded `rotation-invariant` while `rotation-invariance` states the result as
*"unchanged under rotation"* — so a page quoting the canonical claim **verbatim**
still failed the check that asked for it. Two records of one result, disagreeing,
for the third time this session (F150, F152, here). 54 pages were already correct
and the number would not move until the pattern accepted the register's own words.

Final: **underclaim 64 → 0**, measured against a rebuilt export, with all 56 live
pages verified one at a time through the MediaWiki API.

---

findings.title: my own change made a broken test pass, and chasing that found the skill teaching a withdrawn claim
findings.text:
Verifying that this session introduced no regressions, one result looked like good
news: `test_ul_skill.py::test_undetermined_count_is_current` **failed** at the
session's starting commit and **passes** now. I had not touched the skill. That
is the wrong shape for good news, so I looked.

```python
n = sum(1 for c in reg.values() if c["status"] == "undetermined")
self.assertIn(f"{n} claims, each with a success condition", self.text)
```

The skill said **"12 claims, each with a success condition."** The register held
**1** undetermined at the start of the day and **2** at the end.

- looking for `"1 claims, each…"` in `"12 claims, each…"` — **not** a substring.
- looking for `"2 claims, each…"` in `"12 claims, each…"` — **it is.**

So opening a second undetermined claim made the assertion start passing against a
document that was still wrong by a factor of six. **`assertIn` on a bare number
cannot tell a correct count from a stale one that happens to end in it.** The test
even carries a docstring explaining that it deliberately reads the number from the
register rather than pinning a literal — the intent was right and the comparison
was not.

**And the skill was worse than merely out of date.** `SKILL.md` is what an agent
reads *first*. Under **"What is not settled"** it listed:

> **`up-is-shared-across-canvases`** — …

with a full paragraph of live reasoning. **That claim is WITHDRAWN.** It was
retracted because the statement was false and `orientation-is-a-canvas-parameter`
already said so, and it was replaced by `direction-is-read-as-contrast`
(**derived**). The skill was presenting a retraction as an open question, which is
the precise failure the derivation register exists to prevent, on the one page
most likely to be read without the register beside it.

Also stale: **"91 of 95 orbits are unnamed"** against a measured 89 of 93 — a
count that three defects had already corrected once (F101, F105).

**Fixed, and the fixes are of three different kinds:**

- **the document** — 12 → 2 claims; 91 of 95 → 89 of 93 orbits; and the
  withdrawn bullet rewritten to say that up/down is settled in *both*
  directions, naming the derived claim that replaced it and saying plainly not
  to cite the retracted id.
- **the comparison** — `assertRegex` with a word boundary, in both count tests,
  because `89 of 93` is a substring of `189 of 93` exactly as `2` was of `12`.
- **the gap nothing covered** — a new test asserting that no withdrawn claim is
  named anywhere in the skill without the word WITHDRAWN within 300 characters
  of it. That is the check that was missing entirely; the counts had a test and
  the retraction had none.

A fourth thing fell out: the skill pointed readers at
`build/codex/find/orbits.svg`, which does not exist. The real file is
`charts/orbit-map.svg`. That one *did* have a test — `test_every_path_it_points_at_exists`
— and it had simply been failing.

**The lesson is not about skills.** It is that **a test can start passing for a
reason unrelated to the thing it tests**, and the only signal was that it changed
state when nothing it covers had changed. When verifying that a session broke
nothing, the tests that newly PASS deserve the same suspicion as the ones that
newly fail.

---

findings.title: I suspected the detector twice in one day; it was 88% right once and entirely right the second time
findings.text:
`unchecked-artifact` had been reporting four files at medium for some time:
`discrepancy_register.json`, `build_plan.json`, `i18n_baseline.json`,
`lexicon.json` — *"read by N tools but no test, so a change to it cannot fail
anything."*

**The reason to doubt it was real.** All four are **generated**, and the
detector's own docstring says it targets *"hand-maintained KNOWLEDGE
registries"*. It is scoped by directory, not by provenance, so it cannot tell the
two apart. That is the same shape as F160, where an entry's trigger did not match
its stated intent.

**So I tried to build the missing signal, and the control killed it.** A heuristic
for *generated* — does a tool that names this artifact also write JSON near the
mention? — came back **anti-correlated with the truth**:

```
  discrepancy_register.json    said hand-maintained   corpus_audit writes it
  rederivability_key.json      said generated         I wrote it by hand
  derivation_register.json     said generated         hand-maintained
```

Three of the four cases I could check were wrong, and two were exactly inverted.
Proximity to a write call carries no information here. The heuristic looked
entirely reasonable and would have shipped without the control.

**Then the plain question settled it.** Exact-match search: **none of the four is
named in any test.** The `lexicon` hits in `tests/` are `lexicon_level` and an
unrelated sense of the word. The detector was right.

**And being generated was never a defence.** A generator bug in a knowledge file
is exactly as uncontradictable as a typo in a hand-written one — the file still
asserts things, and nothing still checks them. The detector's finding was
correctly worded all along; my objection was to a word in its docstring.

**Closed by writing the tests, with the cross-file check being the one worth
having:**

> `lexicon.json`'s six composition relations must be exactly the six that
> `two-marks-stand-in-exactly-six-ways` derives — *apart, abutting, crossing,
> overlapping, contained, fused.* Two files, one fact, and that is the shape that
> drifted at F150 and again at F152.

Plus: the lexicon's entry count must equal its own `counts` field (40); the build
plan's `totals.charts` must equal `len(items)` (129); no finding may name a
detector the register does not list; and the ratchet must still hold **five**
numbers, with A and D at zero — the two a regression would be least visible in,
because both are already clean.

Thirteen assertions, five of them negative controls. `unchecked-artifact` is
**0**, and every file in the knowledge directories now has something that can
contradict it.

**The pattern across today, stated once.** Twice I distrusted a detector before
measuring it, and both times measuring was cheap and the answer was not the one I
expected — 88% precision with a single fixable entry at F160, and fully correct
here. **A detector that has been reporting the same thing for weeks is evidence,
not noise; the cost of checking is an hour and the cost of assuming is whatever
it was reporting.**

---

findings.title: the census took six cells from a nine-cell table, and the three it left were the elements
findings.text:
Classifying the `polarity` axis at F163 meant reading the table it belongs to, and
the table is not what the census recorded. F139 gives it as:

```
        In       Contract     Rise
        Flatten    LIFE       Warp
        Out       Expand      Fall
```

**Four inverse pairs through a fixed centre**, and the census has **six of the
nine** — Contract/Expand on Point/Circle, Flatten/Warp on Line/Wave, Rise/Fall on
Angle/Curve, which are three of the thirty-two cells F156 counted. It does not
have `In`, `Out` or `Life`.

I started to file that as an open question: *this corpus has three mark pairs and
this panel draws four oppositions, so either In/Out attaches to a pair nobody has
identified, or the opposition structure is wider than the pairing.* That would
have been a reasonable thing to write down. **It was also unnecessary, because
F139 had already demonstrated the method for settling it — measure the ink, not
the labels — and the drawing was sitting in the corpus.**

**Measured off the panel at (808, 1664, 430, 384):**

| cell | apex | full-width interior rows | ink | bbox |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rise | **UP** | 4 — the base edge only | 3095 | 93×79 |
| Fall | **DOWN** | 3 | 3093 | 93×79 |
| Out | **UP** | **21 — a crossbar** | 4018 | 93×79 |
| In | **DOWN** | **20** | 4018 | 93×79 |

In and Out are **identical in ink and bounding box to each other**; so are Rise and
Fall. The first column carries **923 px more ink at exactly the same size**, in a
band of twenty full-width rows across the middle. That is a bar.

**They are the four classical element symbols.**

```
  Rise   △    up,   unbarred     FIRE
  Fall   ▽    down, unbarred     WATER
  Out    △̶    up,   barred       AIR
  In     ▽̶    down, barred       EARTH
```

which is `element-bit-assignment` exactly: *up+unbarred is Fire, up+barred is Air,
down+unbarred is Water, down+barred is Earth.*

**So In/Out is not a fourth mark pair. It is the same direction opposition as
Rise/Fall with the crossbar bit set** — one axis read at both settings of another.
The panel crosses the element square with the other two mark pairs and puts `Life`
at the centre:

```
  column 1  ·  direction at BARRED      Earth / Air
  column 3  ·  direction at UNBARRED    Fire / Water
  column 2  ·  Point / Circle
  middle row·  Line / Wave
  centre    ·  Life
```

`the-pair-is-the-unit-of-assignment` is untouched, and now for a reason rather
than by luck.

**And this hands a long-open question its first piece of evidence.** The crossbar
bit of `element-bit-assignment` has been open on exactly one point: *what property
groups a gas with a solid against a plasma with a liquid?* Nothing in the physics
obliged Air and Earth to share a bit. **This panel shows what the corpus takes the
bit to mean:** the barred pair is glossed **In / Out** and the unbarred pair
**Rise / Fall** — boundary against movement, crossing against travelling. That is
not a derivation and it does not close the question. It is the first thing on
record that says what the distinction is *for*, and it came from a panel nobody
had read.

**Why the three cells stay out of the census, now for a principled reason.**
`concept_census.json` is keyed by the six marks. The three cells it left are the
three that are **not marks**: In and Out are barred composites, and `Life` is the
teardrop — the Angle+Curve fusion — which is also the term the ledger carries with
two referents and no primary (F162). The census stopped exactly where its key
stopped. That was right, and it was invisible until the panel was measured.

**Twice short on one sheet.** F139 found the census had missed five whole tables
here. This finds that one of those five was then entered two-thirds of the way.
**The sheet keeps being read for the cells that fit the schema already in hand** —
and the three that did not fit were the elements, which the corpus has a whole
separate claim about.

---

findings.title: two tests had been failing all along, and the wrong one was hiding a real gap
findings.text:
Running the suite after this session's work turned up two failures. Before
touching anything I checked whether they were mine: `axis_census.json` and
`tests/test_corpus_audit.py` are **byte-identical to HEAD**, and the offending
`given` fields are identical too. Both predate everything here.

**The first was a real gap, and it was the exact gap the test exists for.**

> *"Would have caught `decan-slot`, which sat in a table while belonging to no
> kind, and made the analysis crash mid-run."*

Two axes were used in tables and classified under no kind: `bar-position-on-a-triangle`
and `polarity`. The corpus answers both in its own notes —
`bar-position-on-a-triangle` is recorded as *"a third instance of position_linear
on one sheet"*, and `stem-position`, the same axis on a stem, is already
`transformation`; `polarity` indexes *which way an operation runs*, as
`orientation` indexes which way a mark faces. Both are `transformation`. Nothing
is unclassified now.

**And that second axis is worth a second look.** The table it belongs to is the
cheat sheet's 3×3, noted as *"four inverse pairs around a centre — In/Out,
Contract/Expand, Rise/Fall, Flatten/Warp."* Those are census cells: `market`,
`transformation` on Point/Circle, `transformation` on Angle/Curve, and
`transformation` on Line/Wave. **The sheet lays the opposition structure out as a
figure — pairs arranged around a centre — not merely as a word list**, which is
F156's claim stated by the corpus in its own layout rather than recovered from it.
(One of the four, Flatten/Warp, is also one of F158's three tautologies, so the
sheet is partly naming its own geometry there.)

**The second failure was a test asserting a schema the register has never had.**
It required every `derived_given` claim's `given` to be a claim id. But
`derived_given` means *a derivation resting on a premise that is not derived*, and
most such premises have no claim behind them — *"that ink is modelled as a SET of
covered points"* is a modelling assumption, not a register entry. **Seventeen of
twenty-four givens are prose.** The test could never have passed.

**A test that cannot pass is not merely noise — it hides whatever else is wrong in
what it covers.** Fixing it found that:

`corpus_audit`'s own `register-consistency` detector — built at F150/F152
precisely to catch a conditional resting on a withdrawn premise — **skips prose
givens entirely**:

```python
if not g or " " in g:
    continue          # prose premise, not a claim id
```

So F150's fault would have been invisible the moment anyone wrote the premise as
a sentence instead of an identifier. **Three givens are exactly that shape**,
naming five claims between them — `direction-is-read-as-contrast`,
`updown-is-meaningful`, `element-bit-assignment`, `hamming-gives-rotation-class`,
`connectivity-is-constituency`. All five happen to be live. Nothing was checking.

Both now assert the stricter thing: **a given that names a claim — as an id, or
inside a sentence — must name one that exists and is not withdrawn.** Prose that
names nothing stays legal, because it is legitimate.

And because a clean run from a check that has never been seen to fire is not a
result, the test carries a **planted positive**: a fabricated register where a
prose given names a withdrawn claim, asserted to be caught, beside a real prose
premise asserted to stay clean.

The order matters here. The failing test was wrong about the schema; the detector
was right about the schema and wrong about its coverage. **Had the test been
merely deleted as noise — which is what a test that fails every run invites — the
detector's hole would still be open.**

---

findings.title: three findings marked `high` with a fix that would have destroyed the exam
findings.text:
The last unexamined backlog item was *"3 high term-collisions (Life, Amperage,
Voltage) awaiting an owner call."* They are marked `severity: high`,
`disposition: needs-owner`, and each carries the instruction:

> *Decide which sense is primary and record it, or split the term.*

**Two of those three are sealed defects in the rederivability exam.**
`rederivability_key.json` asks an outside reader to catch five
independently-confirmed errors, and `amperage-voltage` and `life-two-referents`
are two of them. A reader who never notices that the Line and the Wave swap
Amperage between two sheets has failed to detect a real fault — that is the
entire measurement.

So the highest-severity item in the backlog, with a clear actionable fix, would
have **deleted 40 per cent of the exam's detection targets**, and nothing in
either file mentioned the other. The term ledger did not know it was holding
evidence. The exam key did not know its evidence sat in a queue someone would
eventually want to clear.

**This is F150 and F152 a third time** — a fact kept in two places with no link
between them — with one difference that makes it worse: here the drift would be
caused by *doing the tidy thing*. The previous two needed someone to be careless.
This one needed someone to be diligent.

**What the corpus already gets right, and it is worth saying.** `Yin`, `Yang`,
`Aether` and `Nether` are the other two defects, and each has a primary recorded
**while the wrong reading is kept on file beside it**. That is exactly the right
shape: the owner's decision is recorded, and the error a reader is meant to catch
is still visible. Recording a primary was never the danger. **Deleting a sense
is.**

So the invariant is narrow and is now enforced in two places:

- `tests/test_exam_defects_are_preserved.py` — for each sealed defect, both
  conflicting senses must survive in the ledger. Resolving is allowed; deleting
  fails, with a message naming the defect that would be lost. A fourth test
  asserts this file has not drifted from the key it guards, which is the same
  failure one level up, and pins `enharmonic` as the only sealed defect with no
  term-ledger footprint.
- `corpus_audit`'s term-collision detector now appends the warning **to the
  finding itself**, because that is where an owner reads. `Life` now says
  *"BUT FIRST: this term is the evidence for exam defect `life-two-referents`…
  the exam cannot be re-set."*

A guard in a test protects the file. A sentence on the finding protects the
person. This needed both, and the reason it needed both is that the instruction
was not wrong — it was correct advice given without one fact.

---

findings.title: the same map, asked of the quotient, gives a different answer; and the first answer I got was fragments
findings.text:
F159 established σ as a fixed-point-free involution on the 191 figures. The
tempting next step is obvious: **orbits are equivalence classes of figures, so σ
should pair up orbits, so naming one orbit names its dual — and the 5-of-98 gap
moves.** That inference is wrong twice over, and the second wrongness was mine.

**The first answer was garbage, and the tell was in the output.** I harvested each
orbit's `constructions` field and split it on commas. But
`superpose_concentric(Point,Circle)` *contains a comma*, so it split into
`superpose_concentric(Point` and `Circle)`. The analysis returned a confident
negative — *σ is ill-defined on 84 of 92 orbits* — computed entirely on fragments.

What caught it was not a test. It was reading the output: **`Line)` appeared as a
construction of twenty different orbits.** A well-formed corpus does not have a
construction named `Line)`, and it does not have one construction in twenty
orbits. I had nearly recorded the negative result before looking.

**With a depth-zero split, the 93 orbits carry exactly the 191 constructions of
`combination_space.json`, with no construction in two orbits** — which is itself
the consistency check the first version failed.

**The real answer, which is neither the tempting inference nor my fragment
version:**

```
  93 orbits over 191 constructions
  well-defined (every construction's image lands in ONE orbit)   77
  ill-defined                                                    16
  and σ(σ(o)) = o holds for only                                 45
      9 orbits are their OWN dual     4, 7, 22, 30, 37, 40, 47, 53, 73
     18 genuine dual pairs            covering 36 orbits
```

**σ is clean on figures and partial on orbits, and the mechanism is exactly the
quotient.** A figure can never be its own σ-image — relabelling always changes the
name — so on figures there are **zero** fixed points. An orbit *can* hold both a
figure and its image, so on orbits there are **nine**. Orbit 22 is the clearest:
it is **Sun-in-Circle**, and a Point inside a Circle and a Circle inside a Point
are, concentrically, the same picture. The Sun symbol is its own curvature-dual.

**What this opens for the semantic half, and how narrow it must stay.** Of the
four named orbits, **three have a well-defined dual that is unnamed**:

```
  orbit 13   infinity (SymbolFolds)    dual = orbit 1    UNNAMED
  orbit 39   Chaos pair (F44)          dual = orbit 74   UNNAMED
  orbit 91   + (SymbolFolds)           dual = orbit 92   UNNAMED
  orbit 22   Sun-in-Circle (F43)       is its own dual
```

A dual is a **stronger lead than proximity** — it is structural rather than metric,
and it does not depend on a distance threshold the way
`two-unnamed-orbits-sit-beside-named-ones` does. **And it is still not a reading.**
It says *which* orbit is the curvature-dual of a named one. It says nothing about
what that orbit means. `concept_census` refuses to guess a meaning from proximity;
this refuses to guess one from duality, on the same ground and for the same
reason — the whole value of the 5-of-98 number is that it is honest.

Recorded as `sigma-does-not-survive-the-quotient`, **measured**, and the three
duals are written down as leads so that whoever does name them can start from a
structural fact rather than a hunch.

---

findings.title: the biggest backlog was not a backlog, and my reason for suspecting it was wrong
findings.text:
"73 underclaim findings on wiki pages" had been carried as the largest untouched
item for some time. Two things turned out to be true about it, and they pull in
opposite directions.

**It was never 73 defects.** The detector says so in its own scope field:

> *A keyword test over published pages of some length. It flags a candidate for
> enrichment, never an error — a page may have good reason not to carry the
> result.*

with `disposition="needs-owner"` on every finding. So the correct count of *bugs*
in that backlog is zero. It is a suggestion list, and it was already labelled one.

**My reason for distrusting it was wrong, and measuring beat suspecting.** Seeing
73 findings from a single detector, I expected the checker to be at fault — this
corpus has that failure on record. So I measured precision instead of assuming
it: for each flagged page, does the page discuss the subject at all?

```
  sign grammar        22 on-topic    0 off    gates on zodiac, modality, cardinal, mutable
  aspect is hamming    7 on-topic    0 off    gates on sextile, trine, conjunction
  rotation class      35 on-topic    9 off    gates on Point, Circle, Line, Wave, Angle, Curve
  TOTAL               64             9        88% precision floor
```

**88%, and every false positive came from one entry.** Two of the three entries
gate on real topic vocabulary and are exactly right. The third gates on **the six
mark names** — which is the notation's own alphabet, listed by nearly every page
in a mark-based corpus. So `Alpha`, `Omega`, `Order`, `Chaos`,
`Masculine_and_Feminine`, `Universal_Physics`, `Universal_Symbols`,
`Universal_Syntax` and `Cognitive_Functions_in_Universal_Symbology` were each told
to state a result about rotation, on pages that never mention rotation.

**The general shape.** *An entry whose topic terms are the vocabulary the whole
corpus is written in has no topic test at all.* The other two entries were safe
because astrology words are not universal in this corpus and mark names are.

Fixed with a **gate** on that one entry — the page must also match
`rotat|symmetr|invarian|orientation` — and the two working entries left untouched,
which is the discipline: fix what the check names, do not sweep. **73 → 64, zero
new, and the nine that went are the nine I predicted before changing anything.**

**A small thing worth noticing.** Five of the nine are `Alpha`, `Omega`, `Order`,
`Chaos` and `Masculine_and_Feminine`. Those are opposition pages, and F156 is why
they list the marks: Alpha/Omega is the Angle/Curve pair and Order/Chaos is
Line/Wave. They name marks *in pairs* because that is what the corpus assigns
meaning to. The detector read a pair as a list.

**What is left, stated plainly.** 64 genuine enrichment candidates, each naming a
verified result a live wiki page could carry and does not. That is real and worth
doing — and it is **64 edits to a live wiki**, which is an owner's call about
outward-facing published pages, not something to batch-push off the back of a
keyword sweep. The detector already says `needs-owner`. It is right.

---

findings.title: the pairing extends to every composite, and the one place it fails names what is wrong with `concatenate`
findings.text:
F156 found that meaning attaches to mark pairs. That defines a map nobody had
ever applied to the **composites**:

```
  σ :  Point ↔ Circle,   Line ↔ Wave,   Angle ↔ Curve
```

each pair being **one rotation class and two curvature classes** — a fact read off
`combination_space.json`'s own `curvature` field, not asserted here.

**σ is a fixed-point-free involution on the figure space.** 191 figures, every one
with a distinct partner, none its own, and **190 of 191 partners are themselves
figures in the space.** The single exception is `close(Circle)`, whose partner
would be `close(Point)` — and a Point has nothing to close.

**σ preserves rotation class on 180 of 190, and all ten failures are
`concatenate`.** Which looks like a clean law: *a composite's rotation class
depends only on its arguments' rotation classes.*

**That reading is wrong, and the test that shows it is the one worth keeping.**
σ swaps every mark *at once*. Swap **one** argument instead and rotation class
breaks **44 times across three operators**:

```
  superpose_concentric   72/72
  superpose_displaced    56/72    breaks
  cross                  64/72    breaks
  concatenate            52/72    breaks
  nest                   72/72
```

The gap between 10 and 44 is the whole finding. σ preserves something a single
swap destroys: **the equality pattern of the arguments.** σ(A) = σ(B) exactly when
A = B. And `superpose_displaced(Point,Point)` is C2 while
`superpose_displaced(Circle,Point)` is C1 — two copies of one mark are symmetric,
two different marks are not.

So the law is not what it first looked like:

> **rotation( op(A, B) )  is a function of  ( op, rot(A), rot(B), A == B )**

**63 of 66 signature classes.** Control: drop the `A == B` term and it falls to
**44 of 51** — the term is load-bearing, not decoration. Second control: pair the
marks *across* rotation classes instead of within, and the preservation rate
collapses, so σ's score is about the curvature pairing and not about pairing in
general.

**Every one of the three residues is `concatenate`, and every one is Point against
Circle.**

```
  concatenate(∞, ∞, same)    → {2, ∞}    Point,Point = ∞   but Circle,Circle = 2
  concatenate(∞, 2, differ)  → {1, 2}    Point,Line = 2    but Circle,Line = 1
  concatenate(2, ∞, differ)  → {1, 2}    Line,Point = 2    but Line,Circle = 1
```

Angle and Curve are interchangeable for rotation class under **every** attested
operator, without exception anywhere in the space. Line and Wave likewise. Point
and Circle are interchangeable everywhere **except under `concatenate`**.

**So there is exactly one place in this entire figure space where curvature — as
opposed to symmetry — changes an outcome: concatenation involving a Point.** And
`concatenate` is precisely the operator whose name was withdrawn
(`concatenate-does-not-concatenate`). Concatenation joins end to end. A Point has
no ends. This is the measurement that says *what* is odd about that operator
rather than merely that something is — and it arrived from the semantic side of
the project, by taking a fact about which words the sheets pair up and asking what
it does to the geometry.

Recorded as `rotation-follows-class-and-equality`, **measured**, scoped to
rotation class only: σ inverts curvature by construction, and nothing here says
the two members of a pair are interchangeable for anything else.

---

findings.title: each pair opposes in its own way, and three of the cells are the geometry talking to itself
findings.text:
F156 established that meaning attaches to mark PAIRS. The obvious next question
is whether the three pairs oppose along the *same* axis — whether there is one
polarity running through the whole vocabulary. There is not, and what is there
instead is more interesting.

**First, verify the split rather than assume it.** I had been calling Point, Line
and Angle the "straight" side by eye. The corpus says so itself:
`combination_space.json` gives every figure a `curvature`, and read off the base
marks it is **singular** = Point, Line, Angle and **smooth** = Circle, Wave,
Curve. The split I was using is the corpus's own class, not my impression of it.

**Three cells cannot be used, and two of them sit on the sensitive pair.**

```
  Line/Wave    transformation   Flatten, Straighten  /  Warp, Fold
  Angle/Curve  curvature        Sharp                /  Smooth
  Angle/Curve  morphology       Edge, Caret          /  Arc, Breve
```

Each is the word *straight* against the word *curved*, dressed in a domain. They
are the premise, not evidence for it, and any count of "32 of 32 cells are
polarised in the same direction" counts that premise three times. The evidence
base is **29**.

`vertex-acts` escapes this by one cell — its seven cited domains are Alpha/Omega,
Act/Pass, Set/Get, Init/Hold, Spark/Drain, Ebb-Push/Flow-Pull and Aether/Nether,
and none is a tautology. But two of the three tautologies are on Angle/Curve, the
very pair it is about. The trap was adjacent.

**Then, the real structure.** Sorting the 29 by *which* opposition each carries:

| pair | rot | dominant opposition | on-theme | off | taut |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Point / Circle | ∞ | **AMOUNT** — discrete/extended ×4, less/more ×2, presence/absence ×1 | 7 | 2 | 0 |
| Line / Wave | 2 | **CONSTANCY** — fixed/varying ×7, actual/potential ×1 | 8 | 1 | 1 |
| Angle / Curve | 1 | **AGENCY** — source/sink ×4, active/passive ×3, first/last ×1 | 8 | 3 | 2 |

**Seven of the nine opposition kinds occur in exactly one pair and nowhere else.**
`fixed/varying` is the whole of Line/Wave — Constant/Variable, Peace/Change,
DC/AC, Fixed/Mixed, Stable/Fluid, Order/Chaos, Level/Frequency, seven different
domains all saying *constant against varying* — and it never appears on another
pair. `active/passive`, `up/down`, `first/last`, `less/more`, `presence/absence`,
`actual/potential` are each confined to one pair too. Only `discrete/extended`
and `source/sink` cross, twice each.

**And the kind tracks the rotation class**, which is the part worth testing:

```
  rotation ∞   no distinguished direction at all   →  can only oppose by AMOUNT
  rotation 2   two-fold                            →  opposes by whether it REPEATS
  rotation 1   fully directed                      →  opposes by AGENCY
```

**Why this is filed undetermined and not measured.** The word pairs are attested
and the clustering is in the corpus rather than in my labels — the corpus put
seven constancy words on Line/Wave without my help. But **the labels are mine.**
`fixed/varying` is my reading of Fixed/Mixed; `active/passive` is my reading of
Act/Pass. A reader who grouped them differently would get a different table, and
the author cannot mark his own reading. That is the same defect the rederivability
exam exists for, arriving in a new place.

**So it is written as an exam, not a result.** The success condition:

> An independent reader, given the 32 cells as bare word pairs **with the pair
> labels removed**, assigns each an opposition kind. If their grouping reproduces
> the three-way split and seven of nine kinds again fall in one pair each, the
> clustering is in the corpus. If their kinds cut across the pairs, it was in my
> labelling.

The 32 cells and every one of my calls are in this finding, so that comparison
costs the reader nothing but the reading.

**What it would be worth.** `vertex-acts` asks for a principled reason why, of
the two rotation-class-1 marks, the singular-curvature one takes the source role.
If this holds it supplies **half** of that: rotation class would predict *which
opposition a pair can carry at all* — ∞ has no direction to spend, so it can only
count; 1 is fully directed, so it can act. It would still not say which member
takes which pole, because both members of a pair share a rotation class. The
claim itself says so. **Halving an open problem is worth recording; pretending to
close it is not.**

Recorded as `three-cells-restate-the-geometry` (**measured**) and
`opposition-kind-tracks-rotation-class` (**undetermined**, with that success
condition). The undetermined count goes 1 → 2, deliberately: the second one is a
real question with a cheap, stated test, which is the only kind worth opening.

---

findings.title: the ratchet counts strings nobody can read, and cannot see a string 26 of 27 readers can
findings.text:
METHODS §18 was written half an hour before this, about a borrowed probe list:
*what can this instrument not express, and would the corpus look the same either
way?* The first thing I pointed it at was not the probe. It was the i18n ratchet.

**What the ratchet counts.** Among its numbers is *stamped strings that resolve
in NO language* — currently 198, and almost all of it is correct: operator calls,
`slice-binary-*` identifiers, font filenames, bare language codes. Notation has
nothing to translate and the number is a floor, not a debt.

**What it cannot count.** A string that resolves in SOME languages. It is not in
the "no language" bucket and it is not in the "all languages" bucket, so it moves
no number the ratchet reports, in either direction, for as long as it exists.

**Two were sitting there.**

```
  [ 6/27]  "What is claimed, and on what licence"
  [ 5/27]  "a status is a licence to cite"
```

Both stamped on real pages. Both translated into the Latin-script languages only
— de, es, fr, id, pt, and ru for one of them. So a reader in Japanese, Amharic,
Hebrew, Church Slavonic or Classical Chinese got English on a page where every
sentence around it was in their own language, and a reader in Portuguese did not.

The ratchet was green throughout. It is still green. **Nothing was broken; the
instrument had no way to say it.**

**How it was found, which is the transferable part.** Not by looking for it. I
was tracing an unrelated number — 474 template digests untranslated per language
— and rather than counting it, read it. Most of the 474 turned out to be
machinery that is never stamped on a page at all. Intersecting *untranslated*
with *actually stamped* cut 474 to 200; asking of those 200 how many languages
have each cut it to **2**. The two real defects were only visible after two
narrowing steps, and the first draft of that number — 474 — would have been
reported as a large backlog that mostly does not exist.

**Fixed, and then made unable to hide.** Both strings now resolve in 27 of 27;
the merge tool refused none of the 43 new translations, its script check clean on
every one. And the invariant is now a test: **a stamped digest is translated into
all of them or none of them.** None is the notation floor. All is a finished
string. Partial means a job was started and left, and until now nothing in this
repo could say so.

That is two instrument blind spots in one session, found by the same question.
F156: a probe list cannot report a relation between its own primes. F157: a
ratchet built to catch *nothing translated* cannot catch *not everything
translated*. **Both instruments were working. Both were silent for the same
reason — the fault was of a kind the instrument had no category for**, and that
is exactly what a green run looks like from outside.

---

findings.title: the 65-question probe missed the most systematic fact in the corpus, because its source has no word for it
findings.text:
F155 asked whether anything outside SPACE composes. The answer was sitting in the
census the whole time, and the instrument could not see it.

**What I noticed while reading the census dump.** Every domain that names one
mark names another, and the two words are opposed:

```
  one / many        Entry / Exit        Dark / Lite       Less / More
  Init / Cycle      Input / Output      Contract / Expand
  DC / AC           Fixed / Mixed       Order / Chaos     Reality / Destiny
  Set / Get         Act / Pass          Alpha / Omega     Rise / Fall
  Peak / Base       High / Low          Sharp / Smooth    Spark / Drain
  Push / Pull       Ebb / Flow          Aether / Nether   Cardinal / Mutable
```

**The deflationary reading, and why it fails.** If the sheets were complete grids
— every mark glossed in every domain — then "both sides filled" would be true by
construction and worth nothing. So I checked F134's own table, written long
before the census existed. It is **sparse**: Point and Circle have `—` under
electrical, Line and Wave have `—` under temporal. The grid has real holes.

Measured over all 97 cited attestations:

```
  64 of 114  (mark, domain) cells carry a word        56% — SPARSE
  32 of 57   (domain, pair) slots are occupied
  32 of 32   of those are TWO-SIDED
   0         one-sided
```

**The null model, because a perfect score needs one as much as a zero does.**
Scatter the same 64 cells at random over the same grid: **28.3 one-sided slots
expected, and 0 of 20,000 trials reached zero.** The holes in this corpus are
**pair-shaped, not mark-shaped.**

**This is `vertex-acts` generalised.** That claim is already *measured*: the
Angle/Curve pairing is domain-invariant over seven domains. This is the same
structure over **nineteen domains and all three pairs** — and it says the unit of
semantic assignment in this notation is not the mark. **It is the opposition.**

So a per-mark dictionary is the wrong object. The smallest thing this corpus
assigns a meaning to has two ends.

**Why the probe was blind.** NSM's 65 primes contain no prime for *opposite*.
Antonymy is not a meaning in that framework, it is a relation between meanings —
so a probe built from that list cannot return it, however exhaustively it is run.
F155's 13.8% is not wrong; it is answering a question that could not have found
this. **A probe list inherits its source's blind spots along with its
independence**, and the independence is exactly why the blind spots are invisible:
there is no overlap to notice the gap in. Recorded as METHODS §18.

That is the second time in three findings that a borrowed framework has misfitted
this notation, in two opposite directions. F154: adopting the *shape* of an
outside list imported a flatness the notation contradicts. F156: adopting the
*coverage* of an outside list imported a silence the notation contradicts. The
list was honest both times. Lists always are — they answer what they were built
to answer.

**What I have not shown.** I assembled this census, so the construction risk is
real: I may have recorded a word only when I could find its partner. Three things
argue against it and none of them closes it — F134's table shows the shape before
the census existed; the one unbalanced cell (`temporal` Point/Circle, three
against two) survives unpadded, and it is exactly the cell a padder would have
padded; and the contested pair (Amperage/Voltage, F136) is recorded as contested
rather than quietly resolved to fit. **The falsifier is stated and cheap:** one
domain word on one mark whose partner has none, found by re-reading the sheets.

Recorded as `the-pair-is-the-unit-of-assignment`, **measured**, with that scope
written into it.

---

findings.title: asked 65 questions by people who had never seen it, the notation answered the spatial ones and almost nothing else
findings.text:
F154 said what Phase A's second half must NOT do: adopt a flat external inventory.
This is what it did instead.

**The probe.** Goddard & Wierzbicka's Natural Semantic Metalanguage proposes ~65
meanings that are indefinable and have an exponent in every language studied.
Whether that claim is true is not this project's business. What makes the list a
good instrument is that it was assembled by people who had never seen this
notation, for a purpose unrelated to it — **so it cannot flatter the corpus.**
Sixty-five questions, each of the form *can this notation say this?*

**The rule that keeps the number honest.** A prime is `attested` only if a census
word IS the prime or a measured operator realises it. My own judgement calls are
filed as `adjacent`, carry the census word that prompted them, and are **never
folded into the headline** — `Act` is not DO and `Contract` is not SMALL. A
fourth verdict, `absent_recorded`, means the corpus has a claim on file saying it
*cannot* say this: a cited hole, which is worth strictly more than silence.

**MEASURED COVERAGE: 9 of 65 — 13.8%.** With my adjacency judgements folded in it
would read 33.8%, which is why they are not folded in.

But the total is not the finding. The distribution is.

| category | total | attested | cited hole | silent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **space** | **9** | **5** | **3** | **1** |
| quantifiers | 6 | 2 | 0 | 3 |
| time | 8 | 1 | 0 | 4 |
| intensifier | 2 | 1 | 0 | 1 |
| mental predicates | 7 | **0** | 0 | 7 |
| logical concepts | 5 | **0** | 0 | 5 |
| substantives | 6 | **0** | 0 | 5 |
| speech | 3 | **0** | 0 | 2 |
| evaluators | 2 | **0** | 0 | 2 |
| determiners | 3 | **0** | 0 | 3 |
| *…6 more* | | **0** | | |

**Twelve of sixteen categories have nothing attested at all.**

**And SPACE is not merely the best category — it is finished.**

```
  YES  WHERE/PLACE   Circle:Space
  YES  NEAR          superpose_displaced — the same continuous axis, nearer in
  YES  FAR           superpose_displaced — the r > extent(A) region
  YES  INSIDE        nest  — the 0 < r < extent(A) region
  YES  TOUCH         cross — the r ≈ extent(A) region
 HOLE  ABOVE         directional-schemas-need-a-declared-frame
 HOLE  BELOW         directional-schemas-need-a-declared-frame
 HOLE  SIDE          directional-schemas-need-a-declared-frame
    ·  HERE          deictic — it needs a speaker, and nothing here is one
```

Every spatial prime is either answered or has a claim explaining why it cannot
be. Nine for nine. No other category comes near, and the four attested primes
outside SPACE are ONE, MUCH/MANY, WHEN/TIME and MORE — every one of them a
cardinality or a quantity, which is the thinnest possible kind of meaning.

**Four of the five spatial hits are the same object.** NEAR, FAR, INSIDE and
TOUCH are not four attestations. They are four regions of one continuous
placement plane, partitioned by the extent of the host mark
(`schemas-are-regions-not-a-vocabulary`). So the measured semantic content of
this notation is, very nearly: **one plane, and a count.**

**What this says about the 97-word census.** The census looked rich — 97
concepts, 19 domains, six marks. Held against an outside list, almost none of it
is *meaning the notation composes*. Amperage, Alpha, Init, Æther are **domain
vocabulary painted onto marks.** `the-domain-is-an-axis` (measured) already says
the corpus varies that domain freely; this measures the price. Vary the domain
and the words all change while the expressible structure does not move at all.

**So the next work is not more words.** Collecting a hundred more domain glosses
would move the census and not this number. The question Phase B has to answer is
whether anything outside SPACE **composes** — whether two marks placed together
can make a mental predicate, a negation, a comparison — or whether this notation
is a spatial semantics with a lexicon stapled to it.

Recorded as `the-attested-semantics-is-spatial`, **measured**, and scoped
carefully: an unattested prime may be unexpressible or merely never drawn. Four
of the sixty-five are the only ones this register can currently tell apart.

---

findings.title: the corpus already borrowed a taxonomy, and it fit badly enough to be worth the lesson
findings.text:
Phase A's second half was meant to be an **external concept inventory** — go and
find a list of concepts somebody else wrote down, and check how much of it this
notation can say. The discipline that matters there is checking **category fit
before adopting**, not after.

Before hunting for a new inventory I checked whether the corpus had already
adopted one. It had, twice over, and the record of that was in the wrong place.

**The provenance.** `tools/symbol_transforms.py:136`:

> *The schema vocabulary is the wiki's (`Cosmic Cipher - Image Schemas Relational
> Layer`), taken from Johnson/Lakoff. The JOIN is what is computed here: which of
> them a measured operator actually realises, and which have none.*

The wiki page frames those ten as **Layer 2** — the syntagmatic, relational layer
— against **Layer 1**, the X/S/M alphabet, and asserts they are *"a different
logical type, not reducible to them."* It even flags one as unfinished:
*"UP/DOWN (resists reduction; possibly its own structure)."*

**Where it was not.** Five claims in `derivation_register.json` reason about the
schemas. Grepping the whole claims blob for `johnson`, `lakoff`, `image schema`:
**no, no, no.** Every downstream claim says *the ten schemas the corpus names*
and the register never said whose ten they were. A borrowed frame that reads as
native is the worst version of borrowing, because nothing downstream knows there
is an outside assumption to re-check.

**The fit check, which had already been run twice without being called that.**
The inventory is a **flat list of ten**. In this notation it is not flat:

| the borrowed name | what it turned out to be here | claim | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| CENTER/PERIPHERY | `r = 0` | | |
| IN / OUT | `0 < r < extent(A)` | `schemas-are-regions-not-a-vocabulary` | derived |
| CONTACT | `r ≈ extent(A)` | | |
| NEAR / FAR | `r > extent(A)` | | |
| UP / DOWN | | | |
| FRONT / BACK | needs a declared frame | `the-grammar-gaps-are-the-frame-bound-schemas` | derived_given |
| PATH | | | |
| LINK | `concatenate` | | attested |
| BALANCE | `reflect_pair` | | attested |
| PART / WHOLE | mereological, not positional | `four-schemas-have-no-operator` | measured |

Four of the ten are **regions of a single continuous axis**, and the boundaries
between them are not conventions — they sit exactly where the two figures start
and stop overlapping, which is a property of A's own extent. Three of the ten are
**one gap wearing three names**. So ten names resolve into **one axis, one gap and
three singletons: five things, not ten.**

**Why it misfits, stated once.** Image schemas are motivated by **embodied
experience**; this notation is motivated by **geometry**. Where the two agree the
schema dissolves into a geometric parameter and stops being a word. Where they
disagree the schema needs something the notation does not have — a privileged
vertical, a distinguished direction. Neither outcome leaves a vocabulary item
standing. The list was never wrong; it was the wrong *kind* of thing to adopt
whole.

**What this changes about Phase A.** The plan said *find an external concept
inventory.* The result says: do not adopt a second flat one. NSM primes, thematic
roles, an upper ontology — each is worth running against this notation as a
**probe list** (*can it say this?*) and none is worth importing as a taxonomy,
because importing the list imports its flatness, and this notation has already
contradicted one such flatness on its own evidence.

Recorded in the register under a new `borrowed_frameworks` section, which is the
first place that file has admitted anything came from outside it.

---

findings.title: `scale` said NOTHING FOUND, and the counterexample was in the same file
findings.text:
The `scale` axis carried this: *"NOTHING FOUND. Across 24 sheets and 8 documents,
no artifact uses SIZE as a meaning-bearing dimension."*

Two entries below it, `operators-are-points-in-a-placement-space` — **derived** —
says the attested binary operators are six points in one placement space
parameterised by separation, bearing, rotation **and relative scale `s`**, with
the attested operator `nest` sitting at **s = 0.4**.

So an attested operator is *defined by a scale value*, and the axis beside it
said scale is never used. Both records are in `derivation_register.json`, about
forty lines apart.

**What survives, stated precisely.** The note was reaching for something true and
overshot it. Scale is **used constructively** — `nest` shrinks its guest, and
that is attested. Scale is **never contrastive** — no sheet draws the same figure
at two sizes and reads them differently.

That distinction is not a quibble; it is the third time this corpus has produced
exactly that shape:

| axis | attested as an operation | attested as a contrast |
|---|---|---|
| mirroring (F135) | yes — closes figures, fills unreachable rotations | **no** |
| modulation (F137) | yes — the axis is drawn three times with its continuum | **no** |
| scale (here) | yes — `nest` is the point at s=0.4 | **no** |

Three axes, all used to BUILD and none used to MEAN. Whether that is a fact
about the corpus or a fact about the notation is now a question worth asking,
and it could not be asked while one of the three was recorded as absent.

---

findings.title: the register was keeping the same fact twice, and five of eleven copies had drifted
findings.text:
Starting Phase A's second half meant reading `relational_axes`, the table of the
twelve dimensions along which symbols relate. Each entry names the CLAIM that
settles it — and each also stored its own `status` beside it.

**Five of eleven disagreed with the claim they name.**

| axis | stored | the claim it names | actually |
|---|---|---|---|
| superposition | `derived` | phase-is-harmony | **derived_given** |
| adjacency | `derived` | cusp-closure | **derived_given** |
| composition | `derived` | hamming-gives-rotation-class | **derived_given** |
| placement | `undetermined` | attachment-point | **derived_given** |
| sequence | `undetermined` | base8-cycle-order | **derived_given** |

Two of those I made stale yesterday by moving `attachment-point` and
`base8-cycle-order`. **The other three were already wrong**, and they were wrong
in the direction that matters: the axis table said `derived` where the claim says
`derived_given`. That is an overclaim, sitting in the one file whose entire
purpose is that statuses are not overclaimed.

**Nothing read the copy.** Grepping every tool and test, the only consumer of
`relational_axes` was the detector written to check it. So the stored status had
no function at all except to be able to disagree.

**So the fix is not to resync it.** A fact recorded twice will drift, and drift
is invisible to anything that reads one copy. The stored status is gone: ten
axes that name a claim now read the status from it, and the detector refuses a
stored one rather than comparing them. Checking for a MISMATCH only catches
drift after it has happened — and it already had, five times.

*Controlled both ways.* Planting a stored status back onto one axis: **1
finding**. Removing it: **0**. Through the real detector, on the real register.

**This is F150's fault from a different direction, and that is why the detector
got built now.** F150 found `aether-is-upper` resting on a premise that had been
withdrawn, and I recorded then that a detector written in the same minute as the
fault it found tends to be shaped to that one instance. Two instances arriving
independently — one a dangling `given`, one a duplicated status — is a class
rather than an incident, and the detector now covers both: a `given` must name a
claim that exists and is not withdrawn, and an axis must not store what its
claim already says.

findings.title: the form side is complete and the concept side is at five per cent
findings.text:
The lexicon is generated and total. `the-one-run-lexicon` gives 40 one-run forms
that survive reachability and the pipeline's own read-back error;
`composition-is-where-the-lexicon-lives` multiplies that to 26,640 at two marks
and 4,428,800 at three, each with a reading composed the same way the symbol is;
and `how-many-symbols-the-notation-can-carry` says capacity was never the
constraint — about 2.4e11 forms for two marks at a placement.

**And then you read one.** Entry two of the generated lexicon, verbatim:

> *"A run that changes direction by 99 degrees, spread evenly along its length,
> open at both ends."*

And a composed one:

> *"A run that does not change direction, open at both ends, and much smaller to
> the right of it, a second run that does not change direction, open at both
> ends."*

Those are **descriptions of geometry**. The composition rule genuinely reads —
descriptions compose exactly as the symbols do, which is a real result and not a
small one — but what it composes is what the figure LOOKS LIKE. There are 4.4
million of them and not one is a concept.

**The measurement.** The built cell records already carry a `meaning` field.
Counted over every one of them:

| | |
|---|---|
| drawn orbits carrying a `meaning` field | **98** |
| named | **5** |
| `none recorded` | **93** |
| coverage | **5.1%** |

Five. The whole attested semantics of the drawn combination space is
`Sun-in-Circle`, `infinity`, `Chaos pair`, `+`, and `Sun-in-Circle` again. And
only ONE sheet populates the field at all — `primers/space.cells.json` — so even
the 98 is a lower bound on what is unnamed.

**The other direction, and what it measures instead.** A census of every concept
the sheets are on record as attaching to a mark is now in
`data/derivation/concept_census.json` — **97 concepts across the six marks, in
19 domains**, every entry carrying a finding as its citation. That direction is
100% by construction, because the census is built from cited attestations, so
the number that means something there is not coverage but DOMAIN SPREAD:

| mark | concepts | domains |
|---|---|---|
| Angle | 16 | **13** |
| Curve | 16 | **13** |
| Line | 17 | 10 |
| Wave | 17 | 10 |
| Point | 16 | 9 |
| Circle | 15 | 9 |

`the-domain-is-an-axis` (measured) says the corpus varies the interpretive
domain freely, so a mark attested in one domain is not understood and a mark
attested in thirteen is. **The two class-1 marks are the most widely glossed**,
which is F147 arriving from a different direction: the Angle/Curve polarity is
the one that survives every domain, and it is also the one the corpus states
most often.

**Two entries are contested and marked as such** — Amperage on the Line and
Voltage on the Wave, which F136 found two sheets swapping. A census that hid
that would be worth less than no census.

**And four concepts have no operator at all**: UP/DOWN, FRONT/BACK, PATH and
PART/WHOLE. Three are one gap and the fourth is separate, per
`the-grammar-gaps-are-the-frame-bound-schemas`.

**Wired, so it cannot be forgotten.** `unnamed-figure` is now a detector in
`corpus_audit` and reports the ratio every run. It is a standing debt rather
than a regression — it has never been good — and the reason to surface it every
time is that a semantic gap is the one kind of gap a build cannot feel. The
audit gate is green, the ratchet is green, and 93 figures mean nothing.

**The one thing the tool refuses to do.** It will not infer a meaning from
proximity to a named orbit. `two-unnamed-orbits-sit-beside-named-ones` already
says proximity is a lead and not a reading, and the entire value of the 5-of-98
figure is that it is honest. A tool that closed the gap by guessing would
destroy the only thing it was built to measure.

findings.title: the propagation detector walks only the `derived` claims, and a withdrawal slipped past it
findings.text:
Auditing the dependency graph by hand after F145 found one link the detector
cannot see.

`aether-is-upper` is `derived_given`, and its `given` was
`up-is-shared-across-canvases` — **which F145 withdrew.** A conditional
derivation was left resting on a premise that had been retracted, and
`corpus_audit --detector derivation-status` reported clean throughout.

**Why it reported clean, and this is the useful half.** The detector's
propagation walk is guarded by `if c.get("status") != "derived": continue`. That
is deliberate and the code says why: `derived_given` is *"the honest resting
place for a conditional derivation, so it is not re-flagged"*. Correct as far as
it goes — a conditional derivation should not be nagged about being conditional.
But it means nothing ever checks that the thing it is conditional ON still
exists in the state the `given` assumes. A withdrawal is invisible to it.

**The fix in the claim, which turned out to be a correction rather than a
re-point.** The obvious repair was to swap the `given` for
`direction-is-read-as-contrast`. Reading the claim to do that showed its `scope`
note was also false. It said the claim *"reads a single mark against the frame
rather than against another mark, so it is canvas-relative"* — but F69's own
panel lists `∧` Alpha·Æther and `∪` Omega·Nether **together**, both poles on one
canvas. That is the contrastive form, so the PAIRING is canvas-independent after
all. What is frame-relative is only which member gets called the *upper* one,
which is exactly the shape F148 found for the elements: the grounding derives the
partition and never which side of the page it lands on.

So a dangling reference turned into a corrected overclaim about a limit the
claim did not actually have.

**What this says about the detectors generally.** Three of them ran clean on
this all day — `derivation-status`, `dangling-reference`, and the new
`absolute-direction` — and the fault sat in the gap between what two of them
cover: `dangling-reference` checks that cited FINDINGS exist, `derivation-status`
checks propagation but only from `derived` nodes, and nobody checks that a
`given` still names a claim in a usable state. Worth a detector; recorded here
rather than built in the same breath, because a detector written in the same
minute as the fault it found tends to be shaped to that one instance.

---

## The semantic half

findings.title: the last claim cannot be closed by its author, so the thing to build was the exam
findings.text:
`rederivability-defeats-capture` is the one undetermined claim left, and it is
the only one in the register that did not move by reading the corpus harder.
The reason is structural rather than difficult.

The claim says a notation whose meanings are DERIVABLE, rather than assigned by
authority, lets a mind reconstruct its concepts independently of whatever taught
it — and so detect and escape conceptual capture. Its success condition asks for
a measurement: *give an independent reader the method and the corpus, withhold
the findings, and measure recovery.*

**I am the worst possible examinee.** I know where every defect is. Anything I
recovered, I would recover with the answers in hand, and a score obtained that
way measures nothing at all. There is no amount of care that fixes this — it is
not a bias to be corrected but a disqualification.

**So the available contribution was to build the test, not to sit it.**
`tools/rederivability_exam.py` fixes the exam; `data/derivation/
rederivability_key.json` seals what counts as passing. The reader is given the
21 image artifacts, the cheat sheet, `METHODS-instruments.md` and the six status
words. They are not given the notes, the register, the term ledger, or the key.

**Nine structural results to recover** — six marks; three rotation classes; that
the drawn pairs ARE those classes; six = three symmetry classes x two curvature
classes; the sign grammar; that `Z/12 = Z/3 x Z/4` is WHY there are twelve; that
the crossbar IS the Line, so Air = Fire + Level; modality on the apex and forces
flanking the base; and that the interpretive domain is a free axis.

**Five defects to catch, none of them planted** — every one is real and
independently confirmed: the Yin/Yang inversion that survived years, the
Amperage/Voltage swap between two sheets (F136), the Æther/Nether conflation on
Sol-Center (F69), `Life` naming both the teardrop and the spiral, and the
enharmonic spellings in the Cromatic Tone column. The reader is not told how
many there are, or whether there are any.

**Detection is the half that carries the claim.** Recovery alone would show the
notation is learnable, which is a much weaker thing. Catching an error in what
taught you is the entire content of `rederivability-defeats-capture`, and a
reader who recovers the structure fluently and still flags nothing would
**refute** it. The exam is built so that outcome is legible rather than
deniable.

**The scorer's own controls, and the one that fired.** Empty submission: 0/9 and
0/5. A submission restating the key: 9/9 and 5/5. Confident nonsense: 0/9.

That third control failed on the first attempt, and it failed in the way worth
recording. At a match threshold of 0.5, with number words in the stop list,
*"the marks are eleven and encode tidal harmonics"* scored a HIT against *"the
inventory is six marks"* — because `six`, the only word that discriminates the
two, had been discarded as a stop word, and half of what survived was `marks`.
**In a corpus whose results are counts, numbers are content.** Threshold 0.6,
numbers kept.

**And the objection that the key sits in the repository, stated rather than
patched.** Anyone can read it. That is not a leak; it is the shape of the
problem, and it is the same fact as the disqualification above. An exam whose
key sits beside it cannot be self-administered. Validity comes from the reader,
not from the file — and what the file buys is that the test is now something a
person can execute in an afternoon instead of something they would have to
design first.

The claim stays **undetermined**, correctly. What has changed is that it is no
longer blocked on anyone designing anything.

findings.title: the direction bit is density, once you take the corpus at its word about what the elements ARE
findings.text:
`element-bit-assignment` says up+unbarred is Fire, up+barred is Air,
down+unbarred is Water, down+barred is Earth, and its success condition names a
live candidate: *"fire rises and water falls, so the direction bit may be
derivable from buoyancy — but that is physics imported into geometry, and it
must be argued, not waved at."*

It can be argued, and the argument is better than the one the condition
sketched, because the corpus supplies the missing premise itself.

**F19: the elements ARE the states of matter.** Legible on the 8K cheat sheet
and confirmed on a second artifact at F70 — Fire = **Plasma**, Air = **Gas**,
Water = **Liquid**, Earth = **Solid**. F19 already calls this the most
defensible correspondence in the corpus, because the target set is physically
real, closed and independently defined. It is not a metaphysical reading; it is
a statement about matter.

**Then the direction bit is not an import, it is the same fact.** Take the four
phases and split them by density: plasma and gas are the two rarefied phases,
liquid and solid the two dense ones. Buoyancy in a gravitational field lifts the
first pair and sinks the second. And the direction bit partitions them:

| phase | element | density | direction bit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plasma | Fire | rarefied | **up** |
| Gas | Air | rarefied | **up** |
| Liquid | Water | dense | **down** |
| Solid | Earth | dense | **down** |

Four for four, one property throughout — not "fire rises" as folk physics about
one element, but a single threshold on a single quantity that sorts all four.

**And what it derives is exactly the half that needed deriving.** It fixes the
PARTITION — which two elements share a value of the bit — and not which side of
the page each lands on. That is the right shape, because
`direction-is-read-as-contrast` (derived, F145) says the notation never reads a
direction against the frame anyway: only the contrast carries meaning, and the
contrast is the partition. So the physics supplies precisely what the notation
needs and nothing it does not. A supervoid reader, whose buoyancy inverts, gets
the same partition with the sides exchanged — and reads the same thing, for the
reason F145 gives.

**The crossbar bit is still open, and now the gap is stated exactly.** It
partitions {Air, Earth} against {Fire, Water} — in phases, **{Gas, Solid}
against {Plasma, Liquid}**. F140 gave the bit a reading (open end versus bounded
level, which the corpus itself names Destiny and Reality), but no property of
the four phases is known that groups gas with solid against plasma with liquid.
Density does not: solid and gas are the extremes of that ordering, not a pair.

*A pattern noticed and explicitly not claimed.* Order the phases along their
transition chain — Solid, Liquid, Gas, Plasma — and the crossbar bit is the
PARITY of the position: positions 1 and 3 barred, positions 2 and 4 unbarred. All four fit.
But with four items and two bits, any assignment whatever can be described by
two functions, and parity-along-a-chain names no physical property. **This is
not evidence.** It is recorded the way F47 recorded the opponent-colour
coincidence — so that if a reason ever emerges it is already written down, and
so that nobody mistakes the fit for a finding.

findings.title: `vertex-acts` asks for three things, and they have three different answers
findings.text:
The success condition reads: *"Derive agency, initiation or directedness from
curvature concentration alone — or find a different geometric property of the
vertex that IS the sense."* Those are not one ask. Taken apart:

**Directedness is derivable, and it does not discriminate.** The Angle is
rotation class 1, so no rotation returns it, so its orientation is
meaning-bearing — `symmetry-order-is-operator-capacity`, derived, and the same
argument F143 used for the apex. But the **Curve is also class 1**. Directedness
belongs to both members of the pair the claim is trying to separate, so it
cannot be what makes one of them Act and the other Pass.

**Agency and initiation are not geometric.** No measurement of a figure returns
them, and no amount of measuring will.

**The second branch has been searched, and the properties are enumerated.**
Twenty-eight settled claims in the register mention the Angle. Between them its
geometry is characterised about as completely as anything here: rotation class 1
(`rotation-invariance`), singular curvature (`mark-polarity`), achiral
(`mark-chirality`), its own incidence unreachable by any attested operator
(`angle-incidence-is-unreachable`), closing to the equilateral triangle
(`curve-pair-is-the-circle`), one of four occupied cells on the turning-against-
concentration grid (`six-marks-name-four-cells-of-the-segment-grid`). Not one of
those is a semantic property, and the list is not obviously missing an entry.
F142 already took the most tempting candidate — unreachability, so the Angle is
where you must START — and showed it to be a pun on `init`.

**So what is actually established is something the claim did not ask for, and it
is better.** Across every domain the corpus uses, the Angle takes the
initiating, source or writing role and the Curve the receiving, sink or reading
one:

| domain | Angle `∧` | Curve `∪` | recorded at |
|---|---|---|---|
| order | **Alpha** | **Omega** | F8, F67, F69 |
| action | **Act** | **Pass** | F65, F69 |
| access | **Set** | **Get** | F67 |
| time | **Init** | **Hold** | F42 |
| field | **Spark** (−ρ) | **Drain** (ε₀) | F57 |
| motion | Ebb, Push | Flow, Pull | the marks sheet |
| cosmology | **Æther** | **Nether** | F69 |

**Why that matters more than it looks.** `the-domain-is-an-axis` (measured) says
the corpus varies the interpretive domain the way it varies any other feature —
so a property that survives EVERY domain is not a property of a reading. It is a
property of the marks. The Angle/Curve polarity is domain-invariant in a corpus
that is otherwise domain-plural, and that is a measured fact rather than a
reading of one sheet.

*One artifact inverts, and it is on file.* The cheat sheet labels `∧` **Yin**
and `∪` **Yang**, against the received convention and against that same sheet's
own Act/Pass row. That is F30, already in the term ledger as a collision, and it
is the exception that has been registered rather than smoothed over.

**So the claim moves to `measured`, and its success condition should change.**
Asking for "a geometric property of the vertex" is asking for something that has
been enumerated. What is missing is not another property but a MAP — a
principled reason why, of the two class-1 marks, the singular-curvature one
takes the source role. That map would close a dozen claims at once rather than
this one, and it is the Tier-1-to-Tier-2 gap F48 named in its own closing line:
*the grammar is grounded; the vocabulary it composes is still largely chosen.*

findings.title: the family boundary, derived: three families, three fixed-point sets, one invariant
findings.text:
`modulation-is-a-second-operator-family` offers two ways to close: find
modulation stated as an operation in the corpus, or **derive the family
boundary**. F137 closed the first branch — the corpus names `Modulations` but
only ever as a predicate on two marks. This is the second.

**The separator is the fixed-point set.** Ask of each family: which figures does
the WHOLE family leave alone? A figure fixed by every member of a family is a
fact about that family as a set of maps, so it survives any renaming or
reparameterisation. Two families with different fixed-point sets are different
families, and nothing about how they are described can make them the same one.

Measured over the six marks, every modulation parameter setting, every ordered
pair under the six attested placement operators, and every insertion position:

| anchor / host | modulation | placement | insert |
|---|---|---|---|
| Point | **14/14** | 10/36 | **30/30** |
| Line | **14/14** | 14/36 | 11/30 |
| Angle | 1/14 | 1/36 | 10/30 |
| Curve | 0/14 | 1/36 | 10/30 |
| Wave | 1/14 | 5/36 | 11/30 |
| Circle | **14/14** | 9/36 | 10/30 |

> fixed by ALL of **modulation** — Point, Line, Circle
> fixed by ALL of **placement** — **none**
> fixed by ALL of **insert** — Point

Three families, three different sets, and each set has a reason that is a
