property of the operation rather than of the implementation:

- **Modulation re-reads an existing variation**, so a figure with none is
  untouched by every member. And its fixed points are exactly the constant-
  profile figures, checkable directly: Line's profile spans **0.0000**, Circle's
  **0.0042** (at the resolution floor), the Point has no profile at all — while
  Angle spans 0.8913, Curve 0.8441 and Wave 1.1000.
- **Insert splices a guest into a stretch of the host's extent**, so the only
  figure it cannot touch is the one with no extent to cut: the Point.
- **Placement adds a second figure**, and no figure absorbs a second figure
  without becoming a different figure. Its fixed-point set is empty.

**And this is sharper than the commutation result.** F131 showed `insert`
commutes with neither family — 0 of 125 placement pairs and 0 of 78 eligible
modulation hosts — which says what insert is NOT. The fixed-point sets say what
each family IS, positively and by an invariant.

**A correction to what I expected.** The first version of this measurement
predicted that placement would have no fixed points at all and stopped there.
It has **40 of 216** — concatenating a Point onto a Line, a Wave or a Circle
reproduces the mark, which is `concatenating-a-point-is-degenerate` arriving
from another direction. So "one family has fixed points and the other does not"
is false and was checked before it was written. What is true is the stronger and
more specific thing: placement's fixed points belong to particular (guest,
operator) pairs, while modulation's belong to the **host alone**. No mark is
fixed by the whole placement family; three are fixed by the whole modulation
family. That is the difference an invariant can see.

**What this does not settle.** The boundary is derived for the families as
IMPLEMENTED, and implementing a family is a design act — `symbol_waveform.py`
says so in its own header. Whether the corpus's `Modulations` is this modulation
is the other half, and F137 answered it as far as the corpus allows: the word is
there, the operation is not.

findings.title: the habit is now a rule, and the claim it was propping up was false anyway
findings.text:
`up-is-shared-across-canvases` asked whether two readers on different canvases
assign the same direction to `up`. They do not, and this corpus has known so
since F103: `orientation-is-a-canvas-parameter` is **derived**, and its own
derivation contains the counterexample — inside a cosmic supervoid the
gravitational pull is outward from every side, so `down` points away from the
observer rather than toward a mass. The sign of the anchor inverts. There is
nothing left to show.

**So the claim as written is false, and the notation never needed it.** F141
measured that every meaning-bearing use of the direction bit in this corpus is
already CONTRASTIVE — both values of the bit drawn on the same page, so what a
reader reads is the relation between two marks and not either mark against the
frame. Three sheets, four uses, no exception.

**And that is enough, provably.** A relation between two marks on one canvas is
invariant under any transformation applied to the whole canvas: reorient the
canvas and both marks move together, so the relation between them is unchanged.
Reading one mark against the frame is not invariant, because the frame is
exactly what moved. So a notation that reads directions only contrastively is
canvas-independent by construction, and the supervoid reader reads the same
thing as the reader on a planetary surface — not because their `up` agrees, but
because neither of them is consulting it.

**A habit is not a rule until something can fail.** F141 established what the
corpus does; this makes it something the corpus cannot stop doing. The new
`absolute-direction` detector in `corpus_audit.py` walks every `*.cells.json`
this build generates and flags any sheet where a directional field —
`apex`, `apex-up`, `direction`, `phase`, `crossbar` — carries only ONE of its
values:

| | result |
|---|---|
| on the real build | **0 findings** — `cells/signs`, `charts/signs-as-waveforms` and `primers/crt` each carry `apex` and `crossbar` at 6 and 6 |
| on a planted sheet with three cells, all `apex: up` | **1 finding, high** — *"3 cell(s) carry `apex` and every one of them says `up` — so the sheet asks the reader to know which way is up, instead of showing the contrast"* |
| with the plant removed | back to **0**, and the register records it as no longer reproducing |

Both directions, through the real detector, on the real tree.

*What it cannot see, written on the detector.* It covers cells that RECORD a
directional field. A sheet that draws a direction without recording one is
invisible to it, so a clean run is evidence about the records and not about the
ink. That is the honest bound and it is in the `scope` line where a reader of a
finding will meet it.

findings.title: the Base 8 cycle ORDER is forced, and the thing that forces it is what the Force set does not contain
findings.text:
`base8-cycle-order` says the cusps run Wave – Fire – Point – Earth – Line – Air –
Circle – Water, and its success condition says: *"Derive the cycle ORDER. That
each element sits between two cusps is structural; which cusp sits where is not
shown."* The order is derivable. Everything needed was already on file.

**The three inputs, all of them already established.**

1. `hamming-gives-rotation-class` (derived_given) does not merely say the mark's
   class is a function of the distance. It says which: **distance 2 → invariant;
   distance 1 by direction → orientation-bearing; distance 1 by crossbar →
   modulating.**
2. The Force set is Point, Circle, Line, Wave, each used once (F52). By F6's
   three captions and `rotation-class-is-symmetry-order` that is **two invariant
   marks and two orientation-bearing marks, and NO modulating mark.** F143
   measured the same thing from the other side: 0 of 24 force marks on the
   Decans sheet are rotation class 1.
3. There are exactly three distinct Hamiltonian cycles on four elements.

**Enumerate them and the answer is forced.** Writing each element as
(direction, crossbar):

| cycle | what its four gaps demand | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Fire – Air – Water – Earth | 2 **modulating** + 2 invariant | excluded — the Force set has no modulating mark |
| Fire – Air – Earth – Water | 2 **modulating** + 2 orientation-bearing | excluded — same, and it leaves two invariants unused |
| **Fire – Earth – Air – Water** | **2 invariant + 2 orientation-bearing** | **matches the Force set exactly** |

The third is the one the corpus draws. The two exclusions are not preferences;
each names a mark class the Force set does not contain.

Checked gap by gap against F52's reading:

| gap | elements | distance | demands | drawn |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Water↔Fire | (1,0)↔(0,0) | 1, by direction | orientation-bearing | **Wave** ✓ |
| Fire↔Earth | (0,0)↔(1,1) | 2 | invariant | **Point** ✓ |
| Earth↔Air | (1,1)↔(0,1) | 1, by direction | orientation-bearing | **Line** ✓ |
| Air↔Water | (0,1)↔(1,0) | 2 | invariant | **Circle** ✓ |

**Why the all-edge cycle was never possible.** Fire – Air – Water – Earth walks
the four edges of the element square, so every gap is distance 1 and no gap
demands an invariant mark. But two of the four Forces ARE invariant. A cycle
that has no place for them cannot be the one that uses all four.

**What is still open, stated exactly.** The class constraint fixes that the two
invariants go in the two diagonal gaps and the two orientation-bearing marks in
the two direction gaps. It does not say **which** invariant goes in which
diagonal gap, or which orientation-bearing mark in which direction gap. That is
two independent binary choices — four arrangements, all class-consistent, and
the corpus draws one of them.

All four put exactly two elements between two marks of the same cardinality
(`cardinality-bit`, derived: Point and Line are the 'one' marks, Circle and Wave
the 'many'). The corpus's arrangement makes that pure pair **Earth and Water** —
the two DOWN elements — with Earth taking both 'one' marks and Water both
'many'. The other two arrangements make the pure pair Fire and Air instead.
Nothing found so far picks between them, and the reading that suggests itself —
that the bounded element takes the 'one' marks and the open one the 'many',
which would run through F140's Destiny/Reality axis — does not survive: Fire is
also open and Air also bounded, and both get mixed pairs.

**So the claim moves.** The ORDER is derived, given element-bit-assignment. The
assignment of individual forces within it is not, and the success condition
should say so rather than asking for the order again.

findings.title: apex-vs-base is not a convention: the apex is the only site that offers a direction, and the modality marks are the only ones that can use one
findings.text:
`attachment-point` says the modality mark rides the apex and the force marks
flank the base, and its success condition asks for a REASON it should be that
way round rather than the reverse. Consistency across two sheets is evidence of
a rule, not of its necessity. The Decans sheet supplies the necessity.

**The structure, measured.** `Base36_Decans` draws twelve composites, each an
element triangle with small marks attached. There are 36 attached marks —
exactly three per composite — and they sit:

| | count | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| one mark on the **apex** side | 12 of 12 | ok |
| two marks flanking the **base** side | 12 of 12 | ok |

**And "apex" means the figure's apex, not the top of the page.** Six of the
twelve triangles point up and six point down. The single mark is ABOVE for the
six that point up and BELOW for the six that point down — 12/12. The rule is
being read off the figure, which is the same self-reading property F138 found in
`To`/`From`.

**What is attached where, and this is the part that derives it.** Two
independent symmetry tests separate the apex marks from the base marks
completely:

| test | apex marks (12) | base marks (24) | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| mirror-symmetric about a vertical axis? | min **0.927** | the 6 Waves max **0.126** | +0.800 |
| returned by a **half-turn**? | 0/12, max **0.476** | 24/24, min **0.814** | +0.337 |

The base marks partition exactly **6 Wave, 6 Point, 6 Line, 6 Circle**. So:

> **Forces** = Point, Circle, Line, Wave = exactly the marks of rotation class
> **∞, ∞, 2, 2**.
> **Modalities** = Angle, Curve, Staple = exactly the marks of rotation class
> **1**.

That split is `rotation-class-is-symmetry-order`, which is **derived**.

**The derivation.** A triangle has one apex and one base. The apex is a vertex
where the outline turns through its sharpest angle: it POINTS. The two base
corners are exchanged by the triangle's own mirror symmetry, so neither of them
supplies a direction the other does not.

`symmetry-order-is-operator-capacity` (derived) says a transformation
distinguishes two states of a figure exactly when it is not in that figure's
stabiliser. A class-1 mark therefore has a meaning-bearing orientation — no
rotation returns it — while a mark a half-turn returns has an orientation that
is free or two-fold and carries nothing.

So the assignment is forced by what the sites afford and what the marks can use:

- put the **orientable** marks at the **one site that offers an orientation**;
- put the marks whose orientation carries nothing at the **two sites that offer
  none**.

The reverse fails twice over. It spends the only oriented site on marks that
cannot read an orientation, and it has to place a single orientable mark at one
of two corners exchanged by a reflection — an unmotivated choice, and one whose
two readings would be mirror images of each other.

Arity says the same thing from the other side: one apex takes the one modality,
two corners take the two forces, and no other assignment fits without a
collision or an empty site.

**What this does NOT settle.** The premise that each composite attaches exactly
one modality and exactly two forces is a fact about the semantic layer, not
about the geometry, so the claim moves to `derived_given` rather than `derived`.
And `base24_cusps` was checked and does NOT provide a second instance: it is a
different construction — a cusp fuses two adjacent signs (`cusp-closure`, F62) —
and 8 of its 48 drawn pieces are half-turn symmetric, so the clean class-1/class-
many split of the Decans is not what that sheet is doing. One sheet, measured
completely, rather than two waved at.

**The instrument, which was wrong first.** The initial run returned **6 of 12**,
with the misses in a systematic pattern that looked like real structure. The
cause was an area floor of 25 pixels, set to keep noise out. The Points are
**21 pixels** — 5x5 — so the floor was deleting a primitive. Every composite
containing a Point read as having one mark too few, and the pattern of misses
was the pattern of where the Points fall.

**In a notation one of whose primitives is a Point, no area floor is safe.** A
threshold chosen against noise cannot be chosen without asking what the smallest
MARK is, and here the smallest mark is smaller than anything one would normally
call signal. The fix was not a better threshold; it was noticing that 30 marks
across 12 composites is not a whole number and going to look.

findings.title: a candidate for `vertex-acts` that looked good and is not one
findings.text:
Recording a rejected candidate, because the appeal of it is the kind that comes
back.

`vertex-acts` wants the Angle's modality sense — Active, Init, Act — derived
from curvature concentration, or from some other geometric property of the
vertex that IS the sense. F130 offers a tempting one: the Angle's own incidence,
two strokes sharing one end and diverging, is **unreachable by any attested
operator**. Nothing composes into it. So in construction order the Angle can
only be a starting point: you have to begin with it. And `Init` means begin.

**That is a pun, and it should be named as one.** "Initial in the construction
order" and "means initiation" are two different senses of the same English word,
and the argument moves between them without earning the step. Unreachability is
a property of the OPERATOR SET, not of the vertex; a different operator set
would change it while the Angle stayed the same figure. And the success
condition asks specifically for something derived from curvature concentration,
which unreachability is not.

What the unreachability does support is what F130's own title says — that the
Angle is irreducible, which is what primitive should mean. That is a real
result and it is already recorded. It is not this one.

**Why write it down.** The sense of having found something and the fact of
having found something feel identical from the inside, and the difference here
is one English word carrying two meanings. The register's habit of demanding the
derivation rather than the resemblance is what catches it, and a rejected
candidate left unrecorded gets re-derived by the next reader — including by me,
twice, in this corpus already.

findings.title: every drawn use of the direction bit is contrastive, and the instrument that tried to prove it could not
findings.text:
`up-is-shared-across-canvases` has a counterexample already on record: a reader
in a cosmic supervoid has a gravitational gradient pointing outward, so "down"
inverts while both canvases stay perfectly good canvases. Its success condition
offers a second exit — **restrict every meaning-bearing use of up/down to
contrastive form**, a relation between marks on one canvas rather than a reading
of one mark against the frame. That is checkable, and the corpus already
satisfies it.

**Where the direction bit bears meaning, both of its values are drawn on the
same canvas.** From the sheets' own labels, not from shape matching:

| sheet | up | down | contrastive? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Base12_signs` / `ZodiacSignSymbols` (F48) | Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, Aquarius | Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, Pisces | 6 and 6, one band |
| `ElementalNature-SolCenter` corners (F133) | the Fire and Air stacks | the Water and Earth stacks | 6 and 6, one sheet |
| `Base12_signs` element markers (F140) | Fire `↑`, Air `⊤` | Water `↓`, Earth `⊥` | 2 and 2, side by side |
| `Base6_rotary` column headers | `↑` | `↓` | both, one header row |

Three sheets, four uses, and not one of them shows a direction without its
opposite on the same page. Nothing in the corpus asks a reader to know which way
is up in the absence of the contrast — so the restriction the success condition
proposes costs nothing, because the corpus is already written that way.

**And now the instrument, which failed, and which is worth recording because it
failed for a reason peculiar to this notation.** The obvious mechanical test is:
for every glyph on a sheet, is its vertical mirror also on that sheet? Run over
all 21 artifacts it returned 36 per cent, flat across every size threshold from
the 0th to the 95th percentile — 43.3, 39.4, 33.4, 35.6, 33.0, 35.5, 34.7, 35.3,
39.2, 35.1. A number that does not move when the threshold moves usually means
the threshold is not the problem, and it was not: **the components include the
letters of the captions**, and a letter is directional and never has its mirror
on the page. The sweep was measuring the presence of text.

Restricting to the glyph sets whose members are known marks did not rescue it,
and the control is why. Planting a negative — each mark's best mirror-match
against a set it does not belong to — gives mean **0.518** and max **0.772**,
against **0.752** mean for the real measurement. The distributions sit on top of
one another and no threshold separates them:

| threshold | marks with a mirror on their own canvas | false positives in the control |
|---|---|---|
| 0.55 | 32/36 | 24/36 |
| 0.65 | 30/36 | 12/36 |
| 0.75 | 18/36 | 4/36 |
| 0.80 | 14/36 | 0/36 |

**The reason is structural, and it is a fact about the notation rather than
about the code.** The corpus draws everything out of six marks. So a glyph's
mirror and a *different glyph that happens to look like it* are the same thing
to a shape comparison, and instance identity is not recoverable from similarity
when the vocabulary is that small. Any test of the form "is THIS mark's
counterpart present" needs the labels; shape alone cannot carry it. That is a
general limit on measuring this corpus by matching, and it did not appear in the
earlier matching results (F133, F135) because there the question was *which of a
known set is this*, a forced choice among twelve, rather than *is a partner
present at all*, which is unbounded.

So the contrastive fact stands on the labels, and it is the labels that should
be cited for it.

findings.title: the crossbar bit had "no candidate at all", and the Base 12 sheet draws one
findings.text:
`element-bit-assignment` records that the direction bit has a live candidate —
fire rises, water falls — and that **the crossbar bit has none**. It has one,
and it is not an analogy: the sheet marks the four elements with four glyphs
from a notation whose semantics is already derived.

`UniversalSymbology-Base12_signs.png` puts a small marker beside each element
glyph. Measured off the ink, by the row-width profile, with no threshold to
argue about:

| element | row widths, top to bottom | intermediate rows | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fire** | `2 4 6 8 10 11 12 14 14 10 6 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4` | 4 | an **arrow**, head at the top |
| **Water** | `4 4 4 4 4 4 4 6 10 14 14 12 10 10 8 6 4 2` | 4 | an **arrow**, head at the bottom |
| **Air** | `18 18 18 18 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4` | **0** | a **bar** at the top of a stem |
| **Earth** | `4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 4 18 18 18 18` | **0** | a **bar** at the bottom of a stem |

An arrowhead tapers and a bar does not. The two arrows pass through four
intermediate-width rows on the way to their point; the two bars pass through
**zero** — full width, then the stem, nothing between. That is the whole
discriminator and it has no borderline case.

And those four glyphs are exactly the four extreme members of the stem-position
family. `position-on-a-line-is-rank` (F68, **derived**) reads: *"A crossbar's
position along a stem encodes ordinal rank; the two arrow forms are the open
ends."* So:

| | the rank notation says | the sheet's own caption |
|---|---|---|
| Fire, Water | the two **open ends** — unbounded | **Destiny** |
| Air, Earth | the two **bounded levels** — on a rank | **Reality** |

The crossbar bit is open-versus-bounded. That is a reading of the bit rather
than a label attached to it, it comes from a claim that is already derived, and
the corpus makes the connection itself — it draws the four elements with the
four extremes of the rank notation and then names the two resulting classes.
Unbounded is Destiny and a fixed level is Reality, which is the right way round.

**What it does not do, said plainly.** It does not derive that the barred pair
is Air and Earth rather than Fire and Water. Two cells are open and two are
bounded; which names go in which pair is still an assignment. What changes is
that the bit now has a candidate reading at all, and that the reading is
anchored in the notation instead of in a convention table.

**And the direction bit is no longer an import.** The success condition warned
that "fire rises and water falls" is physics carried into geometry and must be
argued rather than waved at. The sheet draws the arrow. `↑` beside Fire and `↓`
beside Water is the corpus's own gloss of the direction bit as motion, in the
same notation as the rest — which does not make the physics a derivation, but it
does move the claim from "we are importing buoyancy" to "the corpus states the
motion, and buoyancy is what would explain its choice".

**One negative, recorded so nobody reads more into this than is there.** The
four markers do NOT reproduce the classical stratification. Taken as positions
they give Fire beyond the top, Air at the top level, Earth at the bottom level,
Water beyond the bottom — and the received order is Fire, Air, Water, Earth,
with Earth lowest. Earth and Water come out swapped. So this is a statement
about two PAIRS, open against bounded, and not a four-level ladder. Anyone who
reads a vertical ordering of the elements off these four glyphs is reading
something the sheet does not say.

findings.title: the census missed five tables on one sheet, and it was the sheet the census read
findings.text:
`axis_census.json` was built to settle a prediction: *"n axes give exactly
C(n,2) 2-D tables, so counting the distinct tables actually drawn gives a lower
bound on the number of axes — including axes never named, only used."* It lists
21 tables across the corpus, of which **two** come from the cheat sheet, both
marked 1-D.

Segmenting that sheet by its own rules — labelling the white regions bounded by
its black borders — gives **25 framed panels**. Most are single glyphs. But five
carry a table the census does not have, and four of those are 2-D:

| panel, at (y, x, w, h) | what it crosses | in the census? |
|---|---|---|
| (754, 8, 438, 438) elements | direction x crossbar, with Angle/Curve/Line/Wave filling the middle row and column the element square has no cell for | no — F69 reads its CONTENT, no table recorded |
| (8, 1664, 430, 384) faculties | the same 3x3 again: Mind/Yin/Spirit, Reality/Aura/Destiny, Body/Yang/Soul | no — F47 reads the content |
| (408, 1664, 430, 384) market | direction (left / neutral / right) x an external domain: Sell/Exit/Credit, Bear/Stock/Bull, Cash/Entry/Buy | **no, not read at all** |
| (808, 1664, 430, 384) transformations | mark-identity x polarity: In/Contract/Rise, Flatten/Life/Warp, Out/Expand/Fall | **no, not read at all** |
| (4, 1204, 142, 1192) the Jump..Dive ladder | bar position on a TRIANGLE — 1-D | **no, not read at all** |

**The ladder is a third modulation strip, and it was measured.** Ten glyphs,
and their ink areas say what they are without any reading of the labels: the
bare triangles come in at 3119, 3121, 3122 and 3122 px — one glyph, four times —
the two bare Lines at 1547 px each, and the composites at 4038, 4038, 4497 and
4499. A triangle and a line laid side by side would be 4669; so 4499 is the two
just touching and 4038 is the bar 631 px deep into the triangle. One mark, one
line, and the line's position varied along the mark's own height, symmetric
about the centre of the column.

So the cheat sheet states the modulation axis **three** times, on three
carriers: along a vertical stem, along a horizontal stem, and along a triangle's
height. That is F137's point made a third time by the same sheet.

**Why this matters beyond the tally.** The census's prediction is a LOWER BOUND
computed from a count, and the count was short. Two of the five were read for
their content years before the census existed (F47, F69) and were never entered
as tables, which is the more interesting failure: the census was populated from
the findings rather than from the sheets, so anything read before the census was
invented could only enter it if someone went back. Two more had never been read
at all.

**What is actually new in the two unread panels.** The market 3x3 glosses
`○` **Exit** and `•` **Entry** — a fifth register for the Point/Circle pair,
after Instance/Object, Period/Cycle, Quanta/Parimeter and Contract/Expand. Five
named readings of one pair of marks, which is F134's argument arriving from a
direction F134 did not use.

And the transformation 3x3 is the corpus's richest operation vocabulary in one
place: **In/Out, Contract/Expand, Rise/Fall, Flatten/Warp**, four inverse pairs
around a centre named Life. Every one of those verbs is attached to a MARK, not
to a pair of figures. Contract glosses the Point, Expand the Circle, Flatten the
Line, Warp the Wave. That is the grammar F137 found and it holds here too: the
corpus is not short of operation words, it attaches them to marks. The absence
of a stated modulation OPERATION is a fact about that grammar, not about the
vocabulary — which makes it a weaker objection to
`modulation-is-a-second-operator-family` than the claim's success condition
assumed.

*One reading checked and dropped.* The `In` and `Out` glyphs look at a glance
like a triangle containing a smaller copy of itself, which would have been the
first instance of the `scale` axis the register records as NOTHING FOUND.
Measured, they are not: `In` and `Out` carry two interior holes of 289+22 and
262+29 px against the bare triangle's single hole of 598, which is a crossbar
splitting one interior in two. They are the Earth and Air glyphs. The `scale`
axis stays where it was.

findings.title: one figure, one Point, two ends, two meanings — and the redundant Point is nowhere
findings.text:
`a-redundant-point-changes-a-figure` asks for a sheet that draws a mark with and
without a Point that adds no ink, and reads them differently. The corpus draws
something very close and it is not that.

**To and From.** The cheat sheet has two adjacent cells holding the same arrow
and the same Point, differing only in where the Point sits:

| cell | distance from the Point to the arrow's HEAD | to its TAIL | gap to the stroke |
|---|---|---|---|
| `To` | **15.4 px** | 121.7 px | 7 px |
| `From` | 118.7 px | **14.9 px** | 3 px |

The Point is the same disc in both — 224 px, 17x17, 0.99 of a filled circle.
Eight to one on the distances; nothing marginal about it. One figure, one Point,
two attachment positions, two meanings.

**And the meaning is read off the figure, not looked up.** The arrow already
carries a direction. A Point at the head is what the arrow arrives at; a Point
at the tail is what it leaves. `To` and `From` follow from the arrow's own
geometry, with no convention table in between. That is the pattern
`attachment-point` needs and has not had: a case where WHERE a mark attaches
bears meaning, and the meaning is recoverable rather than assigned. It does not
derive apex-versus-base for the modality composites — a different figure, and
the arrow's asymmetry is doing the work here — but it moves that claim from "no
instance of the principle anywhere" to "the principle is instantiated, on a
simpler figure, and it is self-reading there".

**The negative, which is the answer to the claim that was asked.** In both cells
the Point is **separate ink**, clear of the stroke by 7 px and 3 px. It is not
redundant. Across the sheets read, the corpus never places a Point where a mark
already passes: `⊙` puts it at a circle's centre, which the circle does not go
through; `!` puts it below a stroke's end; `To`/`From` put it beyond an end.
Every attested Point adds ink.

So the claim's success condition cannot be met by this corpus, and that is now a
measured fact about the corpus rather than an unexamined possibility. Geometry
answered no (F126, separation falling as 1/N at a 32-fold range of sample
density); the corpus declines to ask the question at all.

findings.title: modulation is named, but as a property of two marks, never as an operation
findings.text:
`modulation-is-a-second-operator-family` asks for modulation stated as an
operation somewhere in the corpus. Searched, and it is not there. What IS there
is worth recording precisely, because the shape of the near-miss is the result.

**What the corpus says.** `3CoreSymbolMergers` partitions the six marks into
three pairs by how each pair answers to a parameter, in its own words:

| pair | the sheet's caption | the derived reading |
|---|---|---|
| Point & Shape | "are Geometrically Balanced" | rotation-invariant; orientation is free |
| Line & Wave | "change depending on Orientation" | order-2; orientation bears meaning |
| Angle & Curve | "**are Modulations**" | order-1; each carries a free internal parameter |

That is F6, and the word is right there. But read the grammar: the marks **are**
modulations. It is a predicate on a pair of marks, not an operation you apply to
one. Nothing on that sheet, or any other, says what modulating does.

**What the corpus draws instead is the axis, twice, with its continuum.** The
cheat sheet carries two stem-position strips, and they were counted off the ink
rather than the eye:

| strip | glyphs | composition | the continuum drawn beside it |
|---|---|---|---|
| vertical | 7 | 2 arrows (2502, 2503 px) + **5 crossbars at 2139 px each** | a greyscale ramp, `Light` to `Dark` |
| horizontal | 7 | 2 arrows (1423, 1455 px) + **5 crossbars at 1472 px each** | a spectrum, `Blue Shift` — `Aligned` — `Red Shift` |

The five crossbars in each strip are **identical in area to the pixel**. One
glyph, one parameter moved along its own extent, five times — which is what a
modulation is, drawn. And beside each the corpus draws the parameter as a
CONTINUUM: a brightness ramp on one axis, a Doppler spectrum on the other. A
table of named stops beside a ramp says the stops are samples.

`CrossSet` crosses the two axes into nine cells and names all of them, with the
vertical stops given as verbs — Ascend, Transcend, Descend, Subscend.

**A count to correct.** `position-on-a-line-is-rank` (F68) records its instance
as "7 levels + 2 open ends". Measured, each strip is **5 levels + 2 open ends**,
seven glyphs in total. The likely origin is counting the seven drawn glyphs as
levels and then adding the two arrows again. The derivation — order along a line
IS a total order — does not depend on the count, so this is a stray number in a
metadata field rather than a fault in the claim.

**So the search branch closes negative, and the derivation branch is what is
left.** The corpus states the modulation AXIS (five stops, two open ends, a
drawn continuum, on two orthogonal directions) and states that two of its marks
ARE modulations. It never states modulating as something done to a figure. That
is not evidence against the family; it is evidence that this corpus records
configurations and axes, and leaves operations to be read off them — which is
exactly how the placement operators were obtained (F104: read off the operator
definitions and confirmed by measuring what they emit, not read off a sheet).

findings.title: two sheets swap Amperage and Voltage, and they agree on everything the geometry fixes
findings.text:
Reading the Line & Wave panel for F134 turned up a flat contradiction with F70.

| artifact | Line `\|` | Wave `S` | the product |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PointShapeLineWaveAngleCurve` | **Amperage**, DC, Stable, Bond, Light | **Voltage**, AC, Vibe, Heat | `Current $ Energy` |
| `CheatSheet-ReferenceImage` | **Voltage**, Value | **Amperage**, Liquidity | `$ Energy / Power / Currency / Money` |

**Measured, not squinted at.** On the marks sheet the Line box spans rows
113-267 and the Wave box rows 283-437. `Amperage` sits at rows 137-155 and `DC`
at 162-180 — both inside the Line box's span and more than a hundred rows above
the Wave box. `AC` sits at 373-391 and `Voltage` at 403-426, inside the Wave
box's span. There is no alignment ambiguity: the nearest competing box is over
100 px away in both cases.

**Where they agree and where they do not is the interesting part.** Both sheets
agree that the two marks multiply to energy — `3CoreSymbolMergers` writes it out
as `Power(W) = Voltage(V) x Amperage(I)`, which is correct physics. Both agree
which mark is constant and which alternates. The marks sheet says so twice over,
in two registers at once: `Constant`/`Variable` in the computing column and
`DC`/`AC` in the electrical one, and DC-versus-AC is a fact about a signal's
time profile, which a straight stroke and a sine settle between them.

What they disagree about is Amperage versus Voltage — current against potential,
which is **not** a distinction the geometry makes. A Line is no more a current
than a potential.

So the disagreement falls exactly where nothing constrains it, and the agreement
falls exactly where the geometry does. That is the corpus's own stratification
(geometry sound, labels collide) with a mechanism attached rather than just a
tally: a label collides when it is not anchored, and the anchor is the figure.

**Disposition.** Not resolvable by preferring a sheet. `DC`/`AC` is anchored and
citable; `Amperage`/`Voltage` is a term with two referents and belongs in the
term ledger beside Yin/Yang (F30) and the two enharmonic errors.

findings.title: the corpus draws both hands of the Wave, and uses the mirror to reach a rotation it cannot perform
findings.text:
`mirroring-is-meaningful` asked for a sheet that draws both handednesses of one
figure and reads them differently. There is one, and what it does with them is
not what the claim expected.

**Base6_rotary draws the mirror, four times in eight.** The sheet is six marks
against eight directions (`↑ ↓ → ← ↗ ↖ ↙ ↘`). Each cell was matched against the
first cell of its own row under every rotation at 3-degree steps, once as drawn
and once mirrored:

| row | cells reachable ONLY with a reflection | the margin at those cells |
|---|---|---|
| **Wave** (the one chiral mark) | **4 of 8** — columns 2, 4, 6, 7 | 0.16→1.00, 0.16→0.84, 0.11→0.48, 0.12→0.52 |
| Line (control) | 0 of 8 | both routes identical to three decimals |
| Circle (control) | 0 of 8 | both routes 1.00 |
| Angle (control) | 1 of 8 | 0.88→1.00, the 3-degree sampling grid |
| Curve (control) | 1 of 8 | 0.88→1.00, the same |

The controls are the result as much as the Wave row is. Four achiral marks were
put through the identical instrument and the largest mirror advantage any of
them shows is **0.12**, which is the rotation grid and not chirality. The Wave's
four are **0.37 to 0.84**, three to seven times that.

**Why four, and why it had to be four.** `mark-chirality` (F102) records that a
sine is odd: a half-turn returns it. So the Wave's eight rotations collapse to
four distinct figures, and a row of eight direction-cells cannot be filled by
rotation alone. The sheet fills the other four with the mirror. The reflection
is not carrying a meaning of its own — it is standing in for a rotation the
mark's own symmetry makes unreachable.

**SymbolFolds uses reflection the other way, as a constructor.** Its left column
is headed `Reflection` and holds two cells, `Infinity` and `8 Fold`. Each cell
draws a Wave, its mirror, and the figure they close into. Measured:

| cell | how the lower wave relates to the upper | IoU | identity (the control) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Infinity | reflected in a **vertical** axis | 0.996 | 0.097 |
| 8 Fold | reflected in a **horizontal** axis | 0.999 | 0.097 |

The two waves carry 706 and 709 px — the same figure, three pixels apart. The
closed result carries 1270 px against 1415 for the two apart, so 145 px is the
overlap where they join. And the two cells are one construction turned a
quarter: every element matches its partner in the other cell at **0.994 to
0.999** after a 90-degree rotation, against 0.048 to 0.196 as drawn.

So the sheet names `Infinity` and `8 Fold` — and what separates them is a
rotation, not a handedness. Neither hand of the Wave is named anywhere on it.
They appear only as the two halves of one figure.

**The answer, and it is a no with a mechanism.** Reflection is attested twice
and neither use is a contrast. On the rotary sheet it substitutes for an
unreachable rotation; on SymbolFolds it is how a figure is closed. In neither
does one hand carry a meaning the other lacks — and the register's other half
of the evidence points the same way: 30 of 44 chiral orbits have an enantiomorph
the attested operators never build, which is what a notation looks like when
handedness is a by-product rather than a dimension.

findings.title: the domain is an axis, which is why "the" reading was the wrong question
findings.text:
`waveform-reading-is-intended` asked whether the marks are to be read as
waveforms, and its success condition asked for something that would establish the
waveform reading as **the** reading rather than one useful one. Nothing will,
because the corpus makes the domain a free coordinate and says so in its own
layout.

**Five named domains, one set of marks.** `ZodiacSignSymbols` is laid out as five
headed columns — **Chinese**, **Greek**, **Cromatic Tone**, **Arkana**, **Zodiac
Descriptions** — with the twelve marks drawn once among them. The acoustic
domain is present and named: `Cromatic Tone` assigns each sign a pitch, twelve
semitones for twelve signs. It is one column of five, set beside Chinese zodiac
animals and Greek myth, with nothing marking it as primary.

*What the sheet does not settle.* Whether the mark column has a header of its own
or falls under `Arkana` cannot be read off the alignment: the header rules sit
21, 62 and 62 px right of their columns' centres on the three columns where the
answer is unambiguous, and `Arkana`'s rule lands between the two candidate
columns. Nothing here rests on it.

**Three domains in one sheet's title.** `VideoGamesProgrammingReactRedux` names
its three registers in the title and gives each a column: `Triangle/Run`,
`Declare <> Generic Tag`, `∧ Act/Cardinal` on one row; `Circle/Observe`, `Call ()
Tuple Group`, `∪ Pass/Mutable` on the next. Three readings of one code, drawn
parallel and titled.

**Four domains per cell on the mark sheet.** `PointShapeLineWaveAngleCurve`
glosses each mark in several registers at once, and the registers are each
complete across all six marks:

| mark | computing | electrical / signal | temporal | physical |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Point | Init, Input, Instance | — | Period, Start, Time | Less, Dark |
| Circle | Cycle, Output, Object | — | Cycle, Continuity, Space | More, Lite |
| Line | Value, Number, Constant | Amperage, **DC**, Stable, Mean | — | Bond, Light |
| Wave | Range, String, Variable | Voltage, **AC**, Vibe | — | Heat, Fluid |
| Angle | Run, Set, Act | Peak, High | — | Push, Sharp, Rigid |
| Curve | Wait, Get, Pass | Base, Low | — | Pull, Smooth, Flexible |

The Line/Wave panel sets the two marks against each other as **DC against AC**,
with Amperage beside the Line and Voltage beside the Wave, and their composition
labelled `Current / Energy`. Constant against Variable is the same distinction
stated a second time in the computing register, in the same panel.

**The census already recorded this and nobody read it back.** `axis_census.json`
lists `domain` as an axis of three sheets — `PointShapeLineWaveAngleCurve` (F10),
`VideoGamesProgrammingReactRedux` (F18) and `ZodiacSignSymbols` (F39, as
"correspondence-system") — each annotated `external domain`. F139 later found a
fourth on the cheat sheet, which the census had also missed. An axis is listed
there only where a sheet **varies** it to distinguish cells. So the corpus varies
the domain, deliberately, on four tables, and three of them have been written
down since the census was built. A notation that varies the domain cannot have one.

**So the claim splits, and both halves are answerable.**

*Is the waveform reading attested?* Yes, and structurally rather than by
vocabulary count. Sol-Center labels its two lateral axes **Frequency** (the Wave
mark) and **Level** (the Line mark) — the two coordinates of a signal plot — and
names its centre cells **Harmony** and **Discord**. The mark sheet sets Line
against Wave as DC against AC. `ZodiacSignSymbols` carries a `Cromatic Tone`
column. Three sheets, three structural placements, none of them a stray word.

*Is it exact?* Yes, and that is F133: every drawn mark decomposes into waveshape,
phase and datum with no residue, 12/12 on three sheets, and the corpus performs
both of the operations that decomposition implies.

*Is it exclusive?* No, and it could not be. The same three features are the
modality and element of the astrological reading — F46 settled that the geometry
**is** the modality — so the two are not rival readings of the marks, they are
two names for one partition. Asking which is the real one asks which name for a
partition is the real name.

**What this leaves for `phase-is-harmony`.** That claim reads superposition on a
shared centre as Order/Harmony and displacement as Chaos/Discord, on the ground
that in-phase and out-of-phase **is** consonance. What it needs is not that the
waveform reading is exclusive but that it is attested and faithful, and both are
now measured. It needs one thing more, which the sheet supplies directly: at
those two cells Sol-Center writes **Harmony** and **Discord**, which are acoustic
words. The sheet selects the domain at the cell where the derivation runs. That
is a tighter and checkable premise, and it replaces an open one.

**And one thing this cuts against.** The acoustic domain is used two different
ways in two sheets, and smoothing that over would be dishonest. On Sol-Center it
is structural — it names the axes and the cells. On `ZodiacSignSymbols` it is a
correspondence column, sitting beside Chinese and Greek, which is the same
standing as a borrowed system. Those are not the same status, and the corpus
never reconciles them.

findings.title: the sign band is a waveform alphabet, and a third sheet reproduces it blind
findings.text:
F48 fixed the twelve sign glyphs from three features of the index — geometry
(`n mod 3`), direction (`n mod 2`), baseline (`n mod 4 ∈ {2,3}`) — and checked
them 12/12 against `Base12_signs` and the Sol-Center corners. It called the Base
12 strip "a waveform strip" in passing and did not draw the consequence. The
consequence is that those three features are not three arbitrary bits that happen
to fix a glyph. They are **the three parameters of a drawn waveform**: waveshape,
phase, and whether a zero line is drawn under it.

| F48's name | what it is, as a signal |
|---|---|
| geometry, `n mod 3` | waveshape — triangle `∧`, square `⊓`, sine `∩` |
| direction, `n mod 2` | phase — the positive half-cycle or the negative |
| baseline, `n mod 4 ∈ {2,3}` | the datum — whether a zero line is drawn |

**A third sheet, matched blind.** `ZodiacSignSymbols` carries its own column of
the twelve marks and F48 never used it. Each of its twelve glyphs was matched
against each of the twelve Sol-Center corner glyphs by intersection-over-union on
a 48x48 normalisation, assignment by nearest neighbour and not constrained to be
a permutation. It came out a permutation anyway, and it is F48's:

| sign | best match | IoU | runner-up | margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aries | Aries | 0.720 | 0.483 | +0.237 |
| Taurus | Taurus | 0.827 | 0.594 | +0.233 |
| Gemini | Gemini | 0.770 | 0.541 | +0.229 |
| Cancer | Cancer | 0.735 | 0.489 | +0.246 |
| Leo | Leo | 0.760 | 0.381 | +0.379 |
| Virgo | Virgo | 0.767 | 0.541 | +0.226 |
| Libra | Libra | 0.718 | 0.351 | +0.367 |
| Scorpio | Scorpio | 0.786 | 0.403 | +0.384 |
| Sagittarius | Sagittarius | 0.703 | 0.490 | +0.213 |
| Capricorn | Capricorn | 0.715 | 0.352 | +0.363 |
| Aquarius | Aquarius | 0.827 | 0.596 | +0.231 |
| Pisces | Pisces | 0.694 | 0.494 | +0.200 |

12 of 12. Diagonal mean 0.752 against an off-diagonal mean of 0.216, every margin
at least +0.200. Nothing in the test knows about calendar order, modality or
element — it compares ink. Three sheets now agree glyph for glyph.

**The datum bit reads straight off the width, with a 25-pixel gap.** On
`ZodiacSignSymbols` the twelve marks are either 33-35 px wide or 60 px wide, with
nothing between. Wide is the glyph plus two horizontal arms:

| width | signs | element |
|---|---|---|
| 33, 33, 34, 34, 34, 35 | Aries, Cancer, Leo, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Pisces | Fire and Water — all six, and only those |
| 60 x 6 | Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, Libra, Capricorn, Aquarius | Air and Earth — all six, and only those |

12/12, predicted before it was measured. A threshold anywhere in a 25-pixel band
gives the same answer, which is the standard F129 set after a three-pixel shift
nearly flipped a verdict.

**The corpus performs phase inversion as an operation.** Flip the Sol-Center
lower corner stacks vertically and match them against the upper ones:

| pair | IoU of the three correct matches | best wrong pairing |
|---|---|---|
| Fire → Water (no datum) | 0.840, 1.000, 0.856 | 0.547 |
| Air → Earth (on a datum) | 0.987, 0.981, 1.000 | 0.590 |

Leo's `⊓` flipped is Scorpio's `⊔` at 1.000 — pixel-identical, not similar. The
two lower figures at 0.84 and 0.86 are the unbarred triangle and sine, drawn a
little loosely; they still clear the best wrong pairing by half again.

**And datum-addition as an operation.** Every barred corner glyph contains its
unbarred partner at 0.93-1.00 containment, and what it adds is a constant:

| glyph | added ink | left arm rows | right arm rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| Air 1 | 79 px | 404-407 | 404-407 |
| Air 2 | 80 px | 435-438 | 435-438 |
| Air 3 | 82 px | 467-470 | 467-470 |
| Earth 1 | 72 px | 697-700 | 697-700 |
| Earth 2 | 80 px | 728-731 | 728-731 |
| Earth 3 | 78 px | 758-761 | 758-761 |

In all six the two arms occupy **exactly the same four rows** and the same
x-span. That is a datum line: one element, drawn identically under every shape,
four pixels thick, colinear both sides. Not a decoration that happens to be
horizontal.

**Why this is more than a relabelling of F48.** F48 showed the glyph is computed
from the index. This shows the feature set is closed under two operations the
corpus actually performs on the page — reflect the phase, add or remove the
datum — and that both operations are drawn, not inferred. A notation whose
alphabet is generated by waveshape × phase × datum, and which draws the
inversions and the datum-additions out in full, is a waveform notation in the
operational sense and not only the visual one.

**The instrument that failed first, and why.** The first attempt classified each
glyph by fitting square, triangle and arc models to its top-ink-per-column
profile. It returned margins of 1.02x to 1.88x — no separation worth anything —
and returned 0.00 residual for all three models on two glyphs. The zero was the
tell: for an unbarred `⊓` the topmost ink in every column is at the same height,
because the risers' tops are level with the bar. The profile cannot see a
vertical stroke at all, so a square pulse arrives as a flat line and every model
fits it perfectly. Measuring the relations between glyphs — reflection,
containment, width — needs no shape classifier and has no blind direction.

findings.title: the same figure tiles into the wave and closes into the polygon
findings.text:
The triple has three columns — polygons, wave forms, marks — and F129 measured
two of them. The third turns out to be the same figure doing a second job.

    family      tiled                closed                     free proportion
    triangle    Angle  -> triangle   Angle  -> equilateral       apex 60 degrees
                          wave                triangle, 0.045
    square      Staple -> square     Staple -> square, 0.0035    body = upright
                          wave
    sine        Wave   -> sine wave  Wave   -> a lens, not a     --
                                              circle

Tile a generator along its own axis and you get its wave. Close the same
generator — join its free ends with a chord — and you get its polygon. Two of
three families have one figure doing both.

**Each needs its free proportion set, and that is the interesting part.** A
chevron closes to an isoceles triangle at ANY apex angle and to an equilateral
one only at sixty degrees. A staple closes to a rectangle at any ratio and to a
square only when its body equals its uprights. The proportion is not a detail of
the drawing: it is what turns a member of the family into the regular figure the
corpus names.

    apex   aligned distance to an equilateral triangle
    50     0.151
    55     0.074
    58     0.037
    60     0.045
    65     0.113
    90     0.391

The minimum sits at 58 rather than exactly 60, which is instrument noise rather
than geometry — a closed 60-degree chevron IS equilateral by construction, and
58, 60 and 62 all land inside the 0.073 tolerance.

**The sine family is the exception, and consistently so.** The Wave closes to a
lens, not a circle: two arcs meeting at two cusps. And the Circle is already
closed, so there is nothing to close, and it has no waveform at all. This is the
third time that family has come out odd — F129 found its generator (Wave) and its
character member (Curve) differ, and that the Circle belongs to it by character
while generating nothing. The straight families have one figure per job; the
curved one does not.

**An orientation bug, and the control that would not have caught it.** The first
sweep used raw Hausdorff and put a closed 60-degree chevron 0.387 from an
equilateral triangle, with the minimum still at 60. The number was wrong and the
shape of the answer was right, which is the most dangerous combination: a sweep
that minimises in the geometrically correct place looks like a working
instrument. Raw Hausdorff is orientation sensitive and my triangle pointed up
while the reference pointed right — thirty degrees apart. Aligning over rotation
and reflection, which is the group `same_figure` already quotients by, takes
0.387 to 0.045.

What saved it was not a control but reading the number against what geometry
said it should be. A closed equilateral chevron is an equilateral triangle; if
the instrument says otherwise the instrument is wrong. That check is only
available where the answer is known in advance, which is the argument for
constructing cases whose answer is known even when the sweep is the point.

---

## What the marks are a notation FOR

findings.title: insert commutes with neither family, so there are three
findings.text:
The critique asked for four things: a line that becomes a wave, a wave that
becomes a line, and a line with something in its middle, at its side, or at its
edge.

**The first two are one figure, and they were already drawable.** A Wave whose
amplitude is tapered to zero at one end is straight there and varying at the
other; read it left to right and a line becomes a wave, read it the other way
and a wave becomes a line. What it is NOT is modulation of a Line. Modulation
re-reads an existing variation and scales it, and a Line has none — every member
of that family is the identity on a flat profile, which `symbol_waveform` states
in as many words and which is a control in this module: modulating a Line at
three times amplitude returns the Line.

So "make this Line wavy" is not a modulation. It adds a waveform where there was
none, which is placing something rather than varying what is there.

**The third is new, and it is a third family.** `insert(host, guest, at, span)`
replaces a stretch of the host with the guest, scaled and rotated so the guest's
own two ends land exactly on the host's cut points. That last step is what makes
the result one figure: splice without it and you have a mark abutting a mark,
which is `concatenate` and already exists.

Then the question is which family it is in, and the answer is measured rather
than named:

    commutes with PLACEMENT     0 of 125 pairs
    commutes with MODULATION    0 of  78 eligible hosts
                                (of 186 considered; 108 have no profile at all)

Neither, on samples big enough to mean it. Placement puts B somewhere relative
to A; modulation varies a parameter along A's own extent; `insert` does both at
once and is interchangeable with neither.

**The restriction is what makes the modulation number worth reading.** F122
nearly reported a right answer for the wrong reason: its first commutativity run
compared modulated against unmodulated figures in 24 of 45 cases, because those
composites admit no chart and `modulate` is the identity on them. Here the same
trap is bigger — 108 of 186 candidate hosts have no profile — and excluding them
is the difference between 0 of 78 and a meaningless 0 of 186.

**The six marks were also too few.** The first run tested modulation on marks
alone and got 0 of 3, because only Angle, Curve and Wave have a profile at all.
Nought of three is not evidence of anything. Composites have profiles too, so
the population the question is about is the marks and the composites together,
and that is 78.

**What this does to the register.** `modulation-is-a-second-operator-family` has
sat undetermined with the success condition "find modulation stated as an
operation anywhere in the corpus, or derive the family boundary". This does not
find it stated. It does bear on the boundary from an unexpected side: there is at
least one operation that is in neither family, so the boundary is not a
partition of two — and an operator set described as placement-only is missing
more than one thing.

Whether the CORPUS has `insert` is a separate question and this does not answer
it. A figure with something spliced into its middle is drawn all over the source
sheets — a stem with a bar across it, a line with a loop in it — but drawn is not
the same as stated as an operation, which is the distinction the whole register
rests on. So the operator is recorded as measured, and its attestation is not.

findings.title: the Angle's own incidence is unreachable, which is what primitive should mean
findings.text:
The corpus gives Point and Line more semantic weight than any of the other four.
Point is `Existence` at pole Core (S+), dependency rank 0, and "universal
presupposition" — every other primitive requires Points. Line is `Relation` at
pole Order (M+), rank 1, and "introduces directionality, the first asymmetry in
the system". It states compositions too: two Points joined by a Line is
predication, a Point inside an enclosure is containment, reflection of a mark
through a Point is negation.

So these two pairs are where the notation's grammar starts, and nothing here had
mapped them.

**A configuration is not a position.** A position is a continuum and there is
nothing to enumerate. What is finite is the INCIDENCE: which parts of the two
figures meet. A Line has exactly two parts, its ends and its interior, so the
list is short and it is exhaustive — endpoints meet, an endpoint lands on an
interior, the interiors cross, or nothing touches. Crossed with the angle, which
has two distinguished values and a continuum otherwise, that is the grid.

**Point against a Line — every class reachable, half the figures not.**

    configuration                              ink   sym  mirror  class  figure
    at an endpoint                              no    C2       1  yes    yes
    at the midpoint                             no    C2       1  yes    yes
    elsewhere on the line                       no    C2       1  yes    yes
    off it, on the perpendicular bisector      yes    C1       0  yes    no
    off it, on its own extension               yes    C1       1  yes    no
    off it, anywhere else                      yes    C1       0  yes    no

The three on-the-line positions add no ink, which is F126 arriving again from a
different direction: a Point where the Line already passes makes the same
figure, and the three positions are one figure between them.

The three off-line positions are one incidence CLASS and three different
FIGURES — they differ in the symmetry the pair keeps, 0 mirrors on the generic
position and 1 on the Line's own extension. The operator set reaches the class
and none of the three figures, because `superpose_displaced` offsets by a fixed
amount and lands nowhere in particular. Reporting only the class would have said
this space is covered when it is not, which is why both granularities are on the
sheet.

**Line against a Line — six of eleven classes unreachable.**

    interiors cross, perpendicular             reached   cross(Line,Line)
    interiors cross, oblique                   —
    endpoints meet, perpendicular              —
    endpoints meet, oblique                    —
    endpoints meet, collinear                  reached   concatenate(Line,Line)
    endpoint on interior, perpendicular        —
    endpoint on interior, oblique              —
    no shared point, collinear or parallel     reached   superpose_displaced
    no shared point, oblique                   —
    coincident                                 reached   reflect_pair, superpose_concentric

The unreachable six are not scattered. **Every oblique cell is unreachable**,
because the attested operators are angle-poor: `cross` is fixed at a right angle
and everything else is collinear. That is the same gap `rotation-parameter-is-free`
describes, seen from the configuration side rather than the rotation side.

**And endpoints meeting at an angle is unreachable, which is the interesting
one.** That is the Angle mark's own incidence — two strokes sharing one end and
diverging. No composition of two Lines under the attested operators produces it.
Which is what it should mean for the Angle to be a primitive rather than a
composite: not that nobody has composed it, but that the operator set cannot.

That bears on `six-marks-are-complete` from a new side. F91 established the marks
are complete with respect to symmetry ORDER, and F123 that completeness of order
is not completeness of figure. This adds that the Angle is not merely
conveniently primitive: its defining incidence is outside the reach of
composition on Lines.

**Two instruments failed, and the same control caught both.** The first
`adds_ink` took two finished figures and re-normalised them at each "density",
which changes nothing — so the ratio was 1.000 for every configuration and every
one read as adding ink. A Point sitting on a Line is the one case whose answer is
known before any instrument runs, and it is the control that fired. The fix was
to take a builder rather than arrays, so the sampling actually varies.

The second was subtler and would have shipped a wrong negative.
`reached_by` compared FIGURES, and an incidence class has continuous parameters
inside it — the gap between two collinear Lines, the angle between two oblique
ones. So it reported `superpose_displaced(Line,Line)` as reaching nothing, when
what it reaches is two collinear Lines with a gap: the right class, a different
gap. Classifying the operator's own emitted strokes by incidence is the fix, and
it is only possible because `strokes` hands back the parts rather than the
flattened figure — the thing F101 added for a different reason entirely.

**A name collision, caught by looking.** The first version wrote
`charts/incidence.svg`, which `codex_graphs` already writes for a different
chart about which marks are load-bearing across the orbits. It overwrote it. The
build regenerates that file so nothing was lost, but nothing in the build would
have told me either — a generator has to check the name it is taking.

findings.title: three wave families, and two questions the triple was answering at once
findings.text:
A reading of the corpus pairs three polygons, three wave forms and three marks:
triangles with triangle waves and **angles**, squares with square waves and
**lines**, circles with sine waves and **curves**. The pairing is real. What was
not clear — and what the first version of this finding got wrong — is that
**two different correspondences are involved**, and the triple states one of
them while the drawn sources state the other.

**The generative reading: which mark tiles into which wave.** Lay copies of a
mark end to end along its own axis and ask what the run is:

    tiled mark             triangle   square     sine    reading
    Angle,  repeated          0.002    0.565    0.147    IS the triangle wave
    Staple, alternating       0.556    0.005    0.450    IS the square wave
    Wave,   repeated          0.147    0.461    0.002    IS the sine wave
    Curve,  either            0.272    0.699    0.381    none of the three
    Line,   either              flat, no waveform at all
    Circle, either              flat, no waveform at all

Trimmed RMS at unit amplitude over one detected period, phase and polarity free.
The floor is 0.02 — the largest disagreement between an ideal wave and the same
wave at another frequency, over two to six periods — and the closest two ideals
are 0.147 apart. Seven times the floor, so the three readings sit an order of
magnitude inside it.

Generatively, then: **Angle, Staple, Wave**. The Line tiles to a longer Line.

**The characterological reading: which figure shares the wave's structure.**
A different question, and it has a different answer. Curvature class separates
the smooth family; what separates the other two is the direction its straight
runs take:

    figure           curvature   run directions            family
    Angle             singular   45 and 135                triangle
    triangle wave     singular   63 and 116                triangle
    Line              singular   0                         square
    Staple            singular   0 and 90                  square
    square wave       singular   0 and 90                  square
    Curve, Wave         smooth   a continuum               sine
    sine wave           smooth   a continuum               sine

A figure whose every run is axis-parallel or axis-perpendicular keeps its angles
under any axis-aligned stretch, because such a stretch maps 0 to 0 and 90 to 90.
A figure with runs at any other angle does not. So the square family is the
axis-aligned one, and **the Line is in it** — along with the Staple and the
square wave itself.

Characterologically, then: **Angle, Line, Staple, Curve, Wave** — and the
corpus's triple, Line/Angle/Curve, is correct.

**So the two sources are answering different questions, and both are right.**
`UniversalSymbology-Base3_modality.png`, the corpus's own modality sheet, draws
Fixed as a **staple** — a body with an upright at each end — with Cardinal a
chevron and Mutable an arch. That is the generative member.
`Line_Universal_Language` states "Modality Fixed (square wave)" and gives the
triple as Line/Angle/Curve. That is the characterological member. The drawing is
generatively correct; the prose is characterologically correct; neither is a
mistake.

**What this corrects is my own first pass at it.** That version said the corpus
"named the wrong mark" in two of three rows, on the strength of the generative
measurement alone. It was the measurement that was narrow, not the corpus: I had
one relation, found the corpus asserting a different one, and read the
disagreement as an error. The rule this breaks is the one this project exists
for — a measurement licenses a claim about what it measured, and nothing wider.

The residue that is a genuine gap: the **Mutable row has no generative member
among the six**. The arch tiles to a cusped run, 0.272 from a sine, because two
arcs meet with vertical tangents. The Wave generates the sine, and the Wave is
two Curves. So Fixed and Mutable are both rows where the generative member is a
COMPOUND of the characterological one — Staple is Line plus two uprights, Wave
is two Curves — and only Cardinal has one figure doing both jobs. That is a
pattern worth stating, and it was invisible while the two readings were treated
as one.

    family      belongs to it (character)   generates it (tiling)
    triangle    Angle                       Angle
    square      Line, Staple                Staple = Line + two uprights
    sine        Curve, Wave                 Wave = two Curves

**Whether the Staple and the Line are interchangeable where modality is drawn**
now has an answer with a shape. They are not interchangeable, and they are not
alternatives either: the Line is what the Fixed modality IS, and the Staple is
what it takes to make the Fixed modality's wave. A sheet drawing modality should
draw the Staple, which is what the corpus's sheet does.

**Four instruments failed before the generative one, all in the same way.**
Hausdorff on normalised point sets cannot see a waveform: scaling a long run to
unit RADIUS flattens its amplitude to nothing, so every wave came out
equidistant from every other — the controls sat 0.36 apart when they should have
been at opposite ends of the scale, and every candidate read "nearest sine"
because sine was merely the least flattened. A waveform is a function and has to
be compared as one. Phase is not optional either: the first phase-blind attempt
put the Angle 0.69 from a triangle wave purely because the run began on the
opposite half of the cycle.

The last generative correction is worth keeping because tuning would have hidden
it. With an exact match in hand the staple still read 0.099, five times the
floor, and sweeping its proportions across a 32-fold range did not move the
number by a thousandth. The residual was not in the shape: three samples out of
256, sitting exactly at the two transitions and the wrap. A vertical stroke
lives at one value of x, so the bin it lands in is not a sample of y(x) — it is
the average of a jump. Discarding the extreme 2% removes those bins and leaves
the gap between different waves intact, which is the control that matters,
because a trim aggressive enough to fix a match is also aggressive enough to
manufacture one.

**Three more instruments failed on the characterological side**, and the third
is the same lesson a third time. Parallel share — how much of the figure runs
along the axis — looked like the discriminator and is not: a square wave's
vertical transitions are real arc length, so the measure moves with the aspect
ratio and put the square wave in the triangle family. Mean corner turn failed
next, not because the angle moves but because the COUNT does: the detector found
ten corners in a drawn square wave at one stretch and fourteen at another. Run
direction needs neither, and is the property the difference actually is.

**What this does to the signs.** The twelve were read as waveforms by F117 and
F120, and this says what kind: the marks a sign is built from belong to a wave
family by character and generate one by tiling, and the two need not be the same
mark. The three wave families are a property of the ALPHABET rather than of the
twelve, and the waveform reading does not need the zodiac to stand up.


#### Correction (2026-09-13): the closure family is the result, and the Wave is not in it

Operator objection, and it is right: *the three wave forms are modalities that
impact a wave, so you cannot use a wave as a modality modifier.* The finding
above put the **Wave** in the modality triple. A wave cannot modulate itself.

The objection sends you back to what the corpus said before this finding
"corrected" it — circles with **curves** — and that reading now measures.

    completion                           agreement
    Angle closed at 60 degrees   -> equilateral triangle   0.0453
    Staple closed, body=upright  -> square                 0.0035
    Curve + its own half-turn    -> circle                 0.0035
    Wave closed by a chord       -> a lens, 0.9949 from a circle

    controls: circle vs circle 0.0000 · circle vs square 0.2926
              ONE Curve vs circle 0.9602 · Curve closed by a chord 0.5892

Least Hausdorff over rotation and reflection. Two Curves reach the circle at the
same agreement the Staple reaches the square. Nobody had tested it: `polygon_of`
asked the **Wave** to close the sine family, got a lens, and recorded the family
as "the exception" rather than asking whether the wrong figure was being asked.

So the three modality marks are **Angle, Staple and Curve**, completing to
**triangle, square and circle** — three marks, three regular figures, one
relation. The Wave is the carrier a modality modulates.

**And the tiling table above is weaker than it looks.** `Wave` is drawn as
`sin(pi*x)`, `Angle` as `1-|x|`, and the Staple as a literal square half period.
So "tiling the Wave gives a sine" measures whether tiling a sine gives a sine,
and 0.002 is a property of the drawing, not a discovery. The informative rows
are the negative ones — the Curve does **not** tile to a sine (0.272), the Line
tiles to a longer Line — and those stand.

Registered as `curve-pair-is-the-circle`, measured. The generative/
characterological distinction pushed to the wiki this morning is not wrong, but
it is the weaker of the two readings and the wiki now says so.

findings.title: the sections were surfaced into a variable something else had taken
findings.text:
Every sheet page builds its sections into a list called `cols`: how the sheet
was made, its identity, the claims it asserts, what would settle the open ones.
When the cell table arrived with S8, it needed its own column names and wrote
`cols = [k for k, _l in keys][:6]` — same function, same name, forty lines later.

So `<div class="cols">` rendered `grouprealisedmarksorder` and every section
disappeared from all 120 sheet pages. Every claim a sheet asserts, every open
question it carries, and the whole "how this sheet was made" block had been
absent since S8 shipped.

**The build said so and it read as success.** `codex_sheet.py` prints *"10 claims
and 7 open questions surfaced from the twins"* on every run, and that sentence
was true throughout. They were surfaced. Into a variable something else had
taken. A progress message that reports work done at the point the work is
computed, rather than at the point it reaches the output, cannot tell those two
states apart — and this one had been reporting success at the earlier point for
as long as the bug existed.

Nothing else could catch it either. The audit checks that pages have a top bar,
resolvable links, no stray palettes, no tallies in the site's voice — all of
which remained true of a page with its sections silently emptied. A page missing
content it never advertised is indistinguishable, to every check we had, from a
page that had nothing to say.

It surfaced only because a new section was added and did not appear, which made
the absence visible at last. That is the ordinary way this class of defect gets
found: not by looking for it, but by adding something adjacent and noticing that
the new thing is missing too.

**What was behind the sections, once they were visible again.** The twins carry
structured results — `realised` and `empty` on the subgroup lattice,
`per_operator` on commutativity, `nearest_to_named` on the distance chart, `rows`
on capacity — and the page renderer skipped every dict and list outright. So the
richest measured content on each chart was computed, written to the JSON,
shipped beside the page, and never shown. A reader got a drawing and one line of
prose, and had to open the twin to see the finding the chart exists to report.

Rendering it by the data's own shape rather than a template means no two charts
get the same second reading, because no two twins carry the same keys. That is
the only version of "say it another way" that does not become the same way
twice.

findings.title: the build read a file it never wrote, and shipped two partitions at once
findings.text:
F126 moved the orbit count from 95 to 93. The build went green, the audit passed
all eight checks, and the artifact was deployed. It was internally inconsistent,
and the way it was inconsistent is worth more than the correction.

    data/derivation/combination_space.json   95 orbits   (dated the previous day)
    data/derivation/orbit_features.json      93 orbits   (written by this build)

`codex_search.py` calls `enumerate_space()` and recomputes the partition, so it
said 93. Five other stages — `codex_distance`, `codex_graphs`, `codex_matrix`,
`codex_export` and `codex_primer` — read `combination_space.json` instead. That
file is written by `symbol_combinations.py --enumerate`, **which was not one of
the build's stages**. It had been produced by running the module by hand, and
everything downstream had been reading that hand-made file ever since.

So the shipped site carried a 93-orbit feature table beside a 95-orbit distance
matrix, a 95-row incidence chart, and a 95-point meaning-space embedding. Every
count downstream was arithmetic over two different worlds.

**Nothing caught it.** Not the eight audit checks, which read the built HTML and
have no opinion about whether two derivation files agree. Not the distance
cache's own staleness test, which compares the cached orbit list against
`representatives(S, space)` — computed from the same stale `space`, so it agreed
with itself perfectly and returned in half a second. A cache that validates
against its own stale input is not a cache with a staleness check; it is two
copies of the same mistake.

**The fix is that the build derives what it reads.** `symbol_combinations.py
--enumerate` is now the first stage, before anything that consumes its output.
Proof it was the disease and not a guess: with the space regenerated,
`codex_distance` went from 0.5s to 218.9s — the cache invalidated on its own
once it was given a real input to compare against.

A guard sits in `codex_export` as well, because making a thing impossible is
better than remembering it: if the two derived files ever disagree about the
orbit count, the build stops and says which stage ran against stale geometry. It
was tested the only way a guard is worth testing — against the live mismatch,
which it caught before being fixed.

**The general shape of this.** A pipeline that reads a derived artifact it does
not produce has a hidden manual step, and the step is invisible precisely
because it usually does not matter. It matters on exactly the builds where the
derivation moved — which is to say, on every build that was worth checking. This
is F119's lesson relocated from data to process: there, a meaning was attached to
a slot and moved when the slot did; here, a whole partition was attached to a
file nobody regenerated, and stayed put when the geometry moved underneath it.

The deploy that shipped the inconsistency stood for about forty minutes.

findings.title: a Point was making figures angular, and two orbits were never real
findings.text:
`a-redundant-point-changes-a-figure` (F109) had been left as a semantic question
with a geometric preamble: *"the figures are 0.008 to 0.031 apart (Line, Wave,
Circle) against a same-figure threshold of 0.073, so geometry says
near-identical and the corpus says nothing."* Re-measuring after F118 raised the
sampling showed the preamble was wrong in a way that mattered.

**The separation is the sampling, and nothing else.** Measuring a mark against
the same mark carrying a Point where it already passes, across a 32-fold range
of sample density:

    density        120      240      480      960     1920     3840   ratio
    Line       0.01639  0.00826  0.00415  0.00208  0.00104  0.00052   0.032
    Wave       0.01639  0.00826  0.00415  0.00208  0.00104  0.00052   0.032
    Circle     0.02618  0.01309  0.00654  0.00327  0.00164  0.00082   0.031
    Angle      0.30474  0.31046  0.31334  0.31478  0.31550  0.31587   1.036
    Curve      0.14470  0.15039  0.15342  0.15492  0.15568  0.15606   1.078

A 32× increase in density. Pure discretisation would give 1/32 = 0.031; a real
difference would give 1.000. Line, Wave and Circle give 0.032, 0.032 and 0.031 —
the difference **is** the sample spacing, and Circle's separation equals its own
noise floor at every density to four figures. Angle and Curve converge to a
constant, because there the Point lands where the mark does not pass and is not
redundant at all. So "redundant" is not a manner of speaking: it separates the
five cases exactly, and the two that were never redundant were never the
question.

**But the partition had them in different orbits anyway, and the reason was a
defect.** A Point is one sample. `curvature_of_strokes` returned "singular" for
any stroke shorter than nine samples, so a Point anywhere in a figure forced the
whole figure to read as angular:

    mark      alone      with a Point
    Curve     smooth     singular
    Wave      smooth     singular
    Circle    smooth     singular

The bucket key is (symmetry order, curvature class), so a figure and its
point-carrying twin landed in different buckets and `same_figure` was **never
asked** — the 0.004 separation, far inside the 0.073 tolerance, never got a
hearing. Line escaped only because a Line is singular already.

A Point has no extent and therefore no tangent. It is not a corner, and calling
it one asserts a measurement that was not made. A stroke with no extent now
contributes no curvature instead of overriding every other stroke's. A lone
Point is still singular — zero curvature is the singular pole of F88's axis —
and Point-next-to-Angle is still singular, because that corner is real.

**The count moves from 95 to 93.** The register had predicted this number and
rejected the route to it: *"Excluding the Point from concatenate would drop the
count to 93, but it would also remove concatenate(Point,Angle) and
(Point,Curve), which measure 0.31 and 0.15 from their bare marks and ARE
distinct figures — so the cheap fix buys consistency by discarding real cells."*
That was right about the cheap fix and right about the number. Correcting the
measurement reaches 93 without discarding anything: the two genuinely distinct
cells survive as their own orbits, and only the three that were never distinct
merge.

**Sun-in-Circle is the check that matters.** A Point at the CENTRE of a Circle is
a real corpus symbol, and it must not merge with a bare Circle. It does not: it
measures 0.9958 from one, because the centre is a radius away from the nearest
ink. Point-on-the-circle measures 0.0065 and merges. The merge is driven by where
the Point actually is, which is the only thing that should drive it.

All four recorded meanings re-attach, via the same expressions they always used —
they are matched by FIGURE and not by orbit id, which is the arrangement F119
argued for and the reason a count could move today without a meaning moving with
it.
