**What is left of the claim is the part that was always the hard part.** Geometry
now says these are the same figure, not nearly the same. Whether the corpus reads
a mark and that mark carrying a redundant point as different symbols is still
unanswered, and still needs a sheet that draws both. The difference is that the
geometric preamble no longer hedges: if the corpus does distinguish them, it
distinguishes them by something that is not in the figure.

findings.title: twelve is a partition of the icosahedron, not a symmetry of it
findings.text:
S10 needed meaning-space coordinates, and the corpus supplies a candidate: the
Platonic base correspondence, in which Base 12 is the icosahedral tier and the
twelve signs are the icosahedron's vertices. `Icosahedral_Symbolic_Geometry_System`
states it as **"12 vertices = 4 elements × 3 modalities (V₄ × C₃)"**. This codex
states its own version: a sign is read off `(n mod 3, n mod 4)`, which by CRT is
the isomorphism `Z/12 ≅ Z/3 × Z/4`.

Both are direct products of abelian groups of order 12. They are not the same
group — `V₄ × C₃` has no element of order 4, `C₃ × C₄ ≅ C₁₂` has one — so at
most one of them can be the icosahedron's. The answer is neither.

**Computed from the solid.** Build the twelve vertices, find every rotation
carrying the set to itself, and enumerate the order-12 subgroups:

    rotation group order         60
    element orders               {1:1, 2:15, 3:20, 5:24}
    an element of order 12?      NO
    an element of order 4?       NO
    subgroups of order 12        5
    abelian ones acting freely   0
    all five are                 A4 = V4 ⋊ C3, non-abelian, acting freely

A claim of the form "the twelve are A × B" needs a group of order 12 acting
freely on twelve vertices — that is what labels them. Five such subgroups exist
and every one is A₄, the **semidirect** product. `V₄ × C₃` is abelian and is not
a subgroup of the icosahedral rotation group at all. `C₁₂` is worse off still:
the group contains no element of order 4 or 12, so the cyclic structure has
nowhere to live.

**What the corpus gets right is the partition.** Three orthogonal golden
rectangles partition the vertices four-and-four-and-four. Four pairwise-disjoint
faces partition them three-and-three-and-three-and-three. Ten such face-sets
exist, and exactly **two** of them meet each rectangle exactly once — a genuine
4 × 3 grid:

                   rect0  rect1  rect2
      element 0:     4      0      2
      element 1:     7      1      3
      element 2:     5     11      8
      element 3:     6     10      9

So "4 elements × 3 modalities" is a real structure on the icosahedron. It is a
**partition**, and the × is a grid rather than a group product. The parenthetical
`(V₄ × C₃)` is the part that does not hold, and dropping it costs the claim
nothing it was actually using.

**The consequence is sharper than the correction.** The zodiac's cyclic order is
genuinely C₁₂ — twelve signs succeed one another around the ecliptic, and that
cycle is what `(n mod 3, n mod 4)` indexes. **That cycle is not a rotation of the
icosahedron.** There is no rotation of the solid sending each vertex to the
next sign, because there is no rotation of order 12. Twelve signs and twelve
vertices agree in count and in partition, and disagree in the one structure the
sign rule depends on.

This is F91's lesson arriving from a new direction. F91 narrowed
`six-marks-are-complete` on exactly this ground: matching an ORDER is weaker than
being the same figure. Here, matching a COUNT is weaker than carrying the same
group — and a count match is the weakest correspondence there is. Two twelves are
not one twelve.

**What this changes for S10.** The 3D view is built on both, drawn apart. The
icosahedron carries the partition — three rectangles, four triples, twenty faces,
six axes — because that much is real. The cyclic sign order is drawn as a path
THROUGH the vertices rather than as a symmetry OF them, because that is what it
is. And the measured embedding (classical MDS on the orbit distance matrix) is a
separate object with its own stress figure, because a position that comes from
measured distances and a position that comes from an assigned solid are different
kinds of thing and merging them would hide which is which.

Worth stating plainly, since the corpus is the thing being read here: the wiki's
account of the icosahedral tier is substantially right. Twelve vertices, thirty
edges, twenty faces, six five-fold axes, ten three-fold axes, three golden
rectangles, and a 4 × 3 structure over them — all correct. One parenthesis
naming a group is wrong, and it is wrong in the direction of tidiness: a direct
product is the neater thing to write, and the icosahedron does not do neat.

findings.title: the skeleton was the instrument's symmetry, not the letter's
findings.text:
`cross-script-comparison-needs-skeletons` (F99) named its fix precisely:
*"Skeletonise — extract the medial axis or centreline of each letterform,
reducing a filled region to the stroke it represents, then measure THAT on the
same axes."* The claim was right that the filled-region reading proved nothing.
It was wrong that skeletonisation is one operation, and wrong about what the
answer would be.

**The first skeletoniser was wrong and looked right.** Rasterise the outline,
thin it to one pixel with Zhang-Suen, measure the result. It passed four
controls — a filled ring, bar, plus and L all gave the centreline they should.
Then controls of known rotational order were added: annuli whose radius is
modulated k times, so C_k holds by construction.

    rosette     C2   C3   C5   C6   C8
    raster       1    1    1    1    1
    medial       2    3    5    6    8

**A square pixel grid has C4 symmetry, and the skeleton inherits it.** C2 and C4
came through perfectly because they are the lattice's own subgroups; every order
the lattice cannot express collapsed to C1. The instrument was imprinting its
symmetry on the very axis being measured — and the reading it produced, C1 for
almost everything, is exactly the reading F99 recorded from the filled outlines.
Two different artifacts, the same wrong answer, which is the kind of agreement
that feels like confirmation and is not.

**The construction that works has no grid in it.** The medial axis is the locus
of centres of maximal inscribed discs; each such centre is equidistant from two
or more boundary points, so it lies on the Voronoi diagram of the boundary. Take
that diagram, keep the vertices inside the region, drop the short spurs that
finite sampling adds. Nothing is quantised, so there is no lattice to borrow
from. All ten controls pass, and the pruning is not a dial — the controls agree
at 0.0 and 0.2, and above about 0.35 pruning starts removing real axis and a
ring stops reading as continuous. That is a bound, and it is reported rather than
tuned.

**Symmetry order now transfers. Curvature class does not, and not for want of
tuning.** Curvature is defined for a stroke, and the Voronoi vertices arrive
unordered — shuffling a smooth mark's points makes `curvature_class` call it
singular, so the first letterform run reading "singular" 64 times out of 64 was
measuring the vertex ordering. Walking the axis graph into ordered runs fixes
that much. What it cannot fix is this:

    a filled bar -- a thick straight line -- has a medial axis of FIVE runs

The medial axis of a rectangle is a segment plus four diagonal branches out to
the corners. They are real geometry, not sampling noise, and the stroke that
drew the rectangle never had them. **Skeletonisation does not invert
thickening.** A figure whose stroke was smooth reads singular because the
branches corner where the region's corners are. No threshold fixes this, because
there is nothing wrong to threshold away.

So F99's success condition is half achievable. Symmetry order survives
skeletonisation because the branches share the figure's symmetry. Curvature
class does not, because the branches are exactly where curvature is read.

**And the expected answer was wrong.** F99 diagnosed its failure by noting that
Latin O "should sit near (C-inf, smooth)" and measured (C1, singular). On the
medial axis, Latin O in DejaVu Sans measures **C2, smooth**, with an axis whose
radius runs 584 to 693 — an aspect ratio of 1.19.

A typographic O is not a circle. It is an ellipse, and an ellipse is C2. The
original reading was wrong for the reason F99 gave, and the expectation against
which it was judged was also wrong. Getting the instrument right produced an
answer that matches neither — which is the ordinary case when a measurement
starts working, and the reason the expected value should never be the test.

Across 64 letterforms in twelve scripts, the medial axis gives 60 at C1 and 4 at
C2. That is a real distribution now rather than a collapsed one, and it is
available for script-to-script comparison. It still does not license the
UL-to-script comparison: `ul-is-not-phonetic` (F100) blocks that independently,
and it is the harder of the two blocks. This lifts the instrument, not the
category error.

findings.title: the teardrop is not reachable, and the reason is a hole at exactly one corner
findings.text:
`teardrop-reachability` (F94) had sat undetermined with an unusually precise
success condition: *"Enumerate close() composed with binary operators. This is a
scope gap in the search, not evidence of unreachability."* The original depth-3
enumeration had been restricted to rotational families, so the one composition
most likely to produce a closed figure was never tried. The claim was honest
about being a gap rather than a result, and the gap is now closed.

**The enumeration.** 23,424 `close(...)` expressions: all five attested binary
operators, both `reflect_pair` and `close` as unary steps, sub-expressions
nesting one deep on either side of a binary operator, and `close` permitted at
any position. 20,142 of them are closed and enclose area. `tools/symbol_closure.py`
rebuilds the whole thing.

**The result is negative, and the negative is the interesting part.** No figure
in the space is a teardrop. Nearest approach is 0.326 Hausdorff, against a
same-figure tolerance of 0.073 — about four and a half times too far to be a
near miss. But the distribution of corner counts says something stronger than
"this one figure is absent":

    0 corners:  427        1 corner:  none        2 corners:  630
    3:  2864     4:  3567     5:  3539     6:  3281     7:  2465   ...

**Exactly one corner never occurs.** Not rarely — never. The teardrop is absent
because an entire class is absent, and it is the class the teardrop belongs to.

**Why.** `close()` joins the figure's two free ends with a straight chord. A
chord that arrives along the tangent adds no corner; one that arrives across it
adds exactly one. To land on one corner in total you need the chord tangent at
exactly one of the two ends. Measuring the chord against the tangent at both
ends across the binary composites, that almost never happens: the marks are
built symmetrically about their own axes, so a chord that meets one end
obliquely meets the other obliquely too. The ends come in pairs, so the corners
do. Zero or two, never one.

So the teardrop needs a closing stroke that is tangent at one end and not the
other — which a straight chord between two symmetric ends cannot be. Allowing
`close` to join with an *arc* instead does produce single-cornered convex
figures (eleven of them), which confirms the diagnosis: **the missing capability
is a curved join, not a missing mark.** Those eleven still sit 0.52 from the
reference teardrop, so a curved join is necessary and not yet sufficient.

**What this does to the register.** `teardrop-reachability` moves from
`undetermined` to `derived_given` — the teardrop is not reachable, GIVEN that
`close` joins with a straight chord and that composition nests one deep. Both
conditions are recorded, because both are real limits rather than throat-clearing:
a `close` that curved would change the answer, and depth is bounded by
enumeration cost, not by principle.

It also sharpens `six-marks-are-complete`, whose scope note named the teardrop as
unresolved alongside the Spiral. The teardrop is now resolved in the same
direction as the Spiral: **completeness with respect to symmetry order does not
give completeness with respect to figure.** Two unreachable figures, two
different missing capabilities — the Spiral wants scaling, the teardrop wants a
curved join. Neither wants a seventh mark. That is a much more useful statement
than "the six marks are complete", and it is the second time narrowing a claim
has produced more than the claim did.

**Method note: four detector bugs, all caught by controls.** The corner detector
was wrong four times before it was right, and every time a control with a known
answer caught it, never the enumeration.

1. `np.diff` never looks at the seam of a closed array, so a square read 3
   corners and the reference teardrop read 0 — both had a corner at the wrap.
2. My vesica control read 0 corners and I suspected the detector; the control
   was wrong. I had built two half-*ellipses*, which join into a plain ellipse
   with no corners at all. A real vesica is two circular arcs meeting at 60°.
3. A fixed angle threshold cannot work. An elongated ellipse concentrates its
   turning near its ends, so any threshold either calls those corners or misses
   a genuine shallow one. Replaced with a scale test: halve the measuring window
   and a smooth bend's turning halves with it, while a corner keeps its whole
   angle. That is a property, not a tuned number.
4. The first reference teardrop was eyeballed — straight arms that did not meet
   the arc tangentially — so it carried spurious corners and 3% reverse turning.
   Rebuilt from actual tangent lines, so its single corner is true by
   construction rather than by measurement.

A fixed threshold still hides one thing, and it is worth stating rather than
burying: a bend whose curvature radius is small compared with the measuring
window *is* a corner as far as this sampling can tell. The 10:1 ellipse reads as
cornered for exactly that reason. This is F118's noise floor restated for
curvature — resolution bounds what is distinguishable, and the honest move is to
report the bound rather than pick a threshold that hides it.

**Why a zero needed a positive control.** A negative result from a detector that
had been wrong four times is worth nothing on its own. Five teardrops — fat,
thin, rotated, mirrored, reference — were planted in the same screen that
returned zero, and all five were found; a circle and a triangle were correctly
rejected. The screen can see a teardrop. It did not see one here.

The threshold sensitivity was swept too: 27 combinations of window, turn
threshold and scale ratio. Twenty-four return no one-cornered figure at all; the
three loosest return at most 18 of 20,142, of which exactly one is convex — two
concentric circles, 0.575 from the teardrop, whose "corner" is a window artifact.
The hole at one corner is a property of the space, not of a threshold.

findings.title: the waveform reading does not survive composition, and the two families do not commute
findings.text:
Two measurements on the boundary between PLACEMENT and MODULATION. Both operands
drawn from the three marks modulation can move (Angle, Curve, Wave), every
attested binary operator, 45 constructions.

**A. The reading survives composition less than half the time.**

    superpose_concentric   5/9        concatenate   5/9
    superpose_displaced    5/9        nest          5/9
    cross                  1/9        overall      21/45

Both operands admit a waveform reading in every case. The composite keeps one in
21 of 45. `cross` is worst at 1 of 9, and the reason is visible in what crossing
does: two strokes that cut each other fold the figure, and a folded figure is
not a function in any direction.

This bears against `waveform-reading-is-intended` in a way the claim's own
evidence does not reach. `Universal_Symbology_Composition` holds that composition
is one operation at every scale -- inside a symbol and between symbols. If that
is right, a reading which more than half the time fails to survive one step of
composition cannot be THE reading of the notation. It remains a true and useful
reading of the marks, which is what F117 and F120 established.

**B. Modulation does not distribute over placement.**

Asking whether `modulate(place(A,B))` equals `place(modulate A, modulate B)`,
restricted to the 21 composites that have a profile for modulation to act on:

    3 of 21 agree, and all three are superpose_concentric(X, X), at 0.0000

That case is degenerate. `superpose_concentric(X,X)` stacks a figure on itself,
which as a point set is the figure, so there is nothing for the two operators to
interact over and commuting is automatic. Excluding it: **zero of eighteen
non-degenerate pairs commute.** Even `superpose_displaced(X,X)` fails, at 0.27 to
0.31, because displacing produces two lobes and modulating the composite reads
them as one profile.

So the families are not merely distinct in what they do; they do not compose.
That is a real constraint on where the boundary sits, and it is the second one
after F121's fixed points.

**A methodological note, because it nearly went the other way.** The first run
of B reported 3 of 45 and I was about to record "the families do not commute".
24 of those 45 composites admit NO chart, so `modulate` is the identity on them
and the comparison was between a modulated figure and an unmodulated one --
guaranteed to differ, for a reason having nothing to do with commutativity. More
than half the sample was measuring the wrong thing and the headline number would
have been right by accident. Restricting to eligible composites is what turned a
plausible number into a result.

findings.title: modulation has exactly three fixed points, and they are Point, Line and Circle
findings.text:
`modulation-is-a-second-operator-family` distinguishes PLACEMENT ("place B
relative to A", the whole attested set) from MODULATION ("vary a parameter along
A's own extent"), and notes only placement is documented. With a waveform model
(S7) a figure has a profile, so modulation has something to act on. Implemented
as five operations -- frequency, amplitude, phase, taper, chirp -- acting in
whichever chart the figure admits.

Measured, every one of them is the IDENTITY on three of the six marks:

    mark     chart        resolution   profile spread   modulation
    Point    degenerate      —              —           fixed point
    Line     cartesian       0.00209        0.00000     fixed point
    Angle    cartesian       0.00264        0.89129     moves
    Curve    cartesian       0.00277        0.84406     moves
    Wave     cartesian       0.00329        1.09996     moves
    Circle   polar           0.00654        0.00416     fixed point

The reason is structural rather than incidental. Modulation re-reads and
rescales an EXISTING variation; a constant profile has none. Line's y is zero
everywhere and Circle's r is constant, so there is nothing to re-read and
nothing to scale. Making a circle lobed ADDS a waveform to its profile, which
places something rather than varying what is there -- so it belongs to the
other family. That is a piece of the family boundary the claim asks for, arrived
at from the operations rather than asserted.

**Why the threshold is not a constant.** Circle's r is not exactly constant --
it varies by 0.00416 from interpolation. Against the figure's own resolution of
0.00654 that variation is below what the drawing can express, so it is constant.
A fixed 1e-3 declared it varying and let every modulation warp sampling ripple
into apparent structure. This is F118's lesson a second time: a threshold that
does not know the resolution it is working at will eventually measure the
discretisation instead of the figure.

**An observation, not a claim.** {Point, Line, Circle} is not a partition the
corpus already records -- it cuts across both symmetry order and curvature
class. It is, however, exactly the primitive set of straightedge-and-compass
construction. Whether that is structure or coincidence is not established here
and nothing below depends on it.

**What is still open.** The claim asks for modulation stated as an operation
somewhere in the corpus, or for the family boundary to be derived. Implementing
a family is a design act: it makes the operations concrete, testable, and
drawable, and the fixed-point result is a genuine constraint on where the
boundary can fall. The claim stays `undetermined`.

findings.title: the twelve signs recover their own rule from three waveform axes
findings.text:
Building the waveform model (S7) on F117's two charts and measuring the signs.
All twelve admit the cartesian reading. Measured on the order parameters, they
land on six coincident PAIRS:

    (1,4) angle   (2,11) square   (3,6) arc   (5,8) square   (7,10) angle   (9,12) arc

Each pair shares a geometry and a crossbar and differs only in direction. Every
parameter in the model was built from spectral MAGNITUDES, and magnitude is
invariant under y -> -y, so the model could not see `n mod 2` -- one third of
the rule that generates the signs. A model of the signs blind to a third of
their rule is not a model of the signs, and the signs are what exposed it: on
the six marks the gap is invisible, because no two marks are reflections of each
other.

**Adding phase closes it.** Phase is the argument of the dominant component, and
it is the corpus's own carrier -- it was on the Signal_Manifold list and I had
not implemented it. Measured:

    apex up    phase  +0.004        apex down   phase  -0.996

One half-turn apart, to three figures, which is exactly what a reflection in the
baseline is. All twelve signs then occupy distinct points.

**The three-part rule is recoverable from three axes.** `sign(n)` is built from
`n mod 3` (geometry), `n mod 2` (direction) and whether `n mod 4` is in {2,3}
(crossbar). Measured off the drawing with no knowledge of n:

    phase                  separates direction, 6/6 each way
    (spread, amplitude)    separates geometry x crossbar into exactly 6 cells,
                           each internally consistent:

        angle  no bar  (0.051, 0.286)      angle  bar  (0.055, 0.215)
        arc    no bar  (0.010, 0.193)      arc    bar  (0.107, 0.243)
        square no bar  (0.066, 0.076)      square bar  (0.200, 0.319)

So three waveform coordinates recover all twelve. Note what this is and is not:
the signs are ATTESTED from source cards, and measuring them does not derive
them. What it does is place them as one sampled set in a continuous space, so
that the question "what lies between Aries and Libra" has coordinates to be
asked in. `spread` does not carry geometry alone -- geometry and crossbar are
jointly encoded in the pair -- and saying otherwise would be neater than the
measurement.

**Bearing on `waveform-reading-is-intended`.** With F117 this now reads: the
marks and the signs both admit a waveform reading; it takes two charts; and for
the signs the reading carries the whole generating rule. That is considerably
stronger evidence than the Sol-Center sheet's acoustic vocabulary, which was all
the claim had. It is still not a derivation that the reading is THE intended
one, which is what the claim asks.

**Two model bugs, both caught by controls.** Harmonicity as "share of energy on
the dominant bin and its multiples" is degenerate at k=1, where every bin is a
multiple and any figure scores 1.000 -- a pure sine and a scribble were
indistinguishable. Spectral flatness has no such hole. And amplitude divided by
the profile's own peak, which scales amplitude out entirely: sines of height
0.5 and 0.05 both measured 0.706, because what was being measured was the shape
of a sine.

findings.title: a recorded meaning was attached to a slot, and three of four migrated
findings.text:
Fixing the sampling density (F118) reordered the orbit enumeration. It did NOT
change the partition -- still 95 orbits -- but it changed which index each
figure sits at. Nine orbits' symmetry also corrected:

    before  inf 5   C2 16   C1 71   C4 2   C8 1
    after   inf 5   C2 21   C1 67   C4 2

The spurious C8 is gone, and five figures recorded as having no rotational
symmetry actually have two-fold.

**The damage was elsewhere.** Meanings were carried between builds by index:

    known[o["orbit"]] = o        ...        prev = known.get(oid, {})

An orbit id is `enumerate()` over the enumeration order. When that order moved,
three of the four recorded meanings landed on different figures:

    Sun-in-Circle   superpose_concentric(Point,Circle)   stayed, by luck
    infinity        reflect_pair(Wave)        -> landed on nest(Wave,Line)
    Chaos pair      superpose_displaced(Angle,Angle) -> superpose_displaced(Point,Circle)
    + (SymbolFolds) cross(Line,Line)          -> nest(Circle,Curve)

Nothing raised an error. The artifact simply began stating three false
attributions, and would have shipped them.

**The fix is to key on the construction.** An operator with its operands names a
figure; a position in a list names a slot that a figure currently occupies. Both
failure modes are now fatal rather than silent: if one orbit comes to contain
two differently-named members the partition has merged two named figures, which
is a result needing a decision and not a carryover; and if a recorded meaning
can no longer be placed at all, the build stops rather than dropping what the
corpus knows.

**The same defect existed one level up.** The frontier pages shipped as
`orbit-094.html`, numbered the same way. Ninety-five URLs would have quietly
come to mean different figures -- a bookmark, a citation, or a link from these
notes resolving to something else with no error anywhere. Pages are now named
for the construction: `cross-line-line.html`.

**The general shape.** Positional identifiers are stable exactly as long as
nothing upstream changes, which is a guarantee no derived artifact can make
about itself. This corpus recomputes its own foundations routinely -- that is
the whole point of it -- so any identifier that survives only while the
computation does not move is a defect waiting for the next correction. F116 and
F118 were both corrections that moved a computation; this is what the second one
broke on its way through.

findings.title: a recorded symmetry is a sampling artefact, and the threshold has no headroom
findings.text:
Raising `symmetry_order`'s cap from 8 to 24 changes exactly one of the 95
orbits: orbit 94, `concatenate(Circle, Point)`, recorded as 8-fold. Raising it
further keeps changing the answer -- 48 at cap 48, 96 at cap 96 -- which is the
signature of CONTINUOUS symmetry being reported as whatever the cap allows.

The figure is a circle with a Point that lands on it, 0.992 against a mean
radius of 0.996. It adds no ink. It is a circle.

Why the continuity test misses it:

    TOL = 0.015, and for this figure the distance under rotation measures
    3.75° 0.0131   37° 0.0139   45° 0.0096   83° 0.0135      (all "match")
    90°   0.0162   149° 0.0174   180° 0.0209                 (all "differ")

The test angles are 37, 83 and 149. Two pass and one fails, so the figure falls
through to the finite search, which then returns the cap.

**The threshold has no headroom at this sampling density.** A perfect circle
measured against its own rotation:

    60 pts 0.0518    120 pts 0.0246    240 pts 0.0129
    480 pts 0.0065   960 pts 0.0032   1920 pts 0.0015

At the 240 samples the corpus uses, a figure that is exactly continuous measures
0.013 against a threshold of 0.015 -- 87% of the budget spent on discretisation.
The `Circle` mark itself peaks at 0.0152, OVER the threshold; it classifies as
continuous only because the three test angles happen to land under. At 480
samples both circle and circle-plus-point read continuous with room to spare.

**Consequences.**

  * orbit 94's recorded symmetry (8) is wrong; the answer is `inf`
  * `symmetry_order` returns a plausible divisor when the true order exceeds its
    cap, rather than reporting that it ran out of range. For a 9-lobed figure it
    returns 3. Nothing distinguishes that from a real 3
  * `hausdorff(Circle, Circle+Point)` is 0.008 against a same-figure threshold of
    0.073 -- the corpus's own criterion says they are the SAME figure, at every
    sampling density tested. They are in different orbits because the bucket key
    counts strokes, not because the geometry differs

That last point is direct evidence on `a-redundant-point-changes-a-figure`,
which asks exactly this. Geometrically the redundant point changes nothing and
the corpus's own same-figure test agrees. What separates them is bookkeeping.

**Status.** `measured`. The fix -- denser sampling for the continuity test, and
an honest out-of-range report instead of a divisor -- changes the orbit
partition, so it is recorded here before it is applied.

findings.title: the waveform reading needs two charts, and which one applies is measurable
findings.text:
`waveform-reading-is-intended` says "the marks are to be read as waveforms" and
is undetermined. Measuring it: a waveform reading needs the path to be a
function, so the test is whether the path advances one way along some direction.
Controls first -- a sine and an arc score 1.00, a circle 0.50, a spiral 0.55.

    Line 1.00   Angle 1.00   Curve 1.00   Wave 1.00   Circle 0.50   Point n/a

So four of the six marks ARE function graphs and Circle is not: it doubles back
on every direction. But Circle is not outside the waveform frame -- it is in the
other one. Read in polar form, r as a function of angle about the centre, Circle
is star-shaped with r constant, which is a waveform of period zero.

**Two readings, not one.** Open curves are waveforms in y over extent; closed
curves are waveforms in r over angle. Which applies is decided by whether the
path closes, which is itself measured rather than chosen.

This SHARPENS the claim rather than settling it. "The marks are to be read as
waveforms" is true, and it is not one reading -- and a claim that needs two
charts to be true is a different claim from the one on record.

**This also improves on the source.** `Signal_Manifold` factors emitted sound
into three segmental axes plus four carriers and states that those axes name no
organ. That is right for sound, where there is one parameterisation: time. A
drawn figure has no time, and it can close. Applying the acoustic axes directly
would have imported a single parameterisation that the visual case does not
have. The corpus page is a good reference and this is where the visual case
departs from it.

**Control note.** The first two attempts at this measurement were wrong and the
controls caught both: binning 240 samples into 160 x-columns measures sampling
density, not multi-valuedness; and an ascending search for the angular period
returns 2 for a four-lobed figure, because every divisor of n also satisfies the
shift. Neither error is visible without a figure whose answer is known in
advance.

findings.title: "order matters" was overstated, and the drawing is what caught it
findings.text:
Measured across every ordered pair of distinct marks under each attested
operator, by asking which orbit each construction lands in:

    operator                swaps giving the SAME figure   swaps giving a different one
    cross                            15                              0
    superpose_concentric             15                              0
    concatenate                      12                              3
    superpose_displaced              12                              3
    nest                              5                             10

`cross` and `superpose_concentric` are commutative outright at this depth. And
`nest` -- the operator whose asymmetry is most obvious in words -- is
commutative for a third of its pairs: the exceptions are exactly those where an
operand has no extent to nest into, so `nest(Circle,Point)` and
`nest(Point,Circle)` are the same orbit.

This sharpens, and partly contradicts, the register's existing scope note on
`composition-noncommutative`, which said nest "is not a swap at all -- inner and
outer are different roles." The roles are indeed different; it does not follow
that swapping them always changes the figure, and for five of fifteen pairs it
does not.

**How it was caught.** The landing asserted "B inside A is not A inside B" and
the walk-through illustrated it with `nest(Circle,Point)` vs
`nest(Point,Circle)`. Drawing both from the enumerating code put two identical
figures beside a sentence claiming they differed.

That is the argument for generating every figure from the code that enumerated
it rather than illustrating the prose separately: an illustration drawn to match
a sentence cannot contradict it, and so can never correct it. Here the drawing
and the prose were produced by different routes, they disagreed, and the drawing
was right.

**Status.** `measured` -- a fact about these artifacts at depth 2, not a
necessity. Whether commutativity survives a deeper enumeration is not known and
is not claimed.

findings.title: the application is retired and the codex is the site
findings.text:
The Next.js app at `cosmiccodex-app` is removed. **697 tracked files become
191**, and the derived layer sits at the root.

I argued against this first, and was overruled with a reason worth recording:
*the way it works and teaches was always so heavily contaminated that working on
it constantly required fixing.* That is the correct read of the evidence. What
the app taught:

```
Enclosure  28 mentions      Circle  5        the measurement says Circle
Point      50               Wave    1        the Wave is the only chiral mark
sign grammar · curvature class · rotation order      stated nowhere
theorems: 5 named, 4 of them in no register
```

Every pass over it began by repairing what it asserted — the same shape as the
wiki before F110 and the glossaries before F112. A surface that must be
corrected before it can be extended is not an asset.

**Nothing was destroyed.** The app is in the repository's history, and the
uncommitted work found in its tree — 150 insertions across `theorems.ts`,
`types.ts` and `agent-card.json` — was committed to
`preserve/pre-codex-replacement` and pushed *before* anything was removed. Being
told the history is enough is different from there being no history.

**What replaces it asserts nothing it cannot show.** No server, no framework, no
dependency, no JavaScript. `vercel.json` drops the framework entirely: no build
command, no install step, output at the root. Verified after the move — 186 of
186 checksums, zero broken links, and the shipped CLI still answers from the new
root.

**And the site is now genuinely generated.** Its README says an edit made there
is lost on the next publish, which is only true if publishing is a command
rather than a memory of having copied a directory once. `codex_deploy.py` is
that command. It **replaces** rather than merges — a sheet withdrawn here is
deleted there, or the site slowly stops being the artifact — while leaving the
site's own files alone, and it cannot push. A test requires a clean sync to
propose nothing, so drift between the two becomes a failing test rather than a
discovery.

findings.title: the prose is translatable now, and a promise had quietly broken
findings.text:
F113 established that the notation crosses languages by itself. The prose does
not, and the ask stands: anywhere plain text explains something, it should be
readable in more than one language.

**Fifty-six keyed strings.** Every sentence the landing emits now lives behind a
key, and each generator asks for it rather than holding it. That makes the
English a **default** instead of a hard-coding, which is the whole technical
change — a translation appearing in a language file appears on the page with no
further work.

```
lang  translated  provenance
sw    51 / 56     machine, unreviewed
id    51 / 56     machine, unreviewed
hi    51 / 56     machine, unreviewed
tpi   37 / 56     machine, unreviewed
am    32 / 56     machine, unreviewed
```

Strings I was not confident about were **left absent**, and an absent string
shows in English. Mixed pages are visibly mixed — that is the honest rendering,
not a defect to paper over.

**Everything here is machine-suggested and says so.** Each page carries a banner
stating it is unreviewed and that the drawings and their status marks are *not*
translated because they carry the same meaning in every language. And an
uncomfortable fact worth recording: the pre-existing glossary terms were
`forged_by: copilot-claude-opus-4`, so they are machine too. **Nothing in this
repo has a speaker-reviewed translation.** Refusing to machine-translate would
leave five languages empty forever; passing a machine string off as a
translation would launder a guess. Marking it does neither, which is how the
rest of this corpus treats a claim whose standing is unsettled.

A test requires the drawings to be **byte-identical across languages**. A
translation that altered a glyph would be changing the thing it is supposed to
describe.

**And a promise had broken without anyone noticing.** The landing's own
docstring says it *never scrolls*. It did:

```
1440 x 900   fits
1200 x 800   SCROLLS
 390 x 844   SCROLLS — 1569px of content in an 844px viewport
```

Not caused by translation. The section count went from **9 to 14** over this
session — slices, explore, placement, the frontier, languages — and every
addition was correct on its own while the invariant was nobody's job. Each tile
claimed a minimum height and fourteen of them overflowed. The grid now sizes its
rows from the space it is given (`grid-auto-rows: minmax(0,1fr)`), all three
viewports fit, and a test holds the structure so the next section cannot break
it silently.

findings.title: the status is drawn, so the invariant already crosses languages
findings.text:
F112 concluded that no language was usable because none had a word for
`undetermined`, and that a translated page therefore could not mark an open
claim as open. The operator's question — *the meanings are all supposed to be
derived; why do you need a human to assert definitions arbitrarily?* — is what
exposed that as the wrong measurement.

**The status is drawn, not written.** Six marks, in use on every primer sheet and
cell grid since F63:

```
filled square    derived          barred square   measured
open square      undetermined     circle          conventional
half-filled      derived_given    nothing         withdrawn
```

An open square is an open square in every language. The codex's one invariant —
every assertion carries its licence to cite — **already travels untranslated**,
and so does everything else here that carries meaning: the marks are figures, the
operators are figures, the measured properties are numbers on `data-*`. A reader
with no English can read the notation today. That is the project's whole claim
about itself, and it turns out to hold for its own interface.

**And the notation was never registered.** Zero claims mentioned it. A six-symbol
scheme carrying the project's central invariant went six findings without a
status of its own. Now `status-badges-are-a-convention`, **conventional** — the
shapes are iconic, filled reading as closed and bars as a tally, but iconic is
motivated, not derived, and a different set would carry the same distinctions.
Recorded as a choice so it is cited as one.

**What a speaker actually supplies.** The correction does not abolish the ask, it
relocates it:

> The **meaning** of a mark is derived and already fixed by its geometry.
> A Swahili **word** for that meaning is a fact about Swahili.

That is lexicography, not assertion. Nobody is being asked to decide what the
Wave means. They are being asked what their language already calls a thing whose
meaning was settled by measurement — and a model guessing it would be inventing
a fact about a language, which is a different error from inventing a claim and
no better.

So the honest figure is **prose coverage, 22%**, not a readiness verdict. The
notation is readable now; the sentences wrapped around it are not.

findings.title: the multilingual layer taught a system we no longer hold, and had no word for doubt
findings.text:
The app had **no multilingual support at all**: twenty pages, every one
`lang="en"`, and six non-Latin characters in six megabytes — all of them Hangul,
on one sheet. Against the original brief (South East Asia and the East African
Rift) it delivered none of it.

**The regions were right; the content was not.** Five glossaries cover Kiswahili
and አማርኛ for the Rift, Bahasa Indonesia and Tok Pisin for SE Asia and the
Pacific, plus हिन्दी. The hard part was done. What they taught was a different
system:

```
primitives   5, not 6 — and the missing one is the WAVE, the only chiral mark
operations   a key named `eleven_operations` holding 12 LOGICAL operations
             (predicate, negate, conjoin) disjoint from the six the corpus attests
theorems     5 named; FOUR appear nowhere in the register — full_universality,
             unique_grounding, minimality, compositionality
```

Those four are exactly the unearned grand claims this work replaced with
statements that carry a status. All five glossaries are unreviewed drafts, last
touched 2026-03-31, authored by a different model.

**The gap that matters was not on that list.** Not one glossary translates the
**status vocabulary**. A translated statement is easy; the discipline is that
every assertion carries its licence to cite — and with no word for
`undetermined` in any of the five, a translated codex is exactly where the
hedges fall off and an open question begins reading as a fact. So the payload
carries an explicit rule: **an untranslated status word falls back to English,
never to nothing.** Dropping it would let a translated page assert flatly what
the English page marks as open, which is the one failure a translation can
introduce that the original cannot.

**Nothing was invented.** Terms are regenerated from the register, missing ones
are left `awaiting` and empty. A machine-authored Swahili term for a concept
nobody has checked is the same failure as a machine-authored claim, in a language
the author cannot read to catch it.

`enclosure` became `Circle` when the inventory was measured rather than listed,
and the concept **narrowed**: Kiswahili `Kizingiti` is a doorframe, a threshold —
a good word for an enclosure and not obviously right for a circle. Carried
across, flagged `supplied_needs_review`, not promoted.

```
lang   marks        operators   status words   UI-ready
sw     4 +1? /6     0/6         0/6            no
am     4    /6      0/6         0/6            no
id     4 +1? /6     0/6         0/6            no
hi     4 +1? /6     0/6         0/6            no
tpi    4 +1? /6     0/6         0/6            no
```

**And the regenerator was dangerous.** It read translations from
`geometric_primitives` and wrote them to `marks`; run twice, the second pass
looked for a section its own first pass had removed, found nothing, and **blanked
five languages**. Recovered from git. A tool that rewrites the file it reads must
be able to read its own output, and a test now runs it twice and compares.

A second, subtler one underneath: on a re-run the carried `Circle` term is read
back from `marks`, where the key now matches, so nothing marks it as carried and
the review flag **silently promoted to a plain translation**. Provenance is not
position. It is preserved explicitly now.

findings.title: live on eight pages, and the audit was reading a different wiki
findings.text:
The derived layer is **live**. Backup first, `Base 12` alone, verified against the
live page with a scoped read-only fetch showing no difference, then the other
seven. Eight pages pushed, zero errors, mirror committed and backed up.

**Then the audit did not move, and the reason is a finding.** Four of the eight
pages are in its flagged set, so those findings should have closed. None did —
because the wiki detectors do not read the wiki.

```
MediaWiki mirror, just pushed      6438 pages
static site export, build/wiki/p    729 pages   exported the previous day
                                    the audit reads THIS one
```

**11% of the wiki, from a day-old export**, and the page for the Wave — the one
chiral mark — is not in the export at all. Every underclaim finding said "page is
about this subject but never states the verified result" with a `wiki/` path, and
none of them said that "wiki" meant a published subset rebuilt on its own
schedule. Three surfaces, not two, and the standing rule about never conflating
them applies one layer deeper than it was written.

The detectors now state their own coverage on every finding, computed rather than
described: a reader sees `729 of 6438 pages (11% of the wiki), as exported` and
that an edit does not close a finding until the site is rebuilt.

**And a second defect underneath it.** Making that correction changed nothing on
the 64 rows already on record. The register's merge only advanced `last_seen`, so
**a detector's description was frozen at first sight** — correct the scope and
every existing finding keeps the wrong one forever, while looking maintained. The
merge now refreshes what the detector owns (finding text, evidence, scope,
proposed fix, severity) and preserves what the finding owns (id, first seen,
status, notes). The 64 rows carry the true scope now without losing that they
were first seen on 2026-09-10.

**Not rebuilt.** `wiki_build.py` purges an edge cache by default. That is a live
action nobody asked for, so the static site is left as it stands and the gap is
recorded rather than quietly closed.

findings.title: the results had never reached the authority at all
findings.text:
The audit's 64 `underclaim` findings across 53 pages read as *these pages should
say more*. Measured against the whole 6,440-page mirror, it is worse and simpler:

```
sign = (n mod 3) x (n mod 4)          stated on 0 pages
Z/12 = Z/3 x Z/4, why there are twelve stated on 0 pages
curvature class, the polarity axis     stated on 0 pages
any citation of a runnable check       0 pages
```

**Nothing crossed.** The wiki is the authority and the repo is where the work
happens, and the most strongly verified result in the corpus — 12/12 off the
sheets, three ways, plus a held-out prediction — appeared on no page. There was
no canonical statement for those 53 pages to link *to*, so editing 53 pages was
never the first move. Writing the statement once was.

**Eight pages, generated.** `Universal_Symbology` and `Base_12` carry the two
factorisations; the six mark pages each carry that mark's measured group and what
a rotation or a mirror can say about it. Every block is produced from the
derivation register, so a claim cannot drift from its status, and re-running
replaces its own block rather than appending a second copy.

Each statement carries **the status at the assertion** and the command that
checks it — the invariant the codex has been built on since F63, finally applied
to the wiki. Base 12 states the CRT factorisation as `derived` and the element
labelling as `undetermined` **on the same page**, with what would settle it.

**The tool cannot push.** It writes to the local mirror and only with `--write`;
a test asserts it imports nothing that could reach a network or spawn a process,
after a first version grepped for the string `wiki_sync` and failed on the help
text explaining to a reader how to push — the opposite of a danger. Publishing
stays a separate, backed-up step.

findings.title: what depth 2 cannot reach, and a degeneracy that is a question rather than a bug
findings.text:
Two decisions taken with numbers rather than instinct, and the numbers changed
one of them.

**The redundant point is a semantic question, not a defect.** F107 found that
concatenating a Point onto the Line, Wave or Circle reproduces that mark — the
point lands on the curve and adds no ink. The obvious fix is to bar the Point
from concatenation, on F105's grounds that joining needs an end and a Point has
none. Measured, that fix costs more than it buys:

```
excluding Point from concatenate     95 orbits -> 93
but it also discards
  concatenate(Point, Angle)          0.311 from the bare Angle — DISTINCT
  concatenate(Point, Curve)          0.151 from the bare Curve — DISTINCT
```

So the cheap fix buys consistency by throwing away two real cells. And the
underlying question — does a point sitting where a mark already passes make a
different **symbol**? — is not geometric at all. Geometry says the figures are
0.008 to 0.031 apart against a 0.073 line; the corpus says nothing. Registered as
`a-redundant-point-changes-a-figure`, **undetermined**, and the count of 95 now
carries that assumption explicitly instead of resting on it silently.

What *is* a defect, and stays recorded as one: `concatenate(Point,Circle)` scores
**C∞** while `concatenate(Circle,Point)` scores **C8**, two figures 0.029 apart
that are both a circle. One duplicated sample shifts the centroid and `normalise`
carries it into the rotation test.

**Depth 2 has a ceiling, and it is exactly where the corpus runs out.** A census
over all 191 combinations:

```
C1  131      C2  41      C4  2      C8  1      C-inf  16
```

**No C3 and no C6.** The triangle measures C3 and the hexagram C6, so neither can
appear at this depth — a pair of marks cannot make an odd order, and producing
one needs a third placement. The corpus draws both figures, which is why the gap
matters.

And the single **C8 is an artifact rather than a result**: it is
`concatenate(Circle,Point)`, the degenerate case above, and it is the only 8 in
the entire census. One measurement error, one spurious symmetry order.

**Drawn as the figures, not as the space.** A full depth-3 enumeration is 5700
combinations whose grouping is quadratic — about **44 hours** as this code
stands — and has not been computed. So the sheet shows the specific
constructions that reach C3 and C6 and says outright that nothing is claimed
about the size of depth 3. A chart implying otherwise would be the same overclaim
the build plan exists to catch.

**And a search that came back empty.** `modulation-is-a-second-operator-family`
asks for modulation stated as an operation anywhere in the corpus. Searching
6,440 wiki pages: the word appears for mathematical operators (the Hadamard
product) and as the *name* of two marks in the rotation table (F6) — never as a
symbology operation. The claim stays undetermined, now with a searched-and-not-
found attached rather than an unexamined gap.

findings.title: the last four sheets, and a conflation that had to become a test
findings.text:
S5 and S6 finish the plan. Everything in the catalogue that is not blocked on an
undetermined claim now has a sheet: **51 drawn, 9 covered by a representative, 2
blocked.**

**The relation depth 2 actually has.** The catalogue listed a *reachability
graph* — one orbit reached from another by applying an operator. That needs
depth 3 and is blocked. What exists at depth 2 is **substitution**: two orbits
whose constructions use the same operator and differ in exactly one operand.

```
95 orbits · 269 edges · mean degree 5.7 · 1 isolated
```

It is named for what it is rather than for what was wanted, and the sheet says so
on its face. Laid out on a ring in the **distance dendrogram's order** (S4), so
tree neighbours sit adjacent and the layout carries information instead of being
an arbitrary circle. No force simulation, no dependency — the artifact ships
offline.

**Which marks carry the space.**

```
Curve 36 > Angle 34 > Wave 32 > Circle 26 > Line 23 > Point 16   (of 95)
```

The Point is rarest, and F107 says why: it has no extent, so most placements of
it land on the other mark and add nothing. The incidence sheet and that
degeneracy are the same fact seen twice.

**Two results that had been published without a sheet.** The schema join (F102)
and the frame table (F103) existed only as terminal output. Drawn, they check
each other: the frame-bound rows and the uncovered schemas are the same set
*except* PART/WHOLE, which is frame-free and mereological — F103's claim
verified across two sheets rather than asserted on either.

**And the conflation recurred.** F105's plan caught the catalogue calling seven
layouts "built" with one sheet between them. Landing S3, a rename swept the
schema join up with sheets that really had been drawn, and it claimed **drawn**
with nothing on disk. The plan did not catch it — the plan reads the disk, so it
merely under-counted — and it took a hand audit to find.

> **A status that only a person remembers to check is not a status.**

Every catalogue status is now compared against the filesystem by a test, in both
directions: nothing may claim a sheet that is not there, and nothing may hide one
that is. It would have caught both occurrences, and it found two more while being
written — the distance matrix and the frame table were each drawn and still
listed as merely derivable.

findings.title: a metric on the orbits, and the first two leads into the unnamed
findings.text:
91 of the 95 orbits have no recorded meaning. The only handle on them was a
fingerprint of measured properties (F104) — good for *show me the closed
two-stroke figures*, useless for the question that matters:

> **Is any unnamed orbit NEAR one the corpus actually draws?**

All 4465 pairs measured, by best alignment under rotation and reflection at 36
steps — the resolution `same_figure` searches. A coarser matrix would contradict
the partition it describes, and F101 is the reason to care: at 18 steps no
threshold separates same from different at all.

**Nearest to each figure the corpus draws.**

```
infinity (SymbolFolds)     0.081   orbit 16   superpose_displaced(Circle,Circle)
Chaos pair (F44)           0.078   orbit 42   superpose_displaced(Angle,Curve)
+ (SymbolFolds)            0.358   orbit 8    cross(Line,Wave)
Sun-in-Circle (F43)        0.398   orbit 70   nest(Circle,Angle)
```

The same-figure threshold is **0.073**. The first two miss being *the same
figure* by 0.008 and 0.005.

**The infinity result is the interesting one.** The corpus attests ∞ as
`reflect_pair(Wave)` — a wave against its own mirror. The space says **two
circles set side by side** come within 0.081 of it. Two constructions, from
different marks, arriving at nearly one figure. That is a lead worth chasing and
nothing more: proximity is not meaning, and orbit 16 remains undetermined.

**The second is a known case returning from a new direction.** Chaos pair is
`displaced(Angle,Angle)`; its nearest is `displaced(Angle,Curve)`. That is
exactly the Angle-against-Curve family F101 found sitting at the resolution
limit, where Hausdorff can barely separate a corner from an arc. Reaching it
again by a different route is corroboration, not a new finding.

**Two figures are isolated, and that is equally a result.** The Sun-in-Circle and
the cross have nothing within 0.35. In a space where the typical near neighbour
sits at 0.08, they are distinctive — nothing else the operators build comes close
to either.

**The dendrogram reproduces it without being asked.** Average linkage over the
same matrix puts 13 beside 16 and 41 beside 42 as adjacent leaves. The tree was
computed from the distances alone; that it recovers the nearest-neighbour result
is a consistency check, not a second finding.

**The map states its own loss.** Classical MDS keeps **47%** of the metric in two
dimensions. The other 53% does not fit in a plane and is gone, so the sheet says
so rather than implying the picture is the space. Two points close on it may be
far apart in what it is a shadow of.

**Postscript to F107 — what the matrix says about the partition, and one
degeneracy it exposed.**

Seven pairs of distinct orbits measure closer than the 0.073 line that would
merge them. Every one is held apart by a **derived axis** — symmetry order or
curvature class — which is F105's decision working exactly as intended: the
bucket key blocks a merge the metric would make, because a partition finer than
the metric is the safe direction. The first pair sharing a bucket sits at
**0.0734**, just above the line. So within a bucket the partition is clean, and
across buckets the separations are principled rather than accidental. The test
first written here asserted the wrong invariant and had to be corrected.

**The degeneracy.** Concatenating a Point onto a mark puts it at that mark's own
extremity, where for several marks it lands *on* the curve and adds nothing:

```
concatenate(Point, Line)      0.008 from the bare Line
concatenate(Point, Wave)      0.015 from the bare Wave
concatenate(Point, Circle)    0.031 from the bare Circle
concatenate(Point, Angle)     0.311 — genuinely different
concatenate(Point, Curve)     0.151 — genuinely different
```

Those first three occupy their own orbits despite being the mark over again. And
the Circle case measures **inconsistently**: `concatenate(Point,Circle)` scores
C∞ while `concatenate(Circle,Point)` scores C8, two figures 0.029 apart that are
both, to the eye, a circle. One duplicated sample shifts the centroid, and
`normalise` carries that into the rotation test.

**Left unfixed, deliberately, and for the same reason as F104.** Collapsing these
would move the orbit count a third time, and the count is a published number
that several sheets and three findings now rest on. It is recorded with its
measured size so the decision can be taken rather than stumbled into.

findings.title: concatenate fixed, and every count that rested on the orbit partition moved
findings.text:
F104 found that `concatenate` did not join its marks: it set them 2.10 apart
where `superpose_displaced` sets them 2.20, the same placement under a second
name, and the two shared an orbit in nearly every case. It was left unfixed
deliberately, because changing it moves the orbit count and everything derived
from it, and those have to be re-derived rather than silently updated.

Measured before deciding, rather than guessed:

```
orbits with the gap    80
orbits joined          95        +19%
```

That settled it. Building the operator matrix or the distance matrix on the old
partition would have meant building them twice.

**The fix.** B is shifted by `max(A.x) − min(B.x)`, which brings it into contact
by construction.

```
stroke gap    before        after
Curve+Curve   0.411   ->    0.000
Angle+Curve   0.364   ->    0.005
Line+Line     0.100   ->    0.000
```

Contact to within a fifth of a sampling step.

**What moved.**

```
                                      before   after
orbits                                    80      95
unnamed                                   76      91
chiral orbits                             34      44
  inherited from a Wave                   27      31
  from arrangement alone                   7      13
inventory if mirroring means nothing      80      95
inventory if mirroring means something    88     109
orbits holding both handednesses           8      14
distinct search fingerprints           46/80   48/95
```

**LINK is covered after all.** F102 joined `concatenate` to the LINK schema and
F104 warned the uncovered count might rise to five, because an operator that
leaves a gap does not link anything. Joined, it does. The count stays at **four**
— UP/DOWN, FRONT/BACK, PATH, PART/WHOLE — and F103's result that three of those
four are one gap is untouched, since none of them involves concatenation.

**A scope line the fix exposed.** Joining needs an end to join *at*, and only
**Angle and Curve have distinguishable ends**. Line, Wave, Point and Circle are
returned by a half turn or better (F102), so for those "which end" is not a
canonical choice and the joined figure is well defined only up to congruence.
Orbits quotient by rotation anyway, so the count is unaffected — but a notation
that wanted to name the two ends apart would have to break the symmetry first.
The operator inherits the alphabet's own limitation.

**The old claim is withdrawn, not deleted.** `concatenate-does-not-concatenate`
was true of the implementation as it stood, and is retained so a citation
reaches the correction instead of a missing entry.

**Postscript to F105 — the fix changed what KIND of thing the operator is.**
F104 put the six operators in one placement space as six *points*. After the
fix that is no longer true of concatenate, and the distinction is structural:

```
separation r across all 36 operand pairs      min     max   spread
superpose_concentric                        0.000   0.000    0.000
cross                                       0.000   0.000    0.000
nest                                        0.000   0.000    0.000
superpose_displaced                         2.200   2.200    0.000
concatenate                                 0.000   2.000    2.000
```

Five operators name **coordinates**. Concatenate now names a **condition** —
shift until they touch — and a condition traces a **surface** through the space
where a coordinate marks a point. Its separation moves with the operands because
contact depends on how far each mark reaches.

That matters for the charts: in a slice, a point-operator is one cell and a
surface-operator is a **locus running across it**. The slice renderer has to be
able to draw both, and the placement dial already shows why — CONTACT is the row
where the two figures meet, and that row sits at a different radius for every
pair of marks.

findings.title: the catalogue of charts is not a brainstorm, it is an enumeration of slices
findings.text:
Asked what charts could show transformations of one symbol and relations between
two, the tempting answer is a list of chart types. That list has no end and no
justification. The derivable answer comes from noticing what a chart *is*.

> A chart is a map from a structure to the plane, and it is **faithful** when the
> spatial relations in the display are the structural relations in the data.

So cataloguing charts means cataloguing structures — and for this material almost
every structure is one thing:

```
a cell holds a CONFIGURATION
a grid of cells is a SLICE of configuration space
therefore the catalogue of grids IS the enumeration of slices
```

Which closes the question. With k axes there are k one-axis strips and k(k−1)/2
two-axis grids, and nothing else is planar.

```
unary   which mark · rotation · reflection · scale · count        5 axes
        5 strips + 10 grids                                      15 slices

binary  A · B · separation · bearing · relative rotation ·
        relative scale · reflect-B                                7 axes
        7 strips + 21 grids                                      28 slices
```

**43 planar slices**, plus **19 layouts for a derived quantity** — a group, a
quotient, a metric, a relation — which are not slices and are listed with the
structure that forces each. 62 in total, and the count is derived rather than
brainstormed.

**The six operators are six points in one space.** Reading the definitions and
confirming against what they emit:

```
superpose_concentric   r=0.00   phi=0    s=1.0
cross                  r=0.00   phi=90   s=1.0
nest                   r=0.00   phi=0    s=0.4
superpose_displaced    r=2.20   theta=0  s=1.0
concatenate            r=2.10   theta=0  s=1.0
```

Bearing is undefined where r=0. Neighbouring pairs differ in **exactly one
coordinate**: concentric→cross is φ alone, concentric→nest is s alone,
displaced→concatenate is r alone. The corpus has sampled six configurations out
of a continuum and never looked between them.

**The schemas are regions, not a vocabulary.** Sweep B around A and the ten
"distinct" relational schemas resolve into a partition of one plane:

```
r = 0                   CENTER / PERIPHERY
0 < r < extent(A)       IN / OUT
r ~ extent(A)           CONTACT
r > extent(A)           NEAR / FAR
```

The boundaries are not conventions — they sit where the two figures start and
stop overlapping, which is a property of A's own extent. That changes the open
question from *which schemas are missing* to *which regions have never been
named*. The placement dial (`build/codex/charts/placement-dial.svg`) draws it,
and its own top row is the argument: at r=0 the bearing is undefined, so twelve
cells across are one configuration, and the degenerate axis shows itself.

**A defect the derivation exposed.** Putting the operators in one space made
`concatenate` and `superpose_displaced` adjacent — r=2.10 against r=2.20, a gap
4.5% narrower. They are the same placement, which is why they share an orbit in
almost every case. Worse, **concatenate does not concatenate**:

```
closest approach between its two strokes
   concatenate(Angle,Curve)   0.668
   concatenate(Curve,Curve)   0.411
   stroke sampling step       0.011
```

Gaps of 37 to 60 sampling steps. `components()` splits every concatenate output
into two pieces. Its own attestation reads *"arch followed by cup = the sine"*
(F42) and a sine is one connected curve. So the operator does not perform the
joining it is named for, and does not realise the LINK schema it was joined to at
F102 — **the count of uncovered schemas may be five, not four.**

**Deliberately not fixed in place.** Changing r would move the orbit count, the
chirality census and the schema join, and those have to be re-derived rather than
silently updated. Recorded as `concatenate-does-not-concatenate`, measured, with
that scope attached. This is a defect in the implementation and not a refutation
of F42: the corpus may well attest joining; this operator does not perform it.

**What the catalogue says is blocked, and why.** Two entries cannot be drawn yet
and both name the claim that blocks them — the depth ladder needs composition
past depth 2, and the modulation strip needs
`modulation-is-a-second-operator-family`, still undetermined. A catalogue whose
gaps carry their own reasons is more useful than one that lists only what is
already possible.

findings.title: up is not undetermined, it is SUPPLIED; and the grammar's gaps are one gap
findings.text:
F102 left four relational schemas without an operator and grouped three of them
loosely as "needing a direction". The operator's argument turns that from a
grouping into a result, and settles an open claim on the way.

**The argument.** A plane has no privileged up — which is why
`updown-is-meaningful` sat undetermined. But **no symbol is ever drawn on a bare
plane.** It is drawn on a *canvas*, and a canvas is a plane **plus a frame**. The
frame is not an addition to the medium; it is part of what makes it a medium.

Two routes, and both hold:

- **Rendered.** The frame is *specified*, not inferred. SVG fixes +x rightward
  and +y downward. Every artifact this project ships therefore has its up pinned
  by a standard, not by an assumption.
- **Physical.** The frame comes from a gravitational anchor, and the anchor
  **recurses without terminating**. Leave Earth and the Sun serves; leave the
  star system and the galactic core serves. Each step *replaces* the anchor
  rather than removing it. Its sign can even invert: inside a cosmic supervoid
  the pull is outward from every side, so down points away from the observer
  rather than toward a mass — and the canvas is still perfectly well oriented.

> **Orientation is always available and never canonical.** That is the structure
> of a gauge choice: it must be fixed before anything can be read, and no canvas
> fixes it canonically.

So the claim was mis-posed. "Is there an up" is answered — yes, by the canvas.
`updown-is-meaningful` upgrades from **undetermined** to **derived_given**.

**What actually survives as open.** Not whether up exists but whether it is
*shared*. The supervoid is the operator's own counterexample and it is a good
one: two readers, both well oriented, opposite signs. Within one canvas any use
of up/down is sound; across canvases only the *contrastive* uses transmit — a
relation between marks, not a reading of one mark against the frame. Registered
as `up-is-shared-across-canvases`, undetermined. `aether-is-upper` reads a single
mark against the frame, so that is the premise it now hangs from.

**The prediction, and the measurement.** If direction is what the canvas supplies,
then the schemas the corpus has *never built an operator for* should be exactly
the ones that need it. Each relation was reduced to the scalar it reads and that
scalar measured before and after turning the whole canvas, eight angles over four
figure pairs:

```
schema               operator                 drift      frame-free
IN / OUT             nest                     4.44e-16   yes
CENTER / PERIPHERY   superpose_concentric     1.33e-15   yes
NEAR / FAR           superpose_displaced      1.11e-16   yes
CONTACT              cross                    1.11e-16   yes
LINK                 concatenate              1.11e-16   yes
BALANCE              reflect_pair             3.49e-02   yes (sampling floor)
UP / DOWN            — none —                 2.20e+00   NO
FRONT / BACK         — none —                 4.40e+00   NO
```

**Every attested operator is frame-free, five of them to machine zero.** The
directional schemas drift by two orders of magnitude more.

> **The operator inventory is closed under change of canvas orientation.**

So the four gaps are not four gaps. **Three are one gap** — UP/DOWN, FRONT/BACK
and PATH need a frame, and were never going to appear in an inventory that does
not carry one. **PART/WHOLE is frame-free and mereological, and is a genuinely
separate absence.** That is a real correction to F102, which filed all four
together.

**Booleans were the wrong instrument.** The first pass asked "does the relation
still hold" and IN/OUT and BALANCE appeared to flip — a threshold sitting next to
a degenerate pair, flipping for numerical reasons and looking exactly like frame
dependence. A scalar has no threshold. The second thing it caught: BALANCE
*is* frame-bound when written as "B is the flip of A about the horizontal"
(drift 0.77) and frame-free when written as "these two are mirror twins"
(drift 0.035). **Naming the axis imports the frame.** The relation does not need
one; the phrasing did.

**What it costs to say the missing three.** They are expressible exactly when the
notation carries its own frame. The corpus already proposes this — "canvas
polarity, which way is positive on the frame, annotatable in the corner of the
canvas when needed" — and files it under *candidate conventions to test*. It is
not a convention and not optional: it is the necessary and sufficient addition
that makes three of the ten schemas sayable. Registered as
`directional-schemas-need-a-declared-frame`.

**Scope.** Measured over the attested operators at N=240. Says nothing about
whether the missing schemas are expressible in principle — only that they cannot
be expressed frame-free, and that a declared frame is what they cost.

findings.title: what a turn can say, what a mirror can say, and why A-beside-B is not B-beside-A
findings.text:
The operator inventory treats rotation and reflection as things you *do* to a
mark. The question never asked was what they can **say** — and the answer is not
uniform across the alphabet, which is the whole point.

> **A transformation distinguishes two states of a figure exactly when it is not
> in that figure's stabiliser.**

That is not a new measurement; it is what the two existing ones *mean*. The
stabiliser of a plane figure in O(2) is its symmetry group, and the number of
distinguishable images is that subgroup's index. F85 measured the rotation half.
The reflection half stood as `mirroring`, **undetermined** — "SymbolFolds shows
chirality; no rule stated". Here it is measured.

**The six marks, as subgroups of O(2).**

```
mark     group   rotation conveys                        mirror conveys
Point    O(2)    nothing — every turn returns it         nothing
Circle   O(2)    nothing — every turn returns it         nothing
Line     D2      an angle, but a half-turn returns it    nothing
Wave     C2      an angle, but a half-turn returns it    A SECOND STATE
Angle    D1      a full turn of distinct states          nothing
Curve    D1      a full turn of distinct states          nothing
```

**Exactly one mark is chiral, and it is the Wave.** A sine is odd, so a half-turn
returns it — that is why it groups with Line under rotation (F85). But no rotation
returns its reflection. Five of six marks cannot express handedness at all.

Calibrated in a gap **0.0799 wide** — the achiral cluster tops out at 0.0725 and
the chiral cluster begins at 0.1524 — and seeded from both sides by construction:
`X ∪ mirror(X)` maxes at 0.0356, while a spiral, an L, a comma and a swept
pinwheel bottom out at 0.1882. Two of my intended positive controls **failed**,
and correcting them was the informative part: a pinwheel of *chevrons* is not
chiral, because n rotated copies of a mirror-symmetric blade give D_n, which has
axes. A pinwheel is chiral only if the blade is swept.

**The Line cannot carry a direction.** The wiki's Line page says the Line
"introduces directionality — from one Point toward another" and is "orientable
(can be signed)". Geometrically the drawn Line is C2: a half-turn maps it to
itself, so *from* and *toward* are indistinguishable on the mark. The direction
belongs to the Line-as-construction (an ordered pair of points), not to the
Line-as-drawn. To make it visible you must break the C2 symmetry, which takes a
second mark — an arrowhead is an Angle, and the result is a composite. **Only
Angle and Curve, the two C1 marks, can carry a direction alone.**

**Composition manufactures handedness.** 1 of 6 marks is chiral; **34 of 80
orbits** are. Of those, 27 inherit it from a Wave operand and **7 have no chiral
part at all** — every operand achiral, the *placement* is not:

```
superpose_displaced(Point,Angle)   superpose_displaced(Curve,Point)
superpose_displaced(Line,Angle)    cross(Angle,Curve)
superpose_displaced(Line,Curve)    superpose_displaced(Curve,Circle)
superpose_displaced(Angle,Circle)
```

Two symmetric marks, set side by side, make a handed figure. The handedness is in
the arrangement.

**`reflect_pair` can never produce a chiral figure — 0 of 6, and it is forced.**
`A ∪ mirror(A)` is symmetric about that mirror by construction. The one operator
named for reflection is the one that cannot express handedness. Chirality enters
this system through *placement*, never through mirroring.

**The operand swap is a reflection.** The orbit structure quotients by rotation
**and** reflection, so it treats a figure and its mirror as synonyms. Re-running
the enumeration by rotation alone gives **88** signs against 80. Only 8 of the 80
split — and in all 8 the two sides are exactly the operand swap:

```
superpose_displaced(Point,Angle)  vs  superpose_displaced(Angle,Point)
superpose_displaced(Line,Angle)   vs  superpose_displaced(Angle,Line)
cross(Angle,Curve)                vs  cross(Curve,Angle)          ... and 5 more
```

> **A-beside-B and B-beside-A are enantiomorphs.**

Which collapses two of the corpus's claims into one. The wiki asserts
*composition is non-commutative: A→B ≠ B→A* and separately that *chirality* is a
transformation-layer member. These are **the same claim**: for the beside-operators
the non-commutativity IS the handedness, so if mirroring carries no meaning those
placements are commutative. The inventory is `80 if mirroring means nothing, 88 if
it does` — and `mirroring-is-meaningful` is registered undetermined, so the count
is `derived_given` on it. I predicted 114 before measuring and was wrong: a chiral
figure does not imply its twin was ever built, and for 26 of the 34 these
operators never construct the enantiomorph.

**The relational schemas, joined to the operators.** The corpus names ten;
six have a measured operator and four do not.

| schema | operator | |
|---|---|---|
| IN / OUT | `nest` | B inside A's region |
| CENTER / PERIPHERY | `superpose_concentric` | shared centre |
| NEAR / FAR | `superpose_displaced` | apart, not touching |
| CONTACT | `cross` | they cut each other |
| LINK | `concatenate` | joined end to end |
| BALANCE | `reflect_pair` | placed against its own mirror |
| **UP / DOWN** | — | needs a privileged vertical |
| **FRONT / BACK** | — | needs a distinguished direction |
| **PATH** | — | needs source told from goal |
| **PART / WHOLE** | — | mereological, not positional |

Three of the four gaps are the same gap: UP/DOWN, FRONT/BACK and PATH all need a
distinguished direction, and direction needs a trivial stabiliser. PART/WHOLE is
a different kind of gap and should not be filed with them. The corpus flags
UP/DOWN independently as "the one schema that does not obviously behave like the
others" because gravity breaks its symmetry — which is the same conclusion my
register reached as `updown-is-meaningful`, undetermined, from the other
direction. Two readings converging on one open question is worth more than either.

**Scope.** Depth 2, N=240 samples. One boundary case: orbit 41,
`superpose_displaced(Angle,Curve)`, measures 0.0725 against a 0.11 chirality
threshold yet splits at 0.0778 against a 0.073 rotation threshold — the single
figure where the two independent measurements disagree, both within 0.006 of
their boundaries. Everything else sits far from any decision.

findings.title: the orbit count was wrong three times over, and a drawn sheet is what caught it
findings.text:
The combination space has been published as **122 orbits, 118 unnamed** since F92.
It is **80 orbits, 76 unnamed**. Three separate defects, each hiding the next,
and none of them visible in the numbers — what exposed them was drawing all the
orbits on one sheet and noticing that several cells looked identical.

**1. The bucket key saw something the equality test ignores.**
`enumerate_space` compares figures only within a bucket, and the bucket key
carried a 12-bin histogram of distances from the centroid. That histogram is
rotation- and reflection-invariant, which is why it looked safe. It is not
invariant to **re-parameterisation**, and `same_figure` is: Hausdorff compares
point *sets* and does not care how densely a curve was sampled. `nest` scales one
copy to 0.4 and moves every radius; `reflect_pair` and `concatenate` lay the same
points down in different densities. Identical figures got different histograms,
landed in different buckets, and were **never compared to each other**.

```
all-pairs sweep of the 122 orbit REPRESENTATIVES
89 pairs were the same figure while sitting in different orbits
```

> **A bucket key must only see what the equality test sees.** Anything finer is
> not an optimisation; it is a silent change to the answer.

**2. The threshold was compensating for an under-resolved search.**
`same_figure` searched rotations in 18 steps — every 20° — and used a tolerance
of 0.14. Calibrating over pairs that are the same *by construction* (stacking
order is not part of a figure: `op(A,B)` versus `op(B,A)`) against pairs the
corpus separates (the six marks; one corner versus two):

```
steps=18   known-same max 0.1847   known-different min 0.0779   NO GAP EXISTS
steps=36   known-same max 0.0684   known-different min 0.0779   gap opens
steps=72   known-same max 0.0657   known-different min 0.0779   gap widens
```

At 20° resolution **no threshold separates them** — two copies of one figure
