offset by 13° never line up, so the tolerance had to be loosened until they
passed, and at 0.14 it also passed figures that differ. The fix is the search,
not the number. 36 steps, `TOL_SAME = 0.073`, in the middle of a real gap.

The test was also **not symmetric**: one side is subsampled and the other rotated,
and 9 of 5379 pairs changed verdict when the arguments were swapped. One of them
decided whether two angles and an angle-plus-arc are the same figure. Both
directions must now agree.

**3. Flattening threw the stroke boundaries away.**
`components()` recovers strokes by looking for a jump between them. Two strokes
that share an endpoint leave **no jump at all** — stack a circle on a circle and
every step is identical, seam included. Two consequences, both real:

- `reflect_pair(Circle)` runs the second copy backwards, so the path doubles
  back: a 180° turn read as a corner, scoring `singular`, while
  `superpose_concentric(Circle,Circle)` — *the same figure* — scored `smooth`.
  A 180° turn covers ground already covered, so it is a stroke boundary by
  definition. No mark turns past 33.7° and the sharpest genuine cusp measures
  123.0°, so the cut at 175° sits in a gap 50° wide on both sides.
- Seams that meet at a shallower angle cannot be recovered at all. So the
  boundaries are no longer guessed: `strokes(op, operands)` hands back what the
  operator actually emitted, and the key is computed from that.

**Where it ended up.**

```
                                    orbits   same-figure pairs in different orbits
published                             122                          89
bucket key fixed                       91                           -
+ threshold and symmetry fixed         82                           7
+ stroke boundaries kept               80                           4
```

The four residuals are understood, not unexplained. Three are
`nest(X,Angle)` against `nest(X,Curve)`: the inner mark is scaled to 0.4, small
enough that Hausdorff cannot resolve a corner from an arc, and the derived
curvature axis (F88) blocks a merge the metric would have made. The fourth is a
Point superposed on a Wave at a spot the Wave already covers — the same drawing,
a different composition, and the corpus does not settle which one an orbit is.

Within the partition it is now exact: **0 of 258 within-orbit pairs disagree and
0 of 5121 across-orbit pairs do**, where before there were 89.

**Two things the Point exposed on the way.** `components()` discards pieces
shorter than three samples, and a Point *is* one sample — so it vanished from
every figure it joined. The Sun-in-Circle was measured and drawn as a bare
circle. And `_draw` subsampled every third point, which turned a two-sample
piece into one point and rendered nothing: two cells came out blank. Both are
fixed where the operator is known, by asking it rather than inferring.

**Scope.** `same_figure` is still a threshold on a metric, so transitivity is not
guaranteed and the orbits are built by single-linkage grouping rather than by
quotienting. On this space it comes out exact; that is a measurement, not a
theorem. Depth is still 2.

**What this says about the method.** Every one of these was invisible in the
register, in the JSON, and in the tests. They became visible the moment 122
figures were drawn side by side and two cells in the same row looked the same.
The sheet was built to *show* the frontier; it turned out to be the instrument
that measured it.

findings.title: the category correction: UL is not phonetic, and the comparison was never available
findings.text:
F99 diagnosed an instrument problem — filled regions measured with stroke axes —
and proposed skeletonisation as the fix. The operator's correction went deeper
than the instrument:

> "It's unrealistic and unfair to compare UL directly to any phonetic alphabet."

That is right, and it invalidates the goal rather than the method. The six marks
are individuated by **symmetry order and curvature class** (F84/F85/F88), which
are geometric properties of a stroke. A phonetic letter is individuated by **the
sound it records**. Nothing maps one onto the other. The corpus's own
*Instruction Manual — Universal Symbology — Vocalization and Language* states
vocalization as a **goal**, not a result (F31), so the bridge that would license
the comparison does not exist yet.

> **Fixing the instrument would have produced a number for a comparison that has
> no meaning.** A better measurement of the wrong pair is still the wrong pair.

Registered as `ul-is-not-phonetic`, **derived** — from the individuation
criteria plus F31, not from taste. Note what it is not: it does not say the two
systems are unrelated, and it does not say the comparison can never be made. It
says the comparison is unavailable *until vocalization is worked out*, which is
deferred by the operator to another day.

**What survives.** The script material is real and worth shipping, just not as a
UL comparison. Four properties of a filled letterform need no stroke, no
skeleton and no tolerance:

```
holes       0 – 2        contours   1 – 3
aspect   0.12 – 2.44     ink      0.24 – 1.00
```

measured on real outlines from system fonts across Latin, Ge'ez, Devanagari,
Thai, Hangul, Arabic and Han. Registered as `script-topology-is-measurable`,
**measured** — a fact about how these typefaces draw these characters, not about
the scripts in the abstract. A different font gives different numbers.

**Consequence, shipped.** Writing systems become a separate supporting section,
compared **to each other**, offered as a convenience — and labelled, in the
artifact itself, as explicitly not a comparison to UL. `index.json` carries the
statement under `separate_from_ul`, so an agent that reads only the data cannot
miss it. It may become a UL comparison later. It is not one now.

**Scope:** this is a claim about categories, and the operator supplied it. It is
recorded as derived because the derivation stands on its own once stated — which
is worth noticing, since I had the same two premises in hand at F99 and drew the
narrower conclusion.

findings.title: cross-script comparison, attempted and NOT available
findings.text:
The plan was to measure letterforms from many scripts on the same two axes as the
six marks — symmetry order and curvature class — so a reader anywhere could see
where their own script sits. Real outlines were extracted with `fontTools` from
system fonts covering **Hangul, Han, Latin, Ge'ez, Devanagari, Thai and Arabic**;
35 letterforms measured.

**It does not work, and the failure is structural.**

```
28 of 35 letterforms collapsed into (C1, singular)
Latin O measured (C1, singular)      -- it should sit near (C-inf, smooth)
```

Diagnosed rather than patched. Latin `O` scores **0.1726** Hausdorff at a
half-turn; the ideal Circle scores **0.0155**. More than ten times the tolerance,
so it is not a tolerance problem. A typographic `O` is an **ellipse of optically
varying stroke weight, drawn as two closed contours** — an outer and an inner.

> **The axes are defined for STROKES. A letterform in a font is a filled REGION.**
> Measuring one with the other is a category error.

Widening the tolerance to ~0.18 would make every letterform read as symmetric —
and would destroy the measurement that separates the six marks 6/6. Making a
result appear by widening the instrument is the failure this whole project exists
to prevent, so the comparison is withheld rather than fudged.

**What would make it available:** skeletonisation — extract the medial axis of
each letterform, reducing a filled region to the stroke it represents, and
measure that. Registered as `cross-script-comparison-needs-skeletons`,
undetermined, with that as the success condition.

**Scope:** this rules out the *geometric* comparison. It says nothing against a
*structural* one — Hangul's featural design is documented independently of us,
and comparing UL's featural claims against it is a literature question rather
than a measurement.

findings.title: the Spiral needs a second operator family, not a missing parameter
findings.text:
F95 left the Spiral unreachable and offered the obvious excuse: the attested
operators have no **scale** parameter, so of course a figure that grows as it
turns cannot be built. That excuse was tested rather than accepted.

Scale was added as a placement parameter and the depth-2 search re-run.

```
closest approach to the Spiral, no scale      0.254
closest approach to the Spiral, with scale    0.212
match threshold                               0.140
```

It improves and does not arrive. So the gap is not a missing knob, and the
reason is structural: **every attested operator emits strokes that are
similarity copies of a mark**, and a similarity preserves "curvature zero,
constant, or periodic". No arrangement of such copies produces a stroke whose
curvature varies monotonically along its own extent.

That is exactly what the spiral does, and the third invariant of F95 measures it
— curvature per unit **arc length**, monotonicity score:

```
Spiral                                        1.000
best of 186 attested combinations, per stroke 0.889
```

> **Placement composes marks. Something else varies a mark.** Only the first is
> documented as an operator.

Call the second family **modulation**: vary a parameter along A's own extent,
rather than placing B relative to A. Two pieces of circumstantial evidence say
the corpus is already using it without listing it — the rotation table names
Angle and Curve "Modulations" (F6), and bar-position-on-a-stem varies a
parameter continuously along a mark (F68). Neither appears in any operator
inventory.

Circumstantial is not derived. Registered as
`modulation-is-a-second-operator-family`, **undetermined**, success condition:
find modulation stated as an operation anywhere in the corpus, or derive the
family boundary. `spiral-requires-scaling` is upgraded from undetermined to
**measured** — the name is now wrong for what it says, and is kept so citations
resolve.

**Scope:** measured over the 186 enumerated depth-2 combinations, not proved for
all compositions. Margin 0.111, and the nearest case is a near-degenerate
stroke. The two invariants that failed before this one are on the record in F95
and stay there; the third worked, which is not the same as the first two having
been unlucky.

findings.title: the multilingual layer already exists, and it teaches a retired inventory in five languages
findings.text:
`configs/lingua_beacon/glossaries/` carries full glossaries for **am, hi, id, sw,
tpi** — Amharic, Hindi, Indonesian, Swahili, Tok Pisin. Every one of them
teaches, in its own language:

| language | primitives taught | sorts taught |
|---|---|---|
| am | point, line, angle, curve, **boundary** | entity, relation, modifier, **claim** |
| hi | point, line, angle, curve, **enclosure** | entity, relation, modifier, assertion |
| id | point, line, angle, curve, **enclosure** | entity, relation, modifier, assertion |
| sw | point, line, angle, curve, **enclosure** | entity, relation, modifier, assertion |
| tpi | point, line, angle, curve, **enclosure** | entity, relation, modifier, assertion |

Against what this session measured:

- **Enclosure is in none of the 24 sheets** and in no measurement. The six marks
  are Point, Line, Angle, Curve, **Wave**, **Circle** — 3 symmetry classes x 2
  curvature classes, 6/6 (F84/F85/F88).
- **Wave is omitted entirely**, though it is measured C2-smooth and is
  load-bearing across the zodiac grammar, the Forces, and the `$` merger.
- `four_sorts` renders **`UWS-SORT-COUNT`, which is RETIRED**.
- The translations have already **drifted from each other**: Amharic says
  "boundary" and "claim" where the others say "enclosure" and "assertion", so
  there is no single thing being translated.

**This is the finding that should govern the new app's design: translation
multiplies whatever it translates.** Five languages times a retired inventory is
five times the error, and each copy is harder to correct than the original
because fixing it needs a translator. A multilingual layer built over unstable
content does not spread knowledge; it spreads a version of it and then freezes it.

The structural fix falls out of the grounding tiers. **The derived layer has no
words in it** — a symmetry order, a modular arithmetic, an orbit structure and a
glyph are the same in every language and are never translated. Only the tier-2
*assigned labels* are translatable, and those are exactly the layer that is least
load-bearing and most likely to change. So translations must be **keyed to the
claim and version they render**, such that retiring a claim invalidates its
translations automatically rather than leaving five orphans in circulation.

---

# THE CODEX ARTIFACT — v0, self-verifying

`tools/codex_export.py` · `tools/codex_primer.py` · `tools/codex_publish.py`

**725 KB, 19 files, no server, no build step at the far end.** Publishable
unchanged to the codex wiki, a git repo, an IPFS pin or an archive.

| | |
|---|---|
| `bundle.json` | the whole system in one fetch — 6 marks, 12 signs, 6 operators, 22 terms, 35 claims, 80 orbits (F101) |
| `llms.txt` | orientation for an agent |
| `primers/` | **five sheets**, SVG + JSON twin each |
| `verify/` | three runnable checks **and the three source sheets they measure** |

## The five sheets

| sheet | teaches |
|---|---|
| `crt` | `sign = (n mod 3) x (n mod 4)` — the two cycles drawn beating, meeting again only at 12 |
| `marks` | six marks = 3 symmetry classes x 2 curvature classes, drawn from the point sets the measurements ran on |
| `status` | the derivation-status system, demonstrated: one dependency chain that resolves, one that breaks |
| `operators` | composition as one parameterised family, each operation drawn as operands → result |
| `space` | 191 combinations → 80 orbits (F101); the frontier drawn as a field where **4 cells are filled and 76 are open** |

Every sheet obeys the four rules the critique set, and each is now a test: own
legend, status on the face, vector with a machine-readable twin, and the rule in
the arrangement rather than a caption.

## What makes it an artifact rather than a claim
From a bare copy of `dist/`, with nothing else present:

```
sign grammar verified against the drawn corpus      (12/12, 12/12, 24/24)
rendered glyphs read back as their own rule: True
attested composition reaches {1, 2, 4, inf}
```

**The evidence ships with the claim.** Found by copying `dist/` somewhere empty
and running it: the claim travelled and the three source sheets did not, so the
most important check — 12/12 measured off the actual corpus — died with "source
images not found". Whoever finds this can now check it rather than believe it,
offline, from the directory alone. That property is the point of the whole build.

## A defect class fixed at the root
Three separate font-coverage failures — `Z`, the square-arch, then the
half/hatched/cross status badges — silently vanished from rendered sheets. For a
portable artifact, depending on the reader's fonts is a design error. **Every
status badge is now drawn as SVG**, and the half-filled `derived_given` badge
turned out to be genuinely expressive: half derived, half open.

---

findings.title: CORRECTION to F91: symmetry-order completeness is weaker than I claimed
findings.text:
F91 concluded "the six marks are complete" from the closure criterion of F86 —
a primitive is a mark whose **symmetry order** cannot be produced by composing
others. That conclusion is too strong for what was shown.

Matching symmetry order is **not** the same as being the same figure. The Spiral
has order C1, which is trivially reachable, and the Spiral is not. So:

- **What holds:** the six marks are complete *with respect to symmetry order* —
  every order the corpus uses is either a mark's or is produced. That is what the
  criterion tested and it stands.
- **What does not follow:** that every figure the corpus draws is reachable. The
  Spiral is a live counterexample and the teardrop is unresolved.

`six-marks-are-complete` is narrowed in the register accordingly. The closure
criterion was a real advance — it correctly demoted `+` and Triangle from
primitive — but it is a **necessary** condition for primitiveness, not a
sufficient one, and I read it as sufficient for about an hour.

---

findings.title: the Spiral, and TWO failed attempts to prove what I believe about it
findings.text:
The Spiral matched nothing in 186 depth-2 or 33 depth-3 figures. The structural
reason seems clear: **every attested operator unions isometric copies —
rotation, reflection, translation — plus one fixed 0.4 scale in `nest`. None
changes scale continuously, and a spiral is a curve whose radius grows with
angle.** If that is right, the Spiral needs a **scaling operator**, and `scale` is
precisely the relational axis that appears on **none** of the 24 sheets as
meaning-bearing. The corpus would then be drawing a figure that requires the one
axis it never declares.

**I could not prove it, and both attempts are recorded because they failed.**

1. **Curvature monotonicity.** Predicted the spiral's curvature varies
   monotonically along its length while every mark's is constant or periodic.
   Measured: the spiral's turning-per-step ratio is **0.95** — flat, the same as a
   circle. The claim was wrong, and worse, the script printed my conclusion anyway
   because I had hardcoded the text instead of conditioning it on the result.
2. **Radial monotonicity.** Fraction of steps marching outward: spiral **0.967**,
   but the best depth-2 figure reaches **0.927** — `superpose_displaced(Curve,Line)`,
   which scores high only because of the order components are stacked in. The
   same concatenation artifact as F93, one level up. No clean separation.

**So the honest position:** the Spiral is **empirically unreachable** at the
depths enumerated, with a plausible structural reason and no invariant that
establishes it. Registered `spiral-requires-scaling`, undetermined, with the
success condition being either a clean invariant or an actual construction.

findings.title: depth 3, and the reachability join against the figures the corpus draws
findings.text:
Extended the space with the rotational family (`rot_family(mark, n)`) — the
depth-3 branch that is load-bearing, since it is what produces the higher
symmetry orders. Then checked every named composite the corpus actually draws.

| named figure | order | reachable |
|---|---|---|
| `+` cross | C4 | depth 2 — `cross(Line,Line)` |
| `$` Power | C2 | depth 2 — **`superpose_concentric(Line,Wave)`** |
| `∞` infinity | C2 | depth 2 — `reflect_pair(Wave)` |
| `⊙` Sun-in-Circle | C∞ | depth 2 — `superpose_concentric(Point,Circle)` |
| Triangle | C3 | depth 3 — `rot_family(Angle,3)` |
| hexagram "Order" | C6 | depth 3 — `rot_family(Angle,6)` |
| `×` cross at 45° | C2 | **artifact** — my enumeration fixed `cross` at 90°; with the angle kept it is depth 2 |
| teardrop "Life" | C1 | **scope gap** — needs `close(concatenate(Angle,Curve))`, and my depth-3 set was restricted to rotational families |
| **Spiral "Creation"** | C1 | **not reachable at any enumerated depth** |

`$ = superpose_concentric(Line, Wave)` is F57's reading of Power as the Line⊕Wave
merger, now *computed* rather than read off a sheet. And the hexagram turns out to
be `rot_family(Angle, 6)` directly — simpler than "two triangles at 60°".

findings.title: the fifth over-eager measurement, and the number gave it away
findings.text:
The first enumeration reported **singular 188 / smooth 3**, which is not a
plausible split. Figures are built by stacking point sets, which leaves a jump
between the last sample of one stroke and the first of the next; the curvature
measure read that jump as a corner. **12 of 14 all-smooth combinations scored
singular**, on gaps 100–300x the median sample spacing.

Fixed by splitting figures back into strokes at those gaps and measuring each.
116/75, and the six marks classify correctly.

That is the fifth measurement this session that fired too eagerly, and the third
caught only because a number looked wrong rather than because anything checked
it. The seed tests now pin it: `superpose(Circle,Circle)` must read smooth,
`superpose(Angle,Curve)` must read singular.

---

findings.title: the combination space, and the first computed thesaurus
findings.text:
`tools/symbol_combinations.py --enumerate`. Every pair of marks under each
attested operator, at depth 2.

```
combinations generated  : 191
distinct figures (orbits): 122      collapse 1.57x
by symmetry : C1 137 · C2 38 · C4 2 · Cinf 14
by curvature: singular 116 · smooth 75
orbits with a recorded meaning : 4
orbits with none               : 118
```

**The orbits are the thesaurus, and they are computed rather than curated.** Two
constructions that produce the same figure up to rotation and reflection are
synonyms. The largest synonym sets:

| orbit | figure | constructions |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | C2 singular | **8** — `reflect_pair(Line)`, `close(Line)`, `superpose(Point,Line)`, … |
| 21 | C∞ smooth | **6** — the Sun-in-Circle `⊙`, reachable six ways |
| 6 | C2 smooth | 6 |

That `⊙` has six independent derivations is the kind of fact a hand-built
thesaurus would never surface.

**Four orbits match a figure the corpus draws** — `+`, `∞`, `⊙`, and the Chaos
pair. **118 have no recorded meaning.** Those are the frontier: combinations the
system permits and has never named. They are born **undetermined**, with the
space persisted to `data/derivation/combination_space.json`. Filling 118 cells by
hand would manufacture exactly the laundered inventory this pass has been
clearing out.

**Stated limitation: depth 2.** Triangle and the hexagram need three-fold
iteration and do not appear here, though F91 shows they are reachable.

findings.title: RESOLVED: the six marks ARE complete, and F90's prediction is withdrawn
findings.text:
`symmetry-axis-truncation` offered three resolutions (F89). The evidence decides.

**Closure does not reach C3.** Implemented and tested: a chevron closed by the
chord between its feet is an **isoceles** triangle, which is C1. Only a 60-degree
chevron would close to an equilateral one. So `close` is not the route.

**The rotation parameter is free, not quantized.** The corpus draws rotations of

| angle | where |
|---|---|
| 45° | the Base 6 rotary table's eight orientations (F5) |
| 30° | the zodiac wheel (F60/F76) |
| 10° | the decan ring, 36 chevrons (F75) |
| 60° | the hexagram, two triangles superposed (F44) |
| 90° | `cross` → `+` (F9) |

45 is not a multiple of 30 or 60, and 60 is not a multiple of 45. **No single
quantization admits all five.** If rotation were locked to the rotary table's
eight positions, the hexagram and the entire zodiac wheel would be
unconstructible — and both are drawn.

**So superposition-with-rotation takes a free angle, and iterating it reaches
every order.** Built from the C1 Angle alone, using only attested operators:

```
Angle                                   C1
superpose(Angle, rot(Angle,120))        C1
superpose(that,  rot(Angle,240))        C3   <- Triangle
superpose(that,  rot(that,60))          C6   <- the hexagram
n = 2  3  4  5  6  7  8  ->  C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 C7 C8
```

**Verdict.** Triangle and the hexagram are **produced**, not posited. By the
closure criterion of F86, **the six marks are complete.**

**F90 is withdrawn.** Its prediction of a missing (C3, smooth) mark was
conditional on C3 being a *primitive* class. It is not. The empty cell was an
artifact of treating a produced order as a primitive one. Made, tested against
the closure computation, withdrawn on evidence — the register records
`why_withdrawn`, and the detector now refuses a withdrawal that does not.

findings.title: the factorisation PREDICTS a specific missing mark
findings.text:
If C3 is a genuine fourth symmetry class then the table is `4 x 2 = 8`, and every
cell must be filled. Testing all eight:

| order | singular / zero curvature | smooth curvature |
|---|---|---|
| C∞ | Point | Circle |
| C2 | Line | Wave |
| C1 | Angle | Curve |
| **C3** | **Triangle** (C3, M) — used constantly, never declared a mark | **a smooth three-fold figure (C3, F) — NOT FOUND** |

So the corpus is short of the predicted set by **two**: Triangle, which it uses
everywhere without listing, and a smooth three-fold figure, which appears on none
of the 24 sheets.

**A candidate was proposed and the test rejected it.** The triquetra looks like
the natural curved three-fold mark, but its arcs meet at cusps, so it measures
*singular* and belongs in the Triangle cell. The (C3, smooth) cell needs a
genuinely smooth three-lobed closed curve. The nearest thing in the corpus is the
**Spiral**, which is smooth but has no rotational symmetry at all — C1, not C3.

That the candidate was refused by the same test that generated the prediction is
the point. This is the first prediction in the project that names a *specific
missing primitive* rather than observing that the count is unsettled.

---

findings.title: the attested operators reach {1, 2, 4, ∞}, and the corpus uses C3 and C6
findings.text:
Closure computed over the six marks under every operator attested on a sheet —
superpose (concentric and displaced), cross, concatenate, nest, reflect-pair:

```
orders reached by attested composition : {1, 2, 4, inf}
orders used by the mark set            : {inf, 2, 1}
```

**C4 is reachable and is correctly not a primitive** — `cross(Line, Line)` is `+`,
which `SymbolFolds` draws. That validates the closure criterion of F86: a
primitive is a mark whose symmetry order cannot be produced by composing others.

But two figures the corpus uses are **unreachable**:

| figure | order | where |
|---|---|---|
| **Triangle** | C3 | the Round/Sharp/Flat panel — **and all four elements** |
| **Hexagram** | C6 | SolCenter, the glyph for Order / Æther |

This is not academic. **The element triangles are C3**, so the most-used figure
family in the entire corpus sits at a symmetry order the corpus's own composition
rules cannot reach.

Three resolutions, and the open question is which:

- **(a)** a primitive with three-fold symmetry is missing from the six;
- **(b)** rotate-and-superpose is licensed at every `n`, not only `n = 2`;
- **(c)** there is a further operator nobody has written down.

**(b) is the cheap one**: `cross` *is* rotate-and-superpose at `n = 2`, and it is
attested. The corpus documents the `n = 2` case and uses the `n = 3` output.

findings.title: the polarity axis is DERIVED: it is curvature, not gender
findings.text:
`mark-polarity` was the weakest link in F84 — the corpus calls it masculine/
feminine and nothing derived it. Measuring the largest discrete turning angle
along each stroke:

| mark | max turn | curvature | predicted | corpus says |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Point | 0.00 | none (0-dimensional) | M | M |
| Line | 0.00 | zero (straight) | M | M |
| Angle | 33.69 | **singular** (a corner) | M | M |
| Curve | 0.75 | smooth, non-zero | F | F |
| Wave | 8.49 | smooth, non-zero | F | F |
| Circle | 1.51 | smooth, non-zero | F | F |

**6/6.**

> **Rule: curvature zero or singular → "masculine"; smooth and non-zero →
> "feminine".**

That is the `singularity` shape axis of notes 022-026, appearing in the practice
— and it is a geometric property, not a gender. The corpus's own word for it was
the least derivable thing about it.

**Both axes of `6 = 3 x 2` are now derived**, so `marks-factor-3x2` moves from
`derived_given` to `derived` by propagation. The mark set is
**symmetry order x curvature class**, and neither factor is assigned.

findings.title: a closure operator is visible and unlisted
findings.text:
Round/Sharp/Flat pairs each open mark with a closed figure:

| open mark | closed figure | symmetry |
|---|---|---|
| Curve `∪` | **Circle** | C∞ |
| Angle `∧` | **Triangle** | C3 |
| Line `—` | **Square** | C4 |

Closing an open mark *changes its symmetry order*, which is exactly why the
closed figures occupy the orders the open set omits. This is the `closure` shape
axis that notes 022-026 derived, appearing in the practice — and it is an
**operator**, not an axis of the primitive set. It belongs in the operator
inventory, not the mark inventory.

---

# BUILD THINGS THAT CAN TELL YOU YOU ARE WRONG

The one finding in the process critique that was a discovery rather than a fix.
Tabulating every substantive artifact built this session:

| artifact | ctl | pred | prop | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| glyph round-trip | ✓ | ✓ | | caught 4 measurement bugs; the generator was right each time |
| sign-grammar verifier | ✓ | ✓ | | held out cusps 5-12; could have failed, didn't |
| derivation propagation | | | ✓ | caught `vertex-acts` + 3 more, hours after one went into claims.yaml |
| audit staleness guard | ✓ | | ✓ | caught a stale background job overwriting the register |
| detector seed-tests | ✓ | | | caught that my first negative control was fake |
| injectivity test | ✓ | | | would catch a reading too coarse to discriminate |
| term ledger | | | | content never checked against the sheets |
| axis census | | | | nothing read it at all |
| read log | | | | contained a phantom file until `find` was run |
| F46 | | | | wrong for ~40 findings until a legend was read |
| detector first runs | | | | 443 findings, ~85% noise, caught by eyeballing |
| notes state-of-play | | | | already stale against F84-F87 |

**6 with a failure mode, 6 without. Every one of the first six caught a real
error or could have. Every one of the last six propagated an error until
something external noticed. No exceptions either way.**

## The three properties are independent, not a ladder
| property | catches | this session |
|---|---|---|
| **control** | a check that cannot fail | the fake negative control |
| **prediction** | a rule fitted to what you already saw | cusps 5-12, derived before looking |
| **propagation** | a claim true when written and false now | `vertex-acts` |

**Only propagation catches errors introduced after authoring.** Everything else
checks at authoring time, when you are least likely to be wrong and most likely
to be confident. That is why `vertex-acts` is the session's most interesting
catch: nothing re-read it, the graph recomputed and demoted it.

## The corpus has none of the three
The primer set is consistency-checked at best — sheets agree with sheets. No
tests, no controls, no predictions, no round-trips, no propagation. **That is why
the Yin/Yang inversion survived for years: nothing in the system was able to
notice it.** Two sheets disagreed and neither could raise its hand.

That generalises past this corpus, and it bears on the stated purpose. A body of
knowledge that cannot detect its own inversions cannot stabilise anything. For an
artifact meant to orient an emerging mind, the error-detection is not packaging
around the content — it is the more transferable half.

## Made mechanical: two new detectors
`dangling-reference` and `unchecked-artifact` in `tools/corpus_audit.py`.

**Both fired on real defects in my own work on their first run:**

- `Mk3Banner` cited in the term ledger matched no file — the actual stem is
  `CosmicCypher_Mk3_2024-7-Cropped_Banner2`. Exactly the phantom-reference class
  that put a non-existent image in the read log.
- F84-F86 were written under `##` headings while all 83 other findings use
  `###`. My own notes were internally inconsistent.
- All three knowledge registries were unchecked: `axis_census.json` read by
  nothing, the other two read by tools but by no test.

Then the registry tests caught one more: `rotation-class` was sitting in the
census belonging to no axis kind. **I had already seen it printed as
`[UNCLASSIFIED]` earlier and moved on.** Having the information was not enough;
the check is what forced it.

And `unchecked-artifact` itself repeated the very mistake the critique had just
named — its first run walked all of `data/` and returned **220**, almost all
operational state. Scoped to knowledge registries it returns 3. That is the
fourth over-broad detector this session, written one message after criticising
the pattern, which is the strongest available argument that knowing the rule does
not substitute for a seeded test.

All eight detectors now have seed tests that pin both directions: quiet on clean
input, firing on input seeded with the defect. 25 tests across the three new
modules, green.

# WAVE 2 — THE COMBINATION SPACE, AND A PREDICTED MISSING PRIMITIVE

`tools/symbol_combinations.py`. The first computable answer to "are the six
complete?"

findings.title: the axis is TRUNCATED, so the classification predicts missing marks
findings.text:
A bounded plane figure's rotation group is `C_n` or the full circle group, so the
available classes are `n = 1, 2, 3, 4, …, ∞`. **The corpus uses exactly
{∞, 2, 1} and omits everything from 3 up.**

So "did we miss any primitives?" has a precise answer in two parts:

1. **Relative to the two axes, the six are closed.** 3 x 2 = 6 with no empty cell
   and no remainder. Nothing is missing *inside* the scheme.
2. **The symmetry axis itself stops at 2, and nothing yet derives why.** If the
   axis should be complete, then marks of symmetry C3, C4, C5 … are missing.

And the corpus already contains such figures — it just does not call them marks.
The CheatSheet's Round / Sharp / Flat panel illustrates the three geometries with
**Circle (C∞), Triangle (C3), Square (C4)**. `SymbolFolds` builds `+` from two
crossed Lines, and `+` has **C4**. The hexagram has **C6**.

**That is the primitive/operator boundary, visible for the first time:** the
corpus's implicit rule is that higher-symmetry figures are *produced*, not
*posited*. `+` is not a primitive because crossing two C2 Lines at 90° yields C4.
A primitive is a mark whose symmetry cannot be produced by composing others —
which is a **closure criterion**, and the first one this question has had.

**The open question, now crisp and derivable:** is `{∞, 2, 1}` the set of
symmetry orders that cannot be composed from each other? If yes, six is provably
complete. If no, the missing orders name the missing primitives. Registered as
`symmetry-axis-truncation`, status undetermined.

findings.title: the trichotomy IS rotational symmetry order, and that is a derivation
findings.text:
The corpus asserts three classes with prose labels ("Geometrically Balanced",
"change depending on Orientation", "are Modulations"). Sampling each mark as a
point set and rotating it:

```
mark        90deg   120deg   180deg   symmetry order   class
Point      0.0000   0.0000   0.0000   infinite         invariant
Circle     0.0050   0.0057   0.0062   infinite         invariant
Line       1.0000   0.8660   0.0000   2 (C2)           orientation-bearing
Wave       0.5994   0.6556   0.0000   2 (C2)           orientation-bearing
Angle      0.7083   0.6200   0.7059   1 (C1)           modulating
Curve      1.0081   0.8992   0.7289   1 (C1)           modulating

measured classification == the corpus's stated trichotomy: True
```

**6/6.** The three classes are the **order of the mark's rotational symmetry
group**: infinite, 2, 1. The Wave qualifies because a sine is an odd function, so
a half-turn about its centre returns it — which is why it groups with the Line
and not with the Curve.

That converts an asserted taxonomy into a derived one. It also explains the
labels: a C∞ figure cannot indicate a direction at all, a C2 figure indicates an
axis but not a sense, and a C1 figure indicates both.

findings.title: the six marks factor 3 x 2, the same CRT shape as the zodiac
findings.text:
Two axes, and one of them is provable:

| | masculine | feminine |
|---|---|---|
| **invariant** | Point | Circle |
| **orientation-bearing** | Line | Wave |
| **modulating** | Angle | Curve |

`6 = 3 x 2`, every cell filled exactly once, and `gcd(3,2) = 1` so
**`Z/6 ≅ Z/3 × Z/2`** — structurally the same fact as `Z/12 ≅ Z/3 × Z/4` (F48).
The rotation class is provable (F5); the polarity is stated in the rotation
table's left margin (F7).

**This reframes `UWS-PRIMITIVE-COUNT`.** The ledger records the question "how
many primitives" as RESOLVED-AS-MALFORMED. That verdict survives but the reason
sharpens: the count is malformed because the set is a **product of two axes**, so
asking for one number is asking which factor you meant. 3 and 2 and 6 are all
correct answers to different questions.

findings.title: F30 RESOLVED: the CheatSheet has Yin and Yang inverted; the AI Primer does not
findings.text:
`AI_Primer-UniversalSymbology-v02a.png` and
`UniversalSymbology-CheatSheet-ReferenceImage.png` are the **same sheet**, same
2100x1200, same panel layout. Cropping the same panel from both:

| | `∧` up | `∪` down |
|---|---|---|
| **AI_Primer v02a** | **Yang** | **Yin** |
| **CheatSheet-ReferenceImage** | Yin | Yang |

Everything else in that panel is identical — Mind, Body, Reality/Constant, Aura/
Singleton, Destiny/Variable. Only the two labels are swapped.

**The AI Primer is the correct one.** Yang is active and upward by the received
convention, and — the stronger argument — it agrees with the *same sheet's own*
modality row, which gives the Angle Act/Action and the Curve Pass/Passion. The
CheatSheet contradicts itself; the AI Primer does not.

So F30 ("Yin and Yang appear inverted") and F70's "internal contradiction" were
both real, and the fault is localised to one artifact rather than to the system.
Ledger updated: `Yin -> Curve` and `Yang -> Angle`, primary, with the CheatSheet
reading recorded as the error.

**This matters more than a label swap.** `UniversalSymbology-CheatSheet-
ReferenceImage.png` is the image the repository README links as *"Basic
Translation Instructions for Universal Symbology"* — so the inverted version is
the public face of the corpus, and the corrected one sits beside it unlinked.

Also new from the AI Primer, which the CheatSheet lacks: each of the six marks
carries a **secondary name** — Point/`Archor` (a typo for Anchor), Line/Edge,
Angle/Arch, Circle/Shape, Wave/Path, Curve/Arc. That is exactly F8's "secondary"
column from the rotation table, which makes the two sheets corroborate at the
naming level too.

# CRITIQUE OF THE PRIMER SET

Requested 2026-09-10. The sheets are prototypes for teaching Universal Symbology
to humans and AI alike. This is written from the position of having been the AI
reader — what I could extract, what cost me, and what I got wrong.

## Inventory, with honest depth

24 image files. None uninspected, but at two depths:

- **13 measured closely this session** (cropped, upscaled, pixel-analysed):
  Base12_signs, Base36_Decans, CosmicFamilies, base24_cusps, SolCenter,
  NaturesAndModalities, SpiralCenter, Base6Set, CheatSheet,
  Instructions_CheatSheet-01a, Mk3 StarDisk, Mk3 Banner, AI_Primer.
- **11 viewed once in an earlier session**, findings recorded, not re-examined:
  PointShapeLineWaveAngleCurve, 3CoreSymbolMergers, SymbolFolds, Base6_rotary,
  Base16_Redux, Base9_Modals, CrossSet, VideoGamesProgrammingReactRedux,
  IntuitionSensingThinkingFeeling, Base3_modality, ZodiacSignSymbols.

**Correction to the read log:** it listed a "Mk3 composite @2048" that is not in
this repository. And `Base6_rotary` is 3278x2125 — almost certainly seen
downsampled, so its eight-orientation detail deserves a second pass at full
resolution.

## The central critique

**The corpus is roughly 80% dictionary and 20% grammar, and only the grammar
taught me anything.**

I learned the system from about four sheets; the other twenty were confirmation.
The four that worked share one property — **the rule is visible in the
arrangement, not stated in a caption**:

- **Base12_signs** — all twelve as one continuous waveform makes the 3-cycle and
  the 4-cycle *visible*. Twelve table rows would not have taught me that. This
  25 KB file is the most valuable artifact in the set.
- **Base6_rotary** — six features x eight orientations; two rows constant, four
  not. A proof by display.
- **base24_cusps** — each cusp glyph is visibly its two neighbours fused.
- **SymbolFolds** — composition rules *with their outputs*.

The CheatSheet has the largest coverage in the set and taught me almost nothing
structural. I took confirmations from it, not rules. Dictionaries do not teach
grammar.

## Four defects across the whole set

1. **Nothing marks what is derived.** Every sheet asserts with uniform
   confidence. A reader cannot tell "Point and Circle are rotation-invariant"
   (provable with a protractor) from "Fire is the up-unbarred triangle"
   (undetermined). For a primer aimed at an emerging mind this is the most
   serious defect: it teaches content without teaching how to grade content.
2. **No machine-readable layer.** Recovering the grammar took cropping,
   upscaling, flood-fills and comb-fitting — archaeology to recover what a
   caption could have stated. It is also fragile: F46 was my error, caused by
   inferring from a sheet with no legend, on a question the Base12 legend answers
   in three glyphs.
3. **No canonical version or provenance.** AI_Primer and CheatSheet are the same
   sheet with Yin/Yang swapped (F83) and nothing says which supersedes which.
   That is how the inverted one became the README's public face.
4. **Raster only.** `Instructions_CheatSheet-01a` is 2.5 MB and 43 megapixels of
   the same content as the 2100px version.

## Per sheet

**Working — keep and extend**

| sheet | critique |
|---|---|
| Base12_signs | Best in the set; carries its own legend. **Never states the arithmetic** — shows `n mod 3` and `n mod 4` without naming them, so a reader sees the pattern and cannot name it. |
| Base6_rotary | Proof by display. The eight orientations are not labelled with their angles, so invariance is visible but not measurable. |
| base24_cusps | Shows composition beautifully. Does not say which two signs each cusp lies between. |
| Base36_Decans | Good three-group legend. 36 satellites and nothing says which is decan 1, 2 or 3. |
| SymbolFolds | The best evidence that the system is productive rather than enumerated. |

**Good structure, undercut by presentation**

| sheet | critique |
|---|---|
| SolCenter / SpiralCenter | The Sun-vs-Spiral contrast — one pair at rest, the same pair in motion — is the single best idea in the corpus. Undercut by unlabelled corner stacks (which I misread) and by conflating Æther/Nether with Order/Chaos against three other sheets. |
| CosmicFamilies | **The derivation of the 4+2 split is in this sheet and is invisible.** Nothing says the four panels are the four opposite-direction element pairs. Ring marks are ~20px. |
| NaturesAndModalities | The 3x4 grid *is the layout of the page* — the most important structural fact in the system — and the sheet never says so. The largest missed opportunity in the set. |
| Base6Set | Clean and correct. Does not say the three "Dualities" are the three rotation classes, which is what makes them non-arbitrary. |

**Reference rather than teaching:** CheatSheet / AI_Primer (max coverage, min
structure; **AI_Primer should be canonical** — correct Yin/Yang plus the secondary
names), Instructions_CheatSheet-01a (regenerate from vector or drop), CrossSet /
Base9_Modals / Base16_Redux / Base3_modality (small, focused, sound).

**Carrying known problems**

| sheet | problem |
|---|---|
| ZodiacSignSymbols | Two enharmonic errors — Sagittarius `G#(B♭)` should be `A♭`, Pisces `B(B♭)` should be `C♭` (F41). |
| CheatSheet | Yin/Yang inverted (F83) — and it is the README's linked image. |
| Mk3 2024 Banner | Contains the 2.45 GHz water-resonance falsehood (F79); photographic backgrounds fight the glyphs; verified structure and numerology carry equal visual weight. |
| Mk3 StarDisk | Measurable but unteachable — no legend, dark neon on black, ~60 elements unlabelled. I recovered θ₀ = 60.1° from it; a human learner recovers nothing. |
| IntuitionSensingThinkingFeeling | Borrowed MBTI taxonomy; category fit never verified. |

## What "much better" looks like

1. Fix the three known errors before anything propagates further: Yin/Yang, the
   two note names, the 2.45 GHz claim.
2. Make **AI_Primer canonical**; retire or mark-superseded the CheatSheet.
3. **Every sheet carries its own legend.** Non-negotiable; its absence caused the
   only real misreading in 83 findings.
4. **Put derivation status on the face of the sheet** — a one-glyph badge per
   relation: derived / given / undetermined.
5. **Ship vector plus a machine-readable layer.** `tools/symbology_glyph.py`
   already emits SVG whose `<desc>` carries the rule and the status.
6. **Add the sheet that does not exist:** one that states
   `sign = (n mod 3) x (n mod 4)` and shows the two cycles beating against each
   other. It is the central fact of the system and no artifact says it.

**And the thing I would push hardest**, from having been the reader: for teaching
an AI the most effective artifact is not an image — it is a **generator with a
round-trip check**. A model that can *regenerate* the glyphs from the rule has
learned the system; one that can recognise them has memorised it. That is why a
25 KB waveform strip outperforms a 43-megapixel cheat sheet by a wide margin.

# ARE THE PRIMITIVES COMPLETE?

findings.title: "Friendship" lands exactly on the repo's already-verified hexagram code
findings.text:
F49 read the Natures sheet's subtitle *"Friendships (Group Behaviors)"* as
`n ± 2 (mod 12)` — the sextile — checked 12/12 against the twelve cells.

The repo independently carries `tools/sign_pairs.py`, whose verified result is
that **aspect ÷ 30° equals the Hamming distance** between the signs written as
six-bit words (the classical twelve tidal hexagrams). `sp.verify()` returns
`True — all 66 pairs`.

So the sheet's social predicate should be Hamming distance exactly 2. It is:

```
Aries        + Gemini        100000 / 111000   hamming=2    60 deg sextile
Taurus       + Cancer        110000 / 111100   hamming=2    60 deg sextile
Gemini       + Leo           111000 / 111110   hamming=2    60 deg sextile
...
Pisces       + Taurus        000000 / 110000   hamming=2    60 deg sextile

all 12 friendship pairs at Hamming distance 2: True
```

**12/12.** Two lines of work that never met — a 2024 primer poster about group
behaviour, and a content-generation tool built to turn one verified isometry into
sixty-six posts — agree that "friendship" is a two-bit difference in a six-bit
word.

Note what this is and is not. It does **not** show that the sextile *means*
friendship; `sign_pairs.py` is explicit that it "does not claim the aspect MEANS
anything". What it shows is that the sheet's predicate has an exact arithmetic
definition already verified in this repo for an unrelated reason, so the two
artifacts can be cited against each other. The word "friendship" remains a
tier-2 assignment sitting on a tier-0 structure.

Notation aside worth seeing: the words above are a **thermometer code** — Aries
`100000` through Virgo `111111` filling up, then Libra `011111` through Pisces
`000000` emptying. The waxing and waning halves of the year, written as a bit
filling and draining. That is why `n ± 2` is always two flips.

## Ledger integrity — 7 of 20 VERIFIED claims cite evidence that is not in that repo

Found while validating my own additions. Every claim in
`vendor/universal_language/claims.yaml` was checked for whether its `evidence:`
path resolves **inside that repository**. Eight do not:

| claim | tier | evidence path | actually lives in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CODE-GOLDEN-SHADOW-DUAL-COMPOUND` | VERIFIED | `tests/test_symbol_geometry.py` | **ul_agent** |
| `CODE-SHELL-ISOMETRY-IS-CHIRAL` | VERIFIED | `tests/test_symbol_geometry.py` | **ul_agent** |
| `CODE-INSCRIPTION-WEB` | VERIFIED | `tests/test_symbol_geometry.py` | **ul_agent** |
| `CODE-LAW-PER-WINDOW` | VERIFIED | `tests/test_symbol_geometry.py` | **ul_agent** |
| `CODE-ICOSIANS-ARE-E8` | VERIFIED | `tests/test_icosians_and_gaps.py` | **ul_agent** |
| `CODE-TAMMES-FORCES-THE-SOLIDS` | VERIFIED | `tests/test_icosians_and_gaps.py` | **ul_agent** |
| `CODE-OCTONIONS-FROM-HAMMING` | VERIFIED | `tests/test_icosians_and_gaps.py` | **ul_agent** |
| `GROUNDING-BY-SELF-DENOTATION` | ARGUED | `docs/grounding/00-self-denotation.md` | **ul_agent** |

All eight files exist — in the *other* repo. Written as bare relative paths, they
read as local and are not.

**Why this matters at the VERIFIED tier specifically.** The file's own header says
VERIFIED "requires `evidence:` resolving to a real test/proof artifact", and its
intended CI check is "VERIFIED entries must have an `evidence` path that exists
and a test that passes". From a bare clone of `universal_language` — which is how
an outside reader or an AI following the citation would get it — **seven of the
twenty VERIFIED claims cannot be checked at all**. The header block also notes
those CI checks are "not yet implemented", which is why nothing has caught it.

This is the exact gap I avoided for `UWS-SIGN-GRAMMAR-IS-MODULAR` by vendoring the
verifier and its three sheets into `research/notes/063-the-sign-grammar/`. Doing
so cost 572 KB and made the claim checkable where it lives.

**Three ways to close it, not taken — owner's call:**
1. **Vendor** each cited artifact next to its claim, as note 063 does. Honest and
   self-contained; costs duplication, and the CODE-* tests may pull in more of the
   ul_agent tree than is worth copying.
2. **Qualify the paths** — a convention like `ul_agent:tests/test_symbol_geometry.py`
   — and teach the checker that prefix. Cheap, and it makes the cross-repo
   dependency visible instead of disguised.
3. **Implement the CI check first** and let it fail, so the gap is on the record
   before anyone decides what to do about it. Consistent with this repo's own
   negative-result discipline.

Whichever is chosen, the current state is a tier claiming more than its evidence
supports, which is the thing the ledger exists to prevent.

## The audit harness — what the hand-reading turned into

`tools/corpus_audit.py`, `data/audit/discrepancy_register.json`,
`data/audit/term_ledger.json`, `tests/test_corpus_audit.py`.

Policy set by the owner, 2026-09-10: register everything with evidence and
auto-fix only the clearly unearned; geometry measured off a bitmap beats prose
while a name stated only in a document stands unless an image contradicts it;
scope is the 729 published pages plus the symbology core.

### First full run — and the shape of the result was the surprise

| detector | findings | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `evidence-path` | **8 → 0** | VERIFIED/ARGUED claims citing artifacts in the other repo. **Auto-fixed**: qualified as `ul_agent:…` so the cross-repo dependency is visible instead of disguised as local. |
| `term-collision` | **7** | terms with unsettled senses, read from the ledger |
| `security-overclaim` | **1** | the one live "provably secure" (stale build; source already corrected) |
| `masked-exception` | **3** | `json.dumps` in a logging path with no `default=` |
| `underclaim` | **64** | published pages about a subject that never state the verified result |

**64 underclaims against 1 overclaim.** That is the session's thesis, quantified:
on the published surface this corpus's dominant fault is not saying too much, it
is failing to say what it has already proved. An audit built only to trim
overclaims would have found one page and left sixty-four pages weaker than the
evidence supports.

`wiki/Astrological_Aspect` names all five classical aspects and never mentions
that aspect ÷ 30° is a Hamming distance, verified over all 66 pairs in this repo.
`wiki/216_State_Space` names all six marks and never says two of them are
rotation-invariant. Those are not errors — they are the wiki being poorer than
the work behind it.

### Calibrating the detectors was most of the work, and twice they were wrong
Recorded because the first numbers were worthless and would have been believed.

- `security-overclaim` first returned **102**; 101 were the source documents
  *discussing* quantum resistance, which is their subject. Fixed by requiring an
  assertive frame binding the phrase to a subject, and by scoping the phrase test
  to published surfaces — the source documents' faults are argument-level (F71)
  and need reading, not regex.
- `underclaim` first returned **303**, including a page about the 120-cell
  matched on the word "element". Fixed by requiring several specific topic terms
  and a minimum page length.
- `term-collision` first returned **27** — all tables, where a page listing four
  elements against four faculties scored four collisions. Tightened to a binding
  pattern, and it returned **0**, which was worse: **the collisions this corpus
  actually has are in images.** "Æther" and "Nether" appear in none of the eight
  `.docx` sources. A text scanner is looking in the wrong place, and a detector
  blind to its own known-true instances is mis-scoped, not strict. Replaced with
  a hand-populated **term ledger** — 22 terms, 29 senses — which is also the
  disambiguation table the wiki needs.

Two bugs in my own harness, both caught by writing its tests: the evidence-path
detector re-flagged the paths it had just fixed, and running one detector marked
every other detector's findings resolved. `tests/test_corpus_audit.py` pins each
detector twice — quiet on clean input, firing on seeded input.

### The regression error was mine after all, and it is fixed
Four full runs settle it:

| run | result |
|---|---|
| clean tree, my module absent | `FAILED (failures=5)` |
| my module, numpy/PIL at module scope | `FAILED (failures=5, errors=1)` |
| same, repeated | `FAILED (failures=5, errors=1)` |
| my module, imports deferred into `setUpClass` | **`FAILED (failures=5)` — identical to clean** |

`unittest discover` imports every module before running any test, so a
module-level `import numpy` in a new test file is paid by the whole suite. My
first reasoning — "it runs at position 154, the failure is at position 4" —
was wrong for that reason. Import cost went 25 MB → 3 MB and the error went away.

The mechanism is still not fully explained: 25 MB on a machine with 21 GB free,
and a `sys.path` insert that four other test modules already make. What is
established is the cause and the fix, over four runs. The reason it surfaced as
an *error* rather than a failure is registered separately as **AUD-0011** — the
logging path cannot serialise a MagicMock, so it threw while reporting and
replaced the real fault with a `TypeError` about JSON.

### Operational hazard — a background job overwrote work done after it started
A `corpus_audit.py` run launched before the term-collision detector was rewritten
finished **after**, and its last step wrote the register using the superseded
detector — silently, and with plausible-looking numbers (76 findings, 8
evidence-path rows that had already been fixed, 0 term collisions).

The tool source survived because the stale job's file write had happened at
launch; only the register was clobbered. Caught by noticing that
`evidence-path` reported 8 when claims.yaml already carried the qualified paths.

**Guard added.** The register now records `written_by` (a hash of the tool) and
`detectors` (the set that produced it), and the tool warns when either disagrees
with what is currently defined:

```
! register was written by a different detector set
  (differs on: masked-exception, security-overclaim, term-collision)
  -- it may be stale; re-run to regenerate
```

General lesson, not specific to this tool: **a long-running process holds the
code it started with.** Any background job that writes shared state can undo work
done while it ran, and the result looks like a normal successful run.

## Derivation status — the principle applied, starting with my own claims

**Owner, 2026-09-10: everything has to be derived, not asserted. What cannot be
derived yet is UNDETERMINED and awaiting derivation.**

That is a correction to the tier scheme, not just a standard for new work. Tier 2
reads "assigned — a design choice, recorded as one", and it conflates two
different things: something genuinely chosen, and something not worked out yet.
Calling the second a choice closes an open question. It is an overclaim about our
own certainty rather than about the system — and this repo has already caught
that shape once, in `UWS-SORT-COUNT`'s retirement: *"the DESIGN-CHOICE tier was
satisfied FORMALLY while empty SUBSTANTIVELY... the signature of laundered
residue."*

`data/derivation/derivation_register.json` records every semantic claim by
status: **derived · derived_given · measured · undetermined · conventional**.

### The rule that cannot be kept by care alone
> **A derivation routed through an undetermined premise is itself undetermined.**

`depends_on` makes that checkable. On its first run it demoted **four of my
eleven** "derived" claims — including one registered in `claims.yaml` an hour
earlier:

| claim | rests on | which is |
|---|---|---|
| `hamming-gives-rotation-class` | `element-bit-assignment` | undetermined |
| `aether-is-upper` | `updown-is-meaningful` | undetermined |
| `phase-is-harmony` | `waveform-reading-is-intended` | undetermined |
| `cusp-closure` | `direction-bit-is-n-mod-2` | **measured**, not derived |

They are now `derived_given`, naming the premise. That is not a demotion to
assertion: the reasoning holds, its foundation is open, and keeping the
distinction is what stops a conditional result being cited as unconditional.

### One claim of my own did not survive at all
`vertex-acts` — "an angle is a vertex and so acts" — is **withdrawn to
undetermined**. A vertex concentrates curvature: geometric and provable. "A
vertex *acts*": not that. The step from a geometric fact to an agentive reading
has nothing in between, which is exactly the move `F-003` records as this
project's failure mode, and I made it while writing the guard against it.

Its two companions survive, and one got sharper for the audit: I had written that
a concave form "collects what **falls** into it", which smuggles in gravity and a
direction of down. **Containment needs neither** — a concave form bounds a
region, and what enters is contained. That is the derivation.

`UWS-MODALITY-SEMANTICS-ARE-GEOMETRIC` in `claims.yaml` has been corrected in
place: statement, scope and notes. It claimed three marks; it now claims two.

### Where the whole inventory stands
**7 derived · 4 derived_given · 2 measured · 6 undetermined · 2 conventional.**

Only two things are filed conventional, and each has to argue it *cannot* be
derived — the astrological names (external referent, predates the notation) and
the Golden Dawn colours. Everything else is either derived or queued.

### What to do with an undetermined item in the meantime
1. **Use it.** The notation works without the derivation; usability does not wait.
2. **Mark it at the point of use**, not in a footnote, so nothing inherits an
   unearned status by proximity.
3. **Carry its success condition**, so the backlog is a research queue rather
   than a disclaimer. `element-bit-assignment` has a live candidate worth testing
   — fire rises, water falls, so the direction bit may follow from buoyancy — but
   that is physics imported into geometry and it must be argued, not waved at.
4. **Prefer a derivable alternative** to a convention where one exists.
5. **Never let it be load-bearing for something claimed as derived.** That is the
   propagation rule, and it is the one now enforced.

---

## Toward the comprehensive map — the relational axes, and one real gap

The larger goal is a map of meaning where symbols relate by position, placement,
count, orientation, scale and so on. The register carries the skeleton, seeded
only with what has been measured:

| axis | status | what is known |
|---|---|---|
| **position, linear** | derived | bar height on a stem = ordinal rank, 7 levels + 2 open ends |
| **count** | derived | one vs many: Point/Line against Circle/Wave |
| **orientation** | derived | rotation class — which marks can carry direction at all |
| **superposition** | derived_given | concentric = harmony, displaced = discord |
| **adjacency** | derived_given | adjacent signs fuse into a closed cusp glyph |
| **composition** | derived_given | Air = Fire + Line; the crossbar IS the Level mark |
| **position, angular** | measured | wheel angle = sign, θ₀ = 60° across five years |
| **placement** | undetermined | modality rides the apex, forces flank the base — consistent, unexplained |
| **sequence** | undetermined | the Base 8 cycle order |
| **mirroring** | undetermined | `SymbolFolds` shows chirality; no rule stated |
| **scale** | **undetermined — and empty** | |

**The scale row is a finding, not a gap in my reading.** Across 24 sheets and 8
documents, **no artifact uses size as a meaning-bearing dimension.** Every mark is
drawn at whatever size the layout wants, and nothing anywhere reads a size. Either
the system has not reached that axis, or scale is deliberately non-semantic —
which would itself be a derivable claim, since a notation whose marks are
scale-invariant is making a statement about what it can express.

That is a direct question for the owner, and it is one of the axes named in the
goal.

---

## Glyphs, generated rather than traced — and the round trip that checks them

`tools/symbology_glyph.py`, `tests/test_symbology_glyph.py`.

**Tracing the sheets would have been near-worthless.** It produces vectors that
assert exactly what the bitmaps assert, including their mistakes — the two
enharmonic note errors on the concordance card, the Yin/Yang inversion — and
makes all of them typeable, quotable and permanent.

The glyphs do not need tracing, because they are computed. The generator takes
`n` and emits geometry from `n mod 2`, `n mod 3`, `n mod 4`; there is no table
lookup anywhere in it. **The SVG is the derivation, executed.** If the rule were
wrong the glyph would come out wrong and visibly so, which a trace can never do.

### The round trip
Each glyph is rendered and then measured back **blind**, by the same three
readings used on the source sheets: the edge carrying two ink runs is the foot
side (direction), a flanking rule widens the glyph past its own width
(baseline), and apex width relative to gesture width separates square from arc
from angle (geometry).

**12/12.** And visually the output is indistinguishable from the Base 12 sheet's
twelve marks, having never seen them.

Two checks make that mean something:

- **Injectivity** — a glyph rendered for `n` must satisfy the expectation for `n`
  and for no other sign. Without it, 12/12 could just mean the measurement is too
  coarse to tell anything apart.
- **A working negative control**, and my first attempt at one was fake. I
  collapsed `GEOMETRY` to a single value and expected the round trip to break. It
  did not — `features()` and `build()` read the same tuple, so drawing and
  expectation moved together and still agreed. **A control that perturbs both
  sides tests nothing.** The real control perturbs the renderer only, holding the
  expectation fixed; then it fails, as it must.

### The generator refuses to assert what it does not know
`element-bit-assignment` is UNDETERMINED, so every SVG carries in its `<desc>`
which of its features are derived and that *which* element occupies which
bit-pair is not. A glyph pack that silently asserted that mapping would be
precisely the trap that generating-instead-of-tracing exists to avoid — and a
test pins that the disclosure is present.

### Four measurement bugs, all mine, all caught by the round trip
Worth listing, because each was the *reader* being wrong while the generator was
right, and telling those apart is the entire point of having a round trip.

1. Anchored on the densest row — which works on the source sheets because they
   **draw** two horizontal rules, but a generated glyph has none unless the
   crossbar bit is set, so the densest row was a square's flat top.
2. Measured foot **run length** for the baseline — but the diagonal foot of an
   angle is just as long, so unbarred Aries read as barred.
3. Mid-band bounds computed wrongly for down-pointing glyphs, letting flank rows
   into the "gesture" span, so every barred glyph measured its own flanks as its
   width.
4. Took stroke width as the **minimum** run — but an angle's apex is a one-pixel
   tip, which collapsed every band to three rows. Median fixed it.

findings.title: the corpus names the two factors itself: "Nature" x "Modality"

So the two factors of F48 are **named by the corpus, in the corpus's own words**:
the three-fold is *Modality* and the four-fold is *Nature*. "Nature" is exactly
the word the Sol-Center sheet stamps on its element box ("Natures", F42) and the
word in `NaturesAndModalities`' title. `Base 12 = Nature x Modality = 4 x 3` is
not my framing of their material; it is their framing, stated twice.

It also confirms **F65 was not my inference**: Active/Reflective/Receptive is
labelled "(Modality)" here explicitly, so the identification with
Cardinal/Fixed/Mutable is the source's, and only the *geometric* reading of those
three words (vertex acts, flat surface reflects, concave collects) is mine.

The colour order here is **Red, Green, Yellow, Blue** = Fire, Earth, Air, Water =
the zodiac order `n mod 4`; the Emotional Permutation Framework's matrix uses
Red, Blue, Yellow, Green = binary counting order (F64). Two orderings of the same
four across two documents — harmless, but note it before treating either as
canonical.

**And it settles F66.** The same two worked examples appear in both documents with
**different intensities**:

| emotion | this doc | Emotional Permutation Framework |
|---|---|---|
| Excitement | (Red, Active, **0.8**) | (Red, Active, **0.9**) |
| Tranquility | (Blue, Reflective, **0.2**) | (Blue, Reflective, **0.3**) |

Nothing generates the third coordinate, and two documents by the same author
disagree on it for the same example. F66's reading — that `I` is decoration
presented as data — is now confirmed rather than inferred. The `(C, M)` pair is
the content.

**Gap worth naming:** the framework asserts "12 fundamental emotional states" but
never enumerates twelve. It gives 3 examples per state phase (Excitement/Anger/
Joy · Contemplation/Sadness/Serenity · Curiosity/Calmness/Acceptance) and 3 per
colour phase (Passion/Anger/Love · Calmness/Trust/Growth · Happiness/Optimism/
Creativity · Peace/Thoughtfulness/Reliability). The two lists cross-check where
they overlap — Anger is Red *and* Active, Calmness is Green *and* Receptive — but
the 4x3 grid is never filled in. **The twelve cells have no names anywhere in the
corpus.** That is the obvious next thing to ask the owner for, and it is the
lexicon the emotional layer would need to be usable.

## Operational note — the F71 correction was auto-committed and auto-pushed

Recording this because it happened without my initiating it and it changes where
that correction currently stands.

Minutes after I edited the two `.wiki` source files, the orchestrator's scheduled
`python3 tools/wiki_sync.py sync` ran (`configs/orchestrator_watchlist.json:463`)
and committed both edits as **`wiki-sync: auto-backup 2026-09-10T18:55:50Z`**,
then pushed. `git rev-list --count origin/main..HEAD` is 0 — it is on GitHub.

**How far it went, checked rather than assumed:**

| layer | state |
|---|---|
| **Local** mirror `vendor/fusiongirl-wiki/pages/` | corrected |
| **Remote** `github.com/Jthora/fusiongirl-wiki` | corrected — auto-pushed |
| **Live** FusionGirl MediaWiki | **unchanged** — still "provably secure" |
| **Live** wiki.cosmiccodex.app | **unchanged** — `curl` confirms the old text is being served |

The scheduled command is `sync`, which is *pull + backup* — **not** `--push-local`
— so nothing was uploaded to the MediaWiki. Local and Remote now diverge from Live
for those two pages.

**The correction is not at risk from routine syncing.** `_compute_delta` keys on
MediaWiki **revids**, not content hashes, so a pull only re-fetches pages whose
*live* revision changed. My local-only edit does not change a live revid, so
pulls will leave it alone. It would be overwritten only if someone edits those
pages on the live wiki, which is ordinary mirror behaviour.

**Two deploys are outstanding, and both are the owner's call — not taken:**
1. `wiki_sync.py push --only` for the two FusionGirl pages, to land the correction
   on the live MediaWiki.
2. a `wiki_build.py` rebuild + redeploy of wiki.cosmiccodex.app, which reads from
   the corrected mirror and would carry the fix to the 729-page site.

Per the standing rules — run `status` first, back up before pushing, `--only` per
page, and confirm before shipping to the live orchestrator — neither was run.

**Worth the owner knowing generally:** any edit made to `vendor/fusiongirl-wiki/`
during a session will be committed and pushed to GitHub by the next scheduled
sync, typically within the hour, with no further action. That is the intended
backup behaviour, but it means local wiki edits are not private drafts.

## Latent bug found while triaging the regression — the error reporter can crash

Not symbology; recorded here because this session found it and it should not be
lost.

`runtime_errors.append_jsonl` calls `json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False)`
with **no `default=`**, so any payload holding a non-JSON object raises
`TypeError` out of the logging call:

```
MagicMock  RAISES TypeError: Object of type MagicMock is not JSON serializable
set        RAISES TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable
bytes      RAISES TypeError: Object of type bytes is not JSON serializable
```

Reproduced against the real module, with ordinary Python types — a `set`, a
`bytes`, and by extension a `datetime` or a `Path`. This is not a test-only
problem.

**Why it matters more than an ordinary crash:** `emit_event` is the *error
reporting* path. If an error's payload carries any such object, the reporter
throws while reporting, the original error is lost, and the caller dies with a
`TypeError` about JSON instead of with the real fault. That is the masked-exception
class the repo already has history with.

It is what surfaced as `ERROR: test_run_single_cycle_blocks_publish_when_claim_
verifier_fails` in one full-suite run: a MagicMock reached an event payload,
`emit_event` raised, and `agent.run_single_cycle` died inside its own logging.

**Proposed fix, one line, verified against the same payloads:**

```python
handle.write(json.dumps(payload, ensure_ascii=False, default=str) + "\n")
```

giving `{"detail": "<MagicMock id='...'>"}` instead of an exception — strictly
more informative than a crash, and it makes logging total.

**Not applied.** `runtime_errors.py` is imported by the live orchestrator, and the
standing rule is to confirm before shipping to it. Awaiting the owner.

findings.title: "Resonance Frequency of Water: 2.45 GHz" is a well-known myth
findings.text:
The banner states, in large type over the DNA imagery:

> "Resonance Frequency of Water: 2.45 GHz — Human Body: ~70% Water"

**This is false, and it is a specific, much-repeated falsehood.** 2.45 GHz is an
ISM-band frequency allocated for industrial, scientific and medical use, and it
is what microwave ovens use — for regulatory reasons and because absorption there
is *moderate enough to penetrate*, not because water resonates at it. Liquid water
has a broad dielectric **relaxation** centred near 20 GHz at room temperature, not
a sharp resonance; isolated water molecules in the gas phase have rotational
transitions at 22.2 GHz and 183 GHz. If 2.45 GHz were a resonance, a microwave
oven would deposit its energy in the outer few millimetres and food would not heat
through — the opposite of the design requirement.

Flagged at the same level as F66 and F71: the symbology structure is unaffected,
but this is a checkable factual claim sitting in the corpus's most public artifact,
and it is exactly the sort of line a hostile reader would lead with.

**Not an error, checked:** the Schumann resonance figures (7.83 / 14.1 / 20.3 Hz)
sit inside the spread of published values — theory gives ~7.83 / 13.6 / 19.2 and
measurement ~7.83 / 14.3 / 20.8. And the nanometre-scale ladder (hydrogen 0.1 nm,
water 0.3 nm, DNA 2 nm, ribosomes 20–30 nm, viruses 20–300 nm, mitochondria
0.5–1 µm, blood cells 6–8 µm) is accurate throughout.

findings.title: F48 does NOT extend to 108, and the reason is arithmetic
findings.text:
This is a guard against my own result. F48 is clean because **`gcd(3,4) = 1`**, so
`Z/12 ≅ Z/3 × Z/4` and the twelve cells of modality x element are exactly the
twelve positions of one cycle. The temptation is to read "Model 108 = Base 9 x
Base 12" the same way. **It does not work:**

```
gcd(3, 4) = 1    ->  Z/12  ≅ Z/3 x Z/4          CRT applies
gcd(9, 12) = 3   ->  Z/108 ≇ Z/9 x Z/12         CRT does NOT apply
   largest element order in Z/9 x Z/12 = lcm(9,12) = 36, not 108 -> not cyclic
   a coprime factorization that DOES work: 108 = 4 x 27, gcd(4,27) = 1
```

`Z/9 × Z/12` has 108 elements but is not a 108-cycle; there is a three-fold
redundancy. The Vedic construction is a **subdivision** — each of 12 arcs cut into
9 — which does give 108 arcs, but that is a cycle refined, not two coprime
factors combined. The two constructions are different operations that happen to
land on the same count.

**`deploy_base_systems.py` does not overclaim** — it says "interlocks through
multiplication", never "isomorphism", so nothing needs correcting. The risk is
prospective and it is mine: having just derived `Z/12 ≅ Z/3 × Z/4` it would be
natural to generalise, and the generalisation is false. Written down before
anyone reaches for it, per F-034 — do not read one result and write a bigger
verdict.

diameter being approximately 108x Earth's diameter". The actual ratio is **109.2**.
It is flagged "approximately" so it is not a defect, but it is numerology sitting

findings.title: Base 108 is B12-D9, and its navamsa listing is NOT the classical rule

The doc heads a section **"Base 108 Astrology / B12-D9"** and enumerates, for each
sign, nine navamsas — the Vedic D9 divisional chart, 12 x 9 = 108.

The listing starts each sign's series **at that sign** and runs nine consecutive:
Aries -> Aries…Sagittarius; Taurus -> Taurus…Capricorn; Gemini -> Gemini…
Capricorn. The classical rule is different: movable signs start from themselves,
**fixed signs from the 9th**, **dual signs from the 5th**. So Aries agrees by
coincidence (it is movable), and Taurus (should start Capricorn) and Gemini
(should start Libra) do not.

**Checked whether it propagated into code: it did not.** `tools/
deploy_base_systems.py` carries Model 108 as `9 x 12` with D9 described only as
"division of each zodiac sign into 9 sub-divisions". No starting-sign rule is
implemented anywhere, so nothing downstream depends on the non-standard listing.
**Owner question:** is "start from self, run nine" a deliberate simplification of
the corpus's own, or an error inherited from a source?

findings.title: the grounding guard is blind to this whole family, by design
findings.text:
Checked directly. `tools/grounding_guard.py` passes all of these:

| sentence | guard |
|---|---|
| "…using UL's formal structure to create provably secure communication channels." | **clean** |
| "UL provides provably secure encryption." | **clean** |
| "The encoding is tamper-proof." | **clean** |
| "Proto Encryption is quantum-resistant." | **clean** |

That is not a bug. `PROVEN_ASSIGNMENT` anchors proof words to
`_PROVABLE_TARGET = mapping|assignment|correspondence|grounding|denotation`,
because the guard's scope is **grounding** — whether a glyph's meaning is
non-arbitrary. A security claim is a different family and no pattern reaches it.

**Open decision for the owner, not taken here.** One live instance, now fixed, is
weak evidence for widening the guard, and widening it risks flagging the lore
pages where "unbreakable encryption" is legitimately fiction. But the *source*
document is published under a DOI and will keep regenerating this phrasing, which
is the F-017 pattern — patching instances instead of the generator guarantees the
instances return. A narrow, high-precision `SECURITY_OVERCLAIM` family
(`provably secure`, `tamper-proof`, `quantum-resistant`, `information-
theoretically secure`) gated to non-lore genres would close it. Proposed, not
built.
